8c9eef3054428c16: NEW DELHI, India, Nov 9 — Toxic air in parts of India’s capital New Delhi soared to more than 58 times the World Health Organisation’s recommended daily limit today, after fireworks for the Hindu festival of Diwali, air monitor data showed.
Millions celebrate the annual festival of lights with fireworks in one of the world’s most polluted capitals, worsening winter smog fuelled by vehicle emissions, farm fires and industry.
The Supreme Court this month allowed the limited use of so-called “green” firecrackers, designed to produce fewer emissions, during Diwali.
But restrictions are routinely flouted, with the city reverberating with explosions.

Early this morning, around eight hours after the peak of the bursting fireworks, levels of cancer-causing PM 2.5 microparticles hit 879 micrograms per cubic metre in the Mandir Marg locality, according to monitoring organisation IQAir, which cited data from a city government station.
Dense smog shrouds an illuminated residential area as seen from the Taragarh Fort in Ajmer on November 8, 2026 on the occasion of Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights. — AFP pic
That is nearly 59 times the WHO’s recommended daily maximum.
Authorities have in recent weeks implemented restrictions on traffic and construction as they seek to curb smog in New Delhi, home to more than 30 million people.
Vehicles account for 23 per cent of Delhi’s winter pollution, while biomass burning, including farm stubble fires, contributes 20 per cent, according to India’s environment ministry.
Industry, including coal-fired power plants, contributes about nine per cent.
The largest share, 27 per cent, comes from secondary particles, formed when gases released by vehicles, industry, power plants and biomass burning react in the atmosphere.
A 2024 study published in The Lancet Planetary Health, a peer-reviewed research journal, estimated that 3.8 million deaths in India between 2009 and 2019 were linked to air pollution. — AFP
b85959d971f9e722: PASIR MAS: The annual threat of flooding has prompted traders in Rantau Panjang to take extra precautions, including reducing stock levels and moving merchandise to higher ground to minimise losses during the monsoon season.

Clothing trader Azila Zanuddin, 45, said most traders were avoiding large purchases of new stock as they normally would towards the end of the year, opting instead to sell existing merchandise before gradually replenishing their supplies.
"It has become a necessity for us traders here towards the end of the year, as the monsoon season approaches.
"We store our merchandise in higher places to prevent damage and losses.

"Likewise, most traders avoid purchasing large quantities of new stock during the monsoon season. We sell our existing stock first, before gradually replenishing our supplies in smaller quantities," she told Bernama.

Another trader, Muhammad Shahmir Amzar Azmi, 25, who sells shoes and slippers, said he was taking precautionary measures by moving his merchandise to a specially built loft at his business premises, to prevent damage in the event of floodwaters entering his shop.
"These preparations are necessary every year, as we do not want to take any chances in the event of sudden flooding.
"Goods which are easily damaged and those of high value will be moved to higher places first, while other items are arranged so that they can be easily relocated if the situation worsens," he said.
He said business equipment and important documents were also kept in safe places in preparation for possible flooding.

Checks by Bernama found that most traders in the town had begun making early preparations for the monsoon season, including moving their merchandise to higher places and setting up storage areas, to minimise the risk of losses.

Meanwhile, residents in several flood-prone villages around Rantau Panjang, including Kampung Gual Periok, Kampung Padang Lincin and Kampung Tok Deh, have also taken early precautionary measures, by preparing fibreglass boats for use as transport during floods.
A resident, Shukri Che Mat, 60, said the fibreglass boats would be used to facilitate residents' movement when floodwaters inundated the village.
"Floodwaters usually rise to chest level in this village, as it is located just a few metres from Golok River.

"Water levels typically rise after two or three hours of continuous heavy rain. Therefore, to avoid a chaotic situation, we make early preparations by moving essential items to higher places," he said.

Meanwhile, checks in several areas around Kota Baru found that the weather had remained overcast from morning until late afternoon today, with no sunshine and intermittent showers occurring at short intervals.

a9830ddebfcc4a96: PUTRAJAYA, Nov 9 — The Ministry of Health (MOH) has prepared 85 Emergency Medical Teams comprising 387 personnel to respond to possible flooding during the 2026/2027 North-east Monsoon (MTL).

In a statement today, the ministry said these comprised 36 Rapid Assessment and Health Rapid Response Teams, 34 Medical Rapid Response Teams and 15 Mental Health and Psychosocial Support (MHPSS) teams.

“The teams will be mobilised as required to conduct health risk assessments, provide medical services and emergency treatment, carry out surveillance and control of infectious diseases, as well as provide mental health and psychosocial support to flood victims,” it said.

The ministry has also made available 128 vehicles to support personnel mobilisation and field operations, while flood-related medicine supplies at warehouses operated by concessionaire suppliers remain stable, with stocks estimated to last between one and three months.

Through the National Crisis Preparedness and Response Centre (CPRC), State Health Departments, District Health Offices and healthcare facilities nationwide, the ministry has also stepped up preparedness to ensure continued healthcare services, particularly in flood-prone areas.

The National CPRC has been in Alert Mode since October 27, with continuous monitoring of flood situations, healthcare facility preparedness and coordination of response measures with State Health Departments and relevant agencies.

The ministry said healthcare facilities at risk of flooding had also been identified, together with alternative facilities in the event of operational disruptions. Plans were also in place for the early transfer of high-risk patients, including pregnant women and those requiring haemodialysis.
As of 6am today, floods had been reported in Selangor and Perak, affecting 987 people from 283 families, who were housed at seven active temporary relief centres (PPS).

Meanwhile, the Malaysian Meteorological Department (MetMalaysia) expects three to five monsoon surges during the North-east Monsoon, which could bring heavy rain, particularly to the eastern and southern parts of Peninsular Malaysia, eastern Sabah, and western and southern Sarawak.
The ministry said the risk of flooding could increase if prolonged rain coincided with high tides.

At relief centres, the ministry provides health assessments, infectious disease monitoring, environmental hygiene inspections, food and water safety checks, vector control, as well as mental health and psychosocial support.
These measures are aimed at reducing the risk of flood-related illnesses, including diarrhoea, food poisoning, leptospirosis and respiratory tract infections.
The ministry also advised the public to use clean and safe drinking water, consume properly cooked food and avoid food contaminated by floodwaters.
People were also advised to maintain personal and environmental hygiene, wash their hands frequently with clean water and soap, and avoid direct contact with potentially contaminated floodwaters.

“Those experiencing symptoms such as fever, diarrhoea, vomiting and muscle pain after exposure to floodwaters are advised to seek immediate medical examination and treatment at healthcare facilities,” the ministry said.

The ministry also reminded patients with chronic illnesses, senior citizens, pregnant women and children to ensure continuity of treatment and adequate medication supplies in the event they need to move to relief centres. — Bernama
56b6ffb245b18672: KUALA LUMPUR: The national men's football team have been hit by a player withdrawal crisis on the eve of their departure for China for international friendlies.

50b5101911bc3494: DHAKA: Bangladesh challenged ousted leader Sheikh Hasina on Monday to seek extradition from India if she was serious about returning home, while reviewing an application to renew her passport.

Hasina, whose 15-year rule was ended by a mass uprising she tried to crush, has vowed to return to Bangladesh in December. She was sentenced to death for crimes against humanity over the 2024 crackdown on protesters.
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed told reporters on Monday that authorities were looking into Hasina's request for a new passport, adding that she was a convicted offender who had taken refuge abroad.
"The legal basis of the application, whether it followed due process, and whether there is a right to apply for a passport – all those matters are being reviewed," he said.
"We had already sent a letter to that country (India) seeking her extradition through due process," he added.
Hasina has said several times that she intends to return, telling AFP in an email that she was "fully aware" she faced being hanged.
Hasina's British lawyers have requested the renewal of her documents following the "reported revocation" of her passport.

A letter by law firm Matrix Chambers, addressed to Bangladesh's high commission in New Delhi and seen by AFP, requested the renewal of her passport but made no mention of when or where she planned to travel.
Md Aminul Islam, chief prosecutor of the court that sentenced Hasina to death in November 2025, dismissed the application as "nothing but political stunt".
Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh's junior foreign minister, said she should simply surrender herself to face justice.
"Let her tell India: 'Yes, there is an extradition treaty. Please hand me over. I killed this many people, and I am ready to face the sentence. Please execute me there'," he told reporters.
"She is a thief, a bandit and a terrorist who fled... How could she, having fled, want to come back?"
Trying to create panic
Hasina fled to old ally India in 2024 and has not been seen in public since, but has taken part in online news conferences by telephone.
She was convicted and sentenced in absentia.
Her continued presence in India has strained ties between Dhaka and New Delhi, which says the extradition request is under legal review.

The government of Tarique Rahman, whose party won elections in February in which Hasina's Awami League was barred from contesting, has said it would ensure the former prime minister receives due legal process in all cases against her should she return.
But Hasina's pledge to return presents a political challenge for Rahman's government.
Many Bangladeshis want to see her hanged, while others fear her return could galvanise her former supporters and trigger a fresh confrontation between rival camps.
Police on Monday said they had arrested 12 people over a series of petrol bomb attacks this month, including attacks on property, an empty bus and police vehicles. No casualties were reported.
Dhaka police spokesman Md Akhtar Hossain said the suspects were members of Hasina's banned Awami League party.
"They are trying to create panic among people," he told AFP. "We are remaining vigilant to deal with any untoward situation."

8ddc6cf925a38182: KOTA BHARU, Nov 9 — A total of 59 members of the Psychological Support Team (PST) from various agencies, including the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Education, will be deployed to temporary evacuation centres (PPS) in Kelantan to help address the trauma and emotional stress of flood victims throughout the Northeast Monsoon (MTL) 2026/2027.

Kelantan Department of Social Welfare (JKM) director Che Samsuzuki Che Noh said that in addition to providing psychological support, the team will also organise various activities to help reduce the emotional stress of the victims while they are at the PPS.
He said that the Kelantan JKM also mobilised 400 officers and staff, 13 counselling officers, and 327 volunteers to ensure the smooth operation of disaster management and aid distribution.
In this regard, he encourages those interested in becoming volunteers to register with the JKM early to facilitate the coordination of assistance during disasters.
In another development, Che Samsuzuki urged the public to register early through the MyIBJKM application to facilitate the process when they are relocated to the PPS.

He said the information that needs to be completed in the application includes details of the Head of Household (KIR), family members, place of residence, and children's schools to enable victim profiling to be done earlier.

“This information is important for facilitating data management and preventing the duplication of information. Once registration is completed, the relevant data will be channelled directly to the National Disaster Management Agency, thereby helping to expedite the provision of assistance, including the Bantuan Wang Ihsan (BWI),” he said.
He added that early registration also helps expedite the BWI payment process, including after the PPS is closed.

So far, a total of 79,455 KIR with a total of 135,616 household members have been recorded in the system, while 69,101 KIR have registered through the MyIBJKM application in its second year of implementation.

He also urged the district-level JKM to intensify the campaign for the application registration during disaster management simulations to avoid congestion and delays in the registration process during floods. — Bernama

6b309ca673fe8897: SEREMBAN: Plans to convene the Negri Sembilan state assembly on Nov 26 without the consent of Yang di-Pertuan Besar Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir could trigger a serious constitutional and administrative crisis, a constitutional law expert has warned.
Universiti Teknologi Mara (UiTM) Negri Sembilan senior lecturer Dr Muhamad Fuad Abdul Karim said there was a clear legal distinction between an official opening ceremony and royal consent.
He said the state assembly could proceed without Tuanku Muhriz physically officiating the opening, as the absence of a royal address would not invalidate its proceedings.
"However, the state assembly cannot convene without Tuanku Muhriz's formal consent through an instrument of summons.
"Without it, the planned Nov 26 sitting would not merely be inappropriate, but invalid.
"If it goes ahead, it would be an unprecedented event," he said when contacted.
The sitting is scheduled for Nov 26, with the 2027 state Budget set to be tabled the following day.
However, the state government has yet to obtain Tuanku Muhriz's consent to convene the sitting.
This follows the State Executive Council's decision to recognise the April 19 proclamation concerning Tuanku Muhriz's removal as Yang di-Pertuan Besar as valid and effective.

Earlier, Menteri Besar Datuk Ismail Lasim said the state government would proceed with its original plan to convene the sitting on Nov 26, followed by the tabling of the 2027 state Budget a day later.
The Juasseh assemblyman said the state government was working to obtain Tuanku Muhriz's consent to officiate the sitting.
Fuad said proceeding with the sitting without resolving the constitutional issues could paralyse its functions.
"Even if the sitting meets the minimum quorum, the absence of exco members could hamper the state government's executive functions.

"The tabling of the 2027 state Budget could also be affected as the menteri besar does not have the constitutional authority to approve budget policies on his own before presenting them to the state assembly," he said.

He said question-and-answer sessions could also be disrupted, as the menteri besar would have to answer questions across portfolios, including religious affairs, housing, the economy and infrastructure, which would normally be handled by the respective exco members.
He said the sitting should not proceed without the proper constitutional procedures being followed.
"The state government must resolve the appointment of a legitimate Exco line-up in accordance with constitutional requirements.
"It must also formally seek and obtain Tuanku Muhriz's consent before issuing any notice to convene the sitting," he said.

ab138347ee884e3e: NEW YORK, Nov 9 — Chips made by US chip titan Nvidia push the boundaries of artificial intelligence, but its leader Jensen Huang is in the spotlight over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Unknown to the public just four years ago, the 63-year-old is a powerful entrepreneur, drawing stadium crowds as he presents cutting-edge components essential to the development of AI tools like ChatGPT.
Media reports last week said US intelligence officials believe Huang grew close to a Chinese executive who was funnelling information to Beijing.
Nvidia’s board said yesterday it had opened a probe into the CEO and co-founder, who acknowledged having been unfaithful to his wife and said he was “deeply sorry.”

Big tech’s insatiable appetite for chips designed by Nvidia, known as Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), has catapulted the California chipmaker to a market valuation of US$4.5 trillion (RM18.2 trillion), among the world’s largest.

Its meteoric rise has made Huang one of the world’s richest people — worth around US$160 billion, according to Forbes — thanks to the roughly four per cent stake he holds in the company he founded three decades ago with two friends in a Silicon Valley diner.
He has become a close informal adviser on AI to Donald Trump, travelling with the US president on Air Force One on a trip to Beijing earlier this year.
That is an area of concern to US officials who believe he has been involved with the alleged spy, Alice Huang, who is linked to a Singapore-based data centre company, according to the New York Times.
Despite their shared surname, the pair are not related.
Early life
Born in Taipei in 1963, Jensen Huang — originally named Jen-Hsun — embodies the American success story.
At nine years old, he was sent away with his brother to boarding school in small-town Kentucky.
His uncle recommended the school to his Taiwanese parents believing it to be a prestigious institution, though it was actually a school for troubled youth.

Too young to be a student, Huang boarded there but attended a nearby public school alongside the children of tobacco farmers. With his poor English, he was bullied and forced to clean toilets — a two-year ordeal that transformed him.
“We worked really hard, we studied really hard, and the kids were really tough,” he recounted in an interview with US broadcaster NPR.
But “the ending of the story is I loved the time I was there,” Huang said.
Brought home by his parents who had by then settled in the north-western US state of Oregon, he graduated from university at just 20 and joined AMD, then LSI Logic, to design chips — his passion.

But he wanted to go further and founded Nvidia in 1993 to “solve problems that normal computers can’t,” using semiconductors powerful enough to handle 3D graphics, he said during an interview on the “No Priors” podcast.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang waves after a welcome ceremony for US President Donald Trump at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing May 14, 2026. Huang has rejected calls to deliberately slow down AI development even as some insiders warn the technology could threaten human existence within a decade. — AFP pic
‘As fast as we can’
Nvidia created the first GPU in 1999, riding the intersection of video games, data centres, cloud computing and now generative AI.
Always dressed in a black T-shirt and leather jacket, Huang sports a Nvidia logo tattoo and has a taste for sports cars.
One former high-ranking Nvidia employee described him to AFP as “the most driven person” he’d ever met.
He has rejected calls to deliberately slow down AI development even as some insiders warn the technology could threaten human existence within a decade.
“That kind of narrative is dramatic, it gets a lot of attention,” but “it’s not grounded on facts,” he told CBS News in September.
“We should go as fast as we can” on AI, but labs should not release products that are not safe, he said.
Street food
On visits to his native Taiwan, Huang is treated like a megastar, with fans crowding him for autographs and selfies as journalists follow him to the barber shop and his favourite night market.
“He has created the phenomena because of his personal charm,” noted Wayne Lin of Witology Market Trend Research Institute.

“A person like him must be very busy and his schedule should be full every day meeting big bosses. But he remembers to eat street food when he comes to Taiwan,” he said, calling Huang “unusually friendly.”
Over the years, Nvidia has taken care to project a drama-free image of Huang.

But the former employee painted a more nuanced picture, describing a “very paradoxical” individual fiercely protective of his employees but also capable, within Nvidia’s executive circle, of “ripping people to shreds” over major mistakes or poor choices. — AFP
1c1de6403d1d7848: MELAKA: Perikatan Nasional (PN) and Pas leaders have defended their electoral cooperation with Barisan Nasional (BN), dismissing criticism that the partnership is fragile or one-sided.
Melaka Pas chairman Zulkifli Ismail dismissed remarks by Amanah president Datuk Seri Mohamad Sabu, who claimed that previous ties between Umno and Pas had never lasted more than three years.
"That is just the view of people who do not want to see this unity work," Zulkifli said at a press conference to present the aspirations of PN candidates for the 16th Melaka election.
"Those of us working on the ground are not planning for three years (only). We want to make sure this partnership lasts for good."
Zulkifli also rejected claims that Umno was playing both sides, describing them as unfair attacks intended to score political points.
With the campaign entering its final days, he said the coalition was focusing on rallies across all 28 state constituencies, culminating in a prayer gathering and a final rally before polling day.
Tangga Batu member of parliament and PN Melaka election director Bakri Jamaluddin dismissed claims that PN was being sidelined by BN under the 'Muafakat Melaka' banner.
"Working together means give and take. It does not mean being bullied," he said.
"We have put together a joint manifesto with six main areas and 113 initiatives, including plans for the first 100 days, one year and five years to bring jobs and investment to Melaka.
"We are looking at the bigger picture for stability here and across the country," he added.
PN Bemban candidate Dr Mohd Yadzil Yaakub said relations among party members on the ground went beyond party affiliations.

"Our relationship is not based on party lines, but on sincerity and doing what is right. That is why it is easy to work together," he said, adding that the team would continue working hard until polling day.

d12db3d2b824a614: When Jane first heard about Memory and Imagination, a rare 1990s documentary about the Library of Congress, she was intrigued. But the Canadian writer in her 30s couldn’t find the movie anywhere — not on streaming services, not on YouTube, not on pirate sites — and her intrigue turned into obsession.

Worried it might become a lost film, Jane decided to scour auction sites, search every library catalog she could think of, and even enlist some of her online acquaintances to find a copy. Her plan was to “share it with other people to help ensure it would be preserved into the future,” as she puts it. Jane knew the perfect tool for the task: a private torrent tracker.
“I am ethically conflicted about piracy. I often feel guilty about it.”

Private trackers are essentially the speakeasies of the online piracy world. Promoted primarily by word of mouth, they rely on secrecy, exclusivity, and strict community rules to shield everything that’s going on behind closed doors from the public’s prying eyes. What unites these communities is that they all use BitTorrent to trade media among like-minded file sharers. But their focuses range widely, from general-purpose trackers with catalogs so broad that they make Netflix look like a niche service to the many specialized communities for categories like Chinese movies, motorsports, visual effects tools, e-learning courses, and Japanese porn. There’s even a private tracker just for Frank Zappa music.

Private trackers are known for massive and meticulously organized catalogs, which they owe to users like Jane, who, like every other pirate I talked to for this story, opted to be identified by a pseudonym due to the terabytes of copyrighted data they’ve been sharing. These are people willing to go the extra mile to find long-forgotten movies, rare concert recordings, or out-of-print books. “Many private tracker users are fully consumed with archive fever,” she says.

At first, Jane had no luck finding a physical copy of that elusive documentary, which includes interviews with Steve Jobs and Julia Child. Nobody was selling it on eBay. Her local public library didn’t have it. Neither did any other public library in North America. And when she finally located a DVD that was available to the public, it was in the Bibliotheca Alexandrina — Egypt’s modern-day re-creation of the ancient library that’s long been synonymous with lost media. “That bowled me over,” Jane says. “This obscure movie I’m looking for is only available in the Library of Alexandria!”

Eventually, Jane found Memory and Imagination for sale on a small online marketplace for historical media. Jane instantly bought a copy and uploaded it. “It looked like a digital rip of a severely degraded VHS tape,” she says. “I was still over the moon [that] I rescued this historically significant documentary.”

Not everyone who uses private trackers shares Jane’s amateur-archivist zeal. Some are simply in it for easy access to pirated movies, TV shows, or other forms of entertainment. “My goal initially was to have a better source for video games,” says Odel, a West Coast-based college student. “I quickly found out that [private trackers] could replace everything else.” Others join trackers in search of a community of like-minded cinephiles or music fans. And as they immerse themselves in a world of illicit media trading that’s largely shielded from public view, many of them seem to catch a peculiar kind of bug.
“There aren’t many closed doors on the internet.”

They painstakingly work their way up the ranks in the trackers they’ve joined and then use their freshly earned social capital to get access to even more exclusive sites, where the same rat race starts all over again. “Exclusivity definitely plays a part,” says Maysay, a private tracker user from Pakistan. “You want to get into those more exclusive ‘elite’ trackers at some point just for the sake of it.”
“There is definitely a constant quest to level up,” says Jane, who maintains active accounts on 14 private trackers.

Among the people I talked to for this story, that’s actually a small number. Some private tracker users maintain dozens of accounts, download terabytes of data, share thousands of torrents at a time, embark on obsessive quests to get their hands on long-lost media, and use automated apps and tools that make everyday piracy seem like child’s play.

In a world where streaming services offer access to countless movies and TV shows for little more than your credit card number, private trackers can seem a bit like a throwback. A nod to a different time, when legal options didn’t really exist and file sharing happened in private chat rooms or on password-protected FTP servers.

“There aren’t many closed doors on the internet,” says Jane, who became interested in joining private trackers after hearing about them from friends. Jane quickly realized that she couldn’t just sign up for the latest and greatest movie trackers, which were only open to vetted users with a history of good behavior on other servers. So she devised a plan to join a more lenient private tracker for audiobooks first and work her way up from there.
Users who fall below certain metrics often find their download privileges curtailed, and especially egregious offenses result in instant bans.

Even getting access to that first server came with some hurdles. Private tracker websites rarely have freely accessible sign-up forms. Some only open their doors to new users every few weeks or months, while others use special vetting processes to make sure applicants are a good fit. Sometimes this means that applicants are required to prove they’re in good standing on other trackers. Sometimes they need to take screenshots of their personal media collections to show they’re actually interested in what the tracker they’re applying to is all about. And sometimes there are even actual interviews applicants have to ace before getting their accounts.

The long-defunct private music tracker What.CD used to quiz applicants about audio formats and MP3 encoder settings, and even published a study guide of sorts to help them prepare for it. And Jane’s very first private tracker required her to first join an IRC chatroom, where admins quizzed her about the server’s rules. “It was so stressful! It felt like a job interview,” she says.

Not every private tracker has these kinds of interviews, but like Jane’s first server, most are big on rules. Users are generally required to keep up a certain upload-to-download ratio, with many sites demanding that they contribute as much bandwidth as they consume. (The exact rules and requirements vary, and many trackers also offer some “freeleech” content — files that can be downloaded without negatively impacting a user’s ratio.) Quickly downloading a file without sharing it is also frowned upon, as is the unvetted distribution of invites to outsiders.

Users who fall below certain metrics often find their download privileges curtailed, and especially egregious offenses result in instant bans. “Invite selling is considered to be a major breach of security,” says Odel. Doing so will not only get you kicked from a server, it will also tarnish your reputation elsewhere. “Staff of the tracker you did it on will typically communicate with the staff of some other trackers, which can result in you getting banned from those places as well,” Odel explains.

If you do follow the rules and share generously, you have a chance to work your way up the ranks, which then opens the doors to other trackers. That alone, and the requirement to keep up a healthy upload-to-download ratio, can lead to people downloading and then redistributing (also known as “seeding” in tracker lingo) files just to maintain their stats. “Some places will require you to seed [a certain amount of] terabytes before you get access to a certain rank,” says Odel. “This can result in a lot of downloading of stuff I wouldn’t ever consume otherwise, just to pump up that number.”
“You have to seed things you aren’t interested in consuming to succeed in the tracker economy.”

Odel estimates that he has downloaded around 500 terabytes of data from the 30 or so private trackers he’s currently active on. In the end, he’s watched very little of it. “Probably less than one percent,” he says.

That discrepancy is not uncommon. “I am seeding over 2,000 torrents, and I have no personal interest in almost any of them,” admits Jane. Maysay tells me that he seeds around 3,000 torrents at any given time and has downloaded things he doesn’t intend to watch “many times.”

“It’s how these sites are built,” Jane explains. “You have to seed things you aren’t interested in consuming to succeed in the tracker economy.” Some private tracker users use automated tools to help them maintain their ratio, like scripts that watch dedicated IRC channels to quickly jump on any newly released torrent, no matter what content it is. This is called “racing” in tracker lingo, and it can help improve one’s ratio; anyone looking to download that file later will get it from those early downloaders. Especially committed users even rent a dedicated seedbox — a private server sitting in some remote data center that is only used for downloading and then seeding torrents.

Being able to download more is only one reason for trying to improve your ratio and standing on private trackers. “I just do it for fun,” Jane says. “It’s kind of like playing a video game and watching your score go up.” And just like with some video games, there is a certain addictive quality to all this. ”Using private trackers reminded me a lot of playing MMORPG games like World of Warcraft or RuneScape where you really have to grind to level up,” Jane says. “It’s slow, tedious, and repetitive. Yet you feel this insatiable compulsion to level up.”

Private BitTorrent trackers emerged soon after BitTorrent itself was created 25 years ago. This was at the height of the file-sharing wars, when Hollywood and the major record labels were taking one peer-to-peer network operator after another to court. Entertainment industry lawsuits resulted in the shutdown of Napster in 2001, Audiogalaxy in 2002, and Kazaa in 2006.

Those closures drove millions of file sharers to embrace BitTorrent, which in turn put torrent sites into the crosshairs of rightsholders and their lawyers. Suprnova, a public torrent site frequented by millions of users, shut down amid legal pressure at the end of 2004. And in 2006, authorities raided The Pirate Bay.

Some torrent site admins responded to the increasing legal pressure by simply pulling up a drawbridge to their piracy communities. Instead of letting just anyone download torrents, they required users to register, and in some cases only admitted new users that had gotten an invite from a trusted community member.

Nobody knows exactly how many private trackers are currently up and running, or how many people use them for their pirated media fix. But while BitTorrent piracy as a whole has declined since the emergence of Netflix, Spotify, and other paid streaming services, private trackers are still going strong.

A live dashboard maintained by a tracker software developer currently lists around 530 private trackers, including some with hundreds of thousands of registered users. One music tracker, listed only as [REDACTED] on this dashboard, is said to host 3.7 million torrents, or works to download. A popular movie tracker included in the list has more than 1 million torrents, which are being traded among just 40,000 registered users.
“Occasionally people will request or ask for something that just isn’t available commercially anymore, or ever, and attach a huge bounty to it.”

One of the first notable private trackers was Oink’s Pink Palace, an invite-only music sharing community with a reported 180,000 registered users. Among them was Nine Inch Nails front man Trent Reznor, who told Vulture in 2007 that the site had been “like the world’s greatest record store,” offering access to “pretty much anything you could ever imagine […] in the format you wanted.”

Many private tracker communities meticulously curate catalogs that put publicly accessible piracy sites to shame. “The private tracker experience is a lot better,” says Marvin, a 23-year-old software developer from the Pacific Northwest. Public torrent sites are often ad-ridden and hard to navigate and search, he says. Maysay agrees, telling me that he appreciates private trackers “not just because of the amount of content [available], but also because of the quality, organization, and how well everything is sorted.”

The curation happening in these private communities is very much a group effort. Many private trackers offer their members a chance to request files they want others to upload, complete with bounties (download credits that you would otherwise have to upload other files for) for the first uploader. The rarer the file, the bigger the bounty. And the bigger the bounty, the more frenzied the hunt for that elusive file.
“Are large corporations to be trusted with archiving our culture?”

One famous quest for such a bounty unfolded in 2013, when a user of the since-shuttered What.CD server put out a request for “The Ocean Full of Bowling Balls,” a story from Catcher in the Rye author J.D. Salinger that the writer himself had refused to publish. For a long time, the only known copy of “The Ocean Full of Bowling Balls” resided in Princeton University’s Firestone Library, where visitors could read but not copy the document.

The intrigue — Salinger didn’t publish a single work for the last 45 years of his life — combined with the fact that there clearly was at least one copy out there set off a frenzy among What.CD users, with the bounty reportedly swelling to a massive 6TB. Some came up with schemes to memorize every word of the story while visiting Princeton’s library, while others scoured the Earth for other copies.

A few months later, a What.CD user was ready to claim the bounty. “It took me many weeks of research to find that this book existed and many more weeks to acquire it,” the user wrote in a note accompanying a torrent featuring a total of three unpublished Salinger stories, including “The Ocean Full of Bowling Balls.” Someone had apparently published the three stories as part of a book that was printed just 25 times in 1999. Years later, one of those 25 copies showed up on eBay, where the What.CD uploader quickly snagged it.

The story of this unlikely act of renegade archiving quickly made headlines worldwide, and to this day is legendary in the private tracker community. (The uploader of the book was ironically never able to claim their massive bounty, as site admins removed the torrent once it got too much outside attention.) But while few other bounty hunts have gotten that much attention, they do happen.
“A great deal of media released today will persist via private servers, much like how a lot of silent films we have today were found as reels stored in people’s attics.”

“Occasionally people will request or ask for something that just isn’t available commercially anymore, or ever, and attach a huge bounty to it,” says Odel. “People will research any potential leads, reach out to random French directors via email, and ultimately come back with nothing. Then, a few years later, somebody will randomly upload whatever was being looked for onto YouTube, with no further explanation.”

Odel told me he doesn’t personally partake in these kinds of media hunts. “But I’ve seen some things which I’d classify as ‘important’ be recovered this way,” he says. “Piracy does happen to be pretty good at preservation.”

UC Berkeley professor Abigail De Kosnik, who has investigated private trackers as part of her research on rogue online archives, agrees. “A great deal of media released today will persist via private servers, much like how a lot of silent films we have today were found as reels stored in people’s attics,” she says. “I think that private torrent trackers, which make possible [to download] many art films, indie films, smaller-budget films, films from many countries, will play a large part in constituting future archives of 20th and 21st century cultural productions.”

Copyright holders, unsurprisingly, often hold less favorable views of the private tracker community. “Private trackers are part of a broader piracy ecosystem,” says Larissa Knapp, executive vice president and chief content protection officer of the Motion Picture Association (MPA). “Content that first appears within a closed community can quickly migrate to streaming sites, cyberlockers, IPTV services, and other unauthorized platforms, significantly amplifying its reach and impact.”

Rightsholder groups have repeatedly gone after private trackers and their administrators with varying levels of success. Oink’s Pink Palace, the popular private music tracker, shut down in 2007 following raids in the Netherlands and the UK. Oink admin Alan Ellis was arrested and charged with conspiracy to defraud as part of the enforcement actions, but was later found not guilty in court. Shuttering the tracker also did little to stop file sharing. Oink was quickly succeeded by What.CD, which remained online for nearly a decade until finally closing down in 2016 following a raid on its data center.

These days, private file sharing communities aren’t as often in the news as they were a decade ago. Part of that is simply a matter of priority. Private trackers often cap the number of registered users; some of the most coveted communities have only 40,000 or fewer active members. Public sites like The Pirate Bay, on the other hand, still attract millions of file sharers, making it easier for commercial copyright enforcers to send out tens of thousands of legal notices to end users at a time — a practice that’s especially common in Europe.

Still, groups like the MPA, and its ACE anti-piracy arm, haven’t given up on going after private file sharing communities and their admins. “Private trackers are not beyond enforcement reach,” Knapp says. “Closed access can make an investigation more difficult, but it does not eliminate the legal or operational exposure for the people who run them. In my years in federal law enforcement, I learned that anonymity is rarely as complete as people believe. A private community is not a safe harbor. Every operation, no matter how closed, still depends on people, hosting and domain services, communications tools, and usually some way to move money. Each of those is a connection, and connections are what investigators follow.”

There’s also the moral questions of engaging in piracy, which don’t get easier to answer when you’re actively sharing thousands of files 24/7. “I am ethically conflicted about piracy,” Jane says. “I often feel guilty about it.” Jane tries to assuage some of her guilt by actively purchasing media she likes.

Others told me a similar version of this, while also stressing that piracy is simply more user-friendly and convenient than legal services. That’s especially true for users in developing countries. “A big part of it for me is accessibility,” says Maysay, whose choices in Pakistan are limited. “There’s a lot of content that simply isn’t easily available legally here.”
“In my years in federal law enforcement, I learned that anonymity is rarely as complete as people believe.”

The fast-moving copyright battle around AI adds further ambiguity to this debate. “Now that the fastest-growing corner of the knowledge industries relies on mass piracy — copying huge amounts of data that they download for free — I think that the anti-piracy rhetoric of the past quarter-century is looking a bit outdated,” says De Kosnik. “If anything, AI [companies] are anti-archival because they strip away attribution from the creators, whereas private trackers are intensely accurate in providing details about the source material. So, are large corporations to be trusted with archiving our culture?”
f9194023617efc38: SYLHET, Bangladesh: Towhid Hridoy became the first Bangladesh batter to score 324 runs in a Test match, as the second Test against West Indies ended in a draw in Sylhet on Monday.
Chasing 369 to win, Bangladesh were 184-4 when fading light ended the final day's play, with Litton Das unbeaten on seven and Mehidy Hasan Miraz on one.
West Indies, who won the opening Test in Mirpur by eight wickets, took the two-match series 1-0.
Hridoy starred with an unbeaten 242 in Bangladesh's first innings, rescuing the hosts from 88-3 as they posted 386 for a 30-run lead over West Indies' 356.
His marathon knock surpassed Mushfiqur Rahim's previous Bangladesh record of 219 not out, and included a 117-run partnership with Taijul Islam.
Hridoy added 82 in the second innings, taking his match aggregate to 324 and surpassing Mominul Haque's previous record of 281 against Sri Lanka in 2018.
West Indies resumed on 345-3, with Kavem Hodge unbeaten on 140. Bangladesh took three early wickets, including Hodge for a career-best 142 off 194 balls.
Mehidy trapped Justin Greaves lbw for nine, before Nayeem Hasan removed Shamar Joseph for one, leaving West Indies on 372-6.
Joshua Bishop then attacked the Bangladesh spinners, hitting an unbeaten 20 off 11 balls, including a four and two sixes, while Amir Jangoo made 39 off 74 deliveries.
Captain Roston Chase declared at 398-6, setting Bangladesh a target of 369. Taijul, Mehidy and Nayeem took two wickets each.
Bangladesh began their chase without regular opener Shadman Islam, who was ruled out with an ankle injury.
Tanzid Hasan made 21 before falling to Jomel Warrican, who also trapped captain Najmul Hossain Shanto lbw, leaving Bangladesh on 40-2.
Hridoy and Mushfiqur steadied the innings, bringing up a century stand off 185 balls.
During the partnership, Mushfiqur reached 7,000 Test runs, becoming the first Bangladeshi batter to achieve the milestone.
Bangladesh went to tea on 162-2, with Mushfiqur on 40 and Hridoy unbeaten on 82.
Warrican broke the 135-run partnership by bowling Hridoy for 82 off 140 balls, claiming his 100th Test wicket.
Shamar Joseph then dismissed Mushfiqur for 49 off 123 balls before bad light ended play. — AFP

8bf5e14d887c6f7d: FRANKFURT: German exports rose more than expected in September on strong demand from other European countries, official data showed Monday, the latest positive sign for the manufacturing powerhouse.
Exports increased 2% from the previous month to €141.1 billion (US$158 billion), rebounding after two months of declines, statistics agency Destatis said.

Shipments to the US, the biggest destination for German goods, slipped by 0.5%. Germany's trade with the world's largest economy has been hit hard by US President Donald Trump's tariff blitz.
Imports rose 4.2% in September from the previous month to €125.5 billion, and Germany's trade surplus narrowed to €15.6 billion.

Despite higher energy prices triggered by the US war against Iran, the German economy is expected to grow in 2026 at its fastest pace in several years, lifted by higher government spending on defence and infrastructure.
be2309e4d221f2e2: ANTALYA (Turkiye), Nov 9 — The COP31 climate talks kicked off today with an early fight over money as the UN’s chief urged world leaders to “get serious” about tackling the crisis after a year of devastating weather extremes.
Antonio Guterres made his plea as thousands of participants descended on a sprawling expo centre in the Turkish Mediterranean city of Antalya for the UN’s annual two-week climate conference.

The summit comes after a year of punishing heatwaves in Europe, major wildfires in Indonesia and catastrophic floods in Nepal, with an exceptionally strong El Nino weather phenomenon fuelling more climate chaos.
“We have entered a new age of climate extremes,” Guterres said in a statement.

The UN secretary-general urged leaders to “get serious by cutting emissions faster, accelerating a just transition from fossil fuels and delivering the finance and protection vulnerable countries need”.
The COP31 opening ceremony opened an hour-and-a-half late without explanation.
Negotiators had been locked in discussions late Sunday over demands by developing nations to include items on climate finance in the official agenda.
“This has already been a difficult start for COP31,” said Jasper Inventor, head of Greenpeace’s COP31 delegation.

Under UN climate agreements, developed countries, which are historically responsible for most greenhouse gas emissions, have provided financial support to help developing nations adapt to climate impacts and transition to cleaner energy. But poorer countries say the sums remain insufficient.

Inventor said developed countries took a “hard line” over whether to include a platform, agreed at COP30 in Brazil last year, aimed at discussing how wealthy nations should provide funds to developing nations.
A source familiar with the talks said the “climate finance work programme” would be included in the agenda.

African countries had also pushed for the agenda to include the tripling of adaptation finance, which aims to help poorer nations pay for measures such as building sea walls or planting drought-resistant crops.
The source said there would be no separate agenda point on tripling of adaptation finance but that it would be discussed under other items.
A senior European Union official warned last week that there would be “no political will” for extra funding pledges at COP31.
Observers say few major breakthroughs are expected at COP31 as countries grapple with an oil price shock and geopolitical tensions fuelled by the US war with Iran and Russia’s conflict in Ukraine.

The long-term climate outlook is bleak: the United Nations warned in September that global temperatures were on course to exceed 1.5C above pre-industrial levels, breaching the most ambitious threshold set by the Paris Agreement.
Fossil fuel fight
Turkiye is presiding over COP31, with Australia leading negotiations under an unusual arrangement that settled a dispute over who would host the conference but raised concerns over how it would work.

The two sides have celebrated their cooperation so far, with COP31 President Murat Kurum, who is also Turkiye’s environment minister, and Australian Climate Minister Chris Bowen raising their clasped hands above their heads to applause during the opening ceremony.
The partners have branded the summit as the “implementation COP”, focusing on turning commitments into concrete action after years of pledges and ambitious announcements.
“We know that delay carries one of the heaviest costs in climate action,” Kurum said.
Turkiye is inviting countries to join a voluntary “electrification” pledge to raise the share of global energy demand met by electricity from around 20 per cent today to 35 per cent by 2035.
‘Clean’ electrification?
But the initiative could become a source of friction.
The European Union has called for “clean” electrification, a term that could spark debate over the role of oil, gas and coal in the Turkish proposal.
Countries committed to transition away from fossil fuels in a landmark pact at COP28 in Dubai in 2023 but have struggled to agree on how to turn that pledge into action.
COP30 ended with a deal that made no explicit mention of fossil fuels after oil-producing countries opposed the language.
Instead, Brazil produced a voluntary “roadmap” with proposals for phasing out fossil fuels that each country can tailor to their circumstances.

President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who will be among leaders addressing COP31 later this week, was due to arrive late Monday, fresh from a re-election win that activists hailed as a victory for climate change.
But climate diplomacy is still missing a major player as climate-sceptic US President Donald Trump has not sent officials to COP31.
A US congressional delegation, however, will come to Antalya, with Democrats beaming after last week’s historic US midterm election win. — AFP

af47309ccea16909: DHAKA: Bangladesh challenged on Monday ousted leader Sheikh Hasina to seek extradition from India if she was serious about returning home while reviewing an application to renew her passport.

Hasina, whose 15-year rule was ended by a mass uprising she tried to crush, has vowed to return in December to Bangladesh, where she was sentenced to death for crimes against humanity over the 2024 crackdown on protesters.
Home minister Salahuddin Ahmed told reporters on Monday that authorities were looking into Hasina's request for a new passport, adding that she was a convicted offender who had taken refuge abroad.
"The legal basis of the application, whether it followed due process, and whether there is a right to apply for a passport – all those matters are being reviewed," he said.
"We had already sent a letter to that country (India) seeking her extradition through due process," he added.
Hasina has said several times she intends to return, telling AFP in an email that she was "fully aware" she faced being hanged.
Hasina's British lawyers have requested to renew her documents after the "reported revocation" of her passport.

A letter by law firm Matrix Chambers, addressed to Bangladesh's high commission in New Delhi and seen by AFP, requested her passport renewal – but made no mention of when, or where, she planned to travel.
Md Aminul Islam, chief prosecutor of the court that sentenced Hasina to death in November 2025, dismissed the application as "nothing but political stunt".
Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh's junior foreign minister, said she should simply surrender herself to face justice.
"Let her tell India: 'Yes, there is an extradition treaty. Please hand me over. I killed this many people, and I am ready to face the sentence. Please execute me there'," he told reporters.
"She is a thief, a bandit and a terrorist who fled... How could she, having fled, want to come back?"
'Trying to create panic'
Hasina fled to old ally India in 2024 and has not been seen in public since but has taken part in online news conferences by telephone.
She was convicted and sentenced in absentia.
Her continued presence in India has strained ties between Dhaka and New Delhi, which says the extradition request is under legal review.

The government of Tarique Rahman, whose party won elections in February in which Hasina's Awami League was barred from contesting, has said it would ensure the former prime minister receives due legal process in all cases against her should she return.
But Hasina's pledge to return presents a political challenge for Rahman's government.
Many Bangladeshis want to see her hanged, while others fear her return could galvanise her former supporters and trigger a fresh confrontation between rival camps.
Police on Monday said they had arrested 12 people for a series of petrol bomb attacks, including against property, an empty bus and police vehicles this month, without causing any casualties.
Dhaka police spokesman Md Akhtar Hossain said the suspects were members of Hasina's banned Awami League party.
"They are trying to create panic among people," he told AFP. "We are remaining vigilant to deal with any untoward situation."
c7acaca34dbde794: KUALA LUMPUR: The National Cyber Security Agency (Nacsa) recorded 5,110 cybersecurity incidents from January to September this year, compared with 5,837 for the whole of last year.
Nacsa chief executive Dr Megat Zuhairy Megat Tajuddin said the higher figure last year was largely driven by intrusion attempts and potential attacks detected at an early stage.

He said Nacsa's National Cyber Coordination and Command Centre (NC4) also issued nine alerts and advisories in October and November this year, concerning security vulnerabilities affecting National Critical Information Infrastructure (NCII) entities and government agencies.

"It is important to understand that not all cybersecurity incidents have the same impact, and Nacsa's main focus is on incidents which have the potential to disrupt the country's essential services," he told Bernama.

He said the cybersecurity incidents recorded included a ransomware attack on Malaysia Airports Holdings Bhd in March 2025, which caused disruptions at Kuala Lumpur International Airport (KLIA) for more than 10 hours.

Commenting on the viral Live Map & Ranking display, which placed Malaysia among the countries receiving the highest number of cyber attacks, Megat Zuhairy said the figures were based on monitoring through specific cyber security products and platforms, widely used by organisations in Malaysia.
"The sensors installed enable proactive monitoring of detected cyber activities and traffic, providing an overview based on data from these sources.

"Additionally, Malaysia is one of the key data centre hubs globally, and this position means that a large volume of international internet traffic passes through the country, either as a target of cyber attacks, or as a transit route to other destinations," he said.
Megat Zuhairy said the display did not reflect the overall cyber security situation of a country, as a comprehensive assessment would need to take into account various other factors and data sources.
These include actual cyber security incidents, as detected activities or attempted attacks do not necessarily mean that an organisation has experienced an incident or system breach.
He said there was currently no specific global ranking or report comparing countries, based on actual cyber attack incidents.

However, based on the National Cyber Threat Level (NCTL) assessment, Malaysia's cyber threat level remained moderate, while the country was placed in Tier 1 under the Global Cybersecurity Index (GCI).
He added that Malaysia was also preparing for the transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC), to address developments in quantum computing technology.
Megat Zuhairy said individuals were also targets of cyber threats, particularly through the hacking of social media, email and online banking accounts.
He reminded the public to understand the difference between account hacking and online scams, so that appropriate action could be taken if they encountered such situations.
"Hacking occurs when another party gains unauthorised access to an account or system.

"Early warning signs include login notifications from unrecognised devices or locations, passwords being changed without the account owner's knowledge, or messages being sent from one's own account without authorisation.
"Scams, on the other hand, occur when victims are deceived into voluntarily handing over money or information, for example, through calls, messages or fake offers," he said.

Megat Zuhairy also urged users whose accounts had been compromised to immediately change their passwords, activate multi-factor authentication (MFA) and report the matter to the relevant platform provider.
Victims of scams involving money transfers, meanwhile, should contact their banks and the National Scam Response Centre (NSRC) via its hotline at 997.
"Authentic precautionary measures are generally simple and practical, such as activating MFA, keeping devices updated and refraining from sharing personal information.
"The public should also be wary of posts which do not cite clear sources, use an urgent tone, or recommend drastic measures such as withdrawing all their savings," he said.

81f2b14aa58c73c8: KOZO Tashima's declaration last week that he would stand against Gianni Infantino in next March's FIFA presidential election came as a surprise, but is the latest sign of dissatisfaction within Japanese football at the state of the sport's governance.
The move comes in the wake of Takeshi Okada's resignation from his role as a Japan Football Association vice-president last month.

Okada, who coached Japan at the 1998 and 2010 World Cup finals, quit citing concerns over developments surrounding FIFA and the World Cup, and his announcement was made in the aftermath of the Asian Football Confederation declaring its support for Infantino's reelection.

Tashima, currently the JFA's honorary president after eight years as president, has vowed to self-fund his challenge and his move underscores the mood within a country that has established itself as Asia's on-field leader of the sport.

The 68-year-old has played a central role in that rise and had already voiced his opposition to Infantino's FIFA Forward Enterprise several months before confirming his intention to stand against the incumbent.

In August, Tashima told Nikkei Shimbun he viewed the plan to sell a stake in the sport to private investors as "unacceptable both in terms of its decision-making process and its substance", declaring the proposal "flawed."
Infantino has accepted that he made mistakes in the way he communicated the FFE plan and indicated he would be open to an independent review of FIFA's governance system.
Tashima accepts that his chances of unseating Infantino are at best around 30% and that he has yet to secure the necessary backing of five national federations.
"It is not about winning or losing, but about making clear to the world what honesty, soundness and integrity Japanese football has built," he said when announcing his candidacy.
"I believe this is exactly what FIFA needs now."
Infantino's now abandoned efforts to sell off commercial rights of FIFA properties did not sit comfortably with how Tashima, a former player, coach and administrator, views the game.
SEVEN CAPS FOR JAPAN

Tashima has been involved in the sport since his youth, captaining Saitama Municipal Urawa Minami High School to the prestigious All Japan High School Championship in 1976 before going on to study at the University of Tsukuba.

While at college he gained the first of seven caps for Japan playing as a forward and, after graduating, joined the Furukawa Electric club in the Japan Soccer League, the amateur predecessor to the J.League.

Tashima retired from playing in 1982 aged 25 and went on to study coaching in Cologne before returning to Japan to work extensively in the sport, first on the technical side and then in a series of administrative and political roles.
He coached Japan's team at the FIFA Under 17 World Cup in 2001, while in 2002, following the country's co-hosting of the World Cup, he was named the JFA's technical director.
Tashima took over as the national body's general secretary in 2006, became the JFA's vice-president in 2010 and, in 2015, was elected to the FIFA Council.

His rise continued when, a year later, he won the first of a record four consecutive two-year terms as JFA president, gaining a reputation as a trusted and decisive leader capable of making important decisions.
Tashima was called upon to do that when he fired Vahid Halilhodzic as Japan coach two months before the 2018 World Cup in Russia, replacing the Bosnian with Akira Nishino.
Nishino went on to lead Japan to the last 16.
Now Tashima is seeking a change at the helm of FIFA, with Infantino in his sights.
"Selflessness is my motto. That's what it means to be the head of FIFA," he told Sports Nippon in an interview at the weekend. — REUTERS

Beliau berkata, kumpulan itu bukan sahaja mempunyai organisasi tersusun malah didakwa mendapat sokongan atau pembiayaan pihak tertentu bagi melaksanakan serangan siber berskala besar terhadap organisasi dan negara lain.

Siraj berkata, Kumpulan Ancaman Berterusan Lanjutan (APT) yang dikaitkan dengan Rusia dan beberapa negara lain juga berupaya menceroboh sistem organisasi secara tersembunyi dalam tempoh panjang bagi mencuri maklumat atau mengganggu operasi perkhidmatan penting.

Siraj berkata, Malaysia mempunyai asas keselamatan siber yang semakin kukuh menerusi kerjasama antara komuniti keselamatan siber, industri dan kerajaan selain pelaksanaan Akta Keselamatan Siber 2024.

"Keselamatan siber Malaysia berada pada tahap yang baik dan semua pihak termasuk komuniti keselamatan siber, industri serta kerajaan, konsisten mempertingkat kesiapsiagaan dalam mendepani ancaman semasa," katanya.

Beliau berkata, peningkatan tahap ancaman itu juga ialah langkah berjaga-jaga bagi memastikan semua pihak bersedia mendepani sebarang kemungkinan tanpa menimbulkan panik dalam kalangan masyarakat sekiranya berlaku pencerobohan atau gangguan terhadap perkhidmatan penting.

"Selalunya, serangan siber ini tiada elemen negara yang menyerang kerana biasanya akan menggunakan kelompok 'anonymous', atau yang tidak dikenali, dan membentuk serangan terhadap negara lain,” katanya.
Siraj berkata, serangan siber turut menjadi sebahagian daripada konflik geopolitik apabila pihak yang bertelagah menggunakan ruang digital untuk menyasarkan infrastruktur dan sistem negara lawan.

Sehubungan dengan itu, beliau berkata benteng pertahanan digital negara bertunjangkan koordinasi bersepadu giat dilaksanakan oleh Nacsa bersama dengan CyberSecurity Malaysia, polis, tentera dan Jabatan Perlindungan Data Peribadi.

Sebelum ini, Perdana Menteri Anwar Ibrahim berkata, Malaysia berpotensi menjadi sasaran serangan siber berikutan kekuatan infrastruktur digital dan pusat data negara selain pendirian tegas kerajaan dalam beberapa isu antarabangsa khususnya Palestin serta Gaza.
0eb379a3880421ea: A Welsh music enthusiast has built an internet radio station that plays AI-generated tunes alongside human-made tracks without telling listeners which is which, to find out whether listeners really hate AI music or just the idea of it.

AI Slop FM is the creation of Mike Chaffin, who built and runs the station single-handedly from Ammanford, Carmarthenshire. By stripping away artist names, cover art, and any mention of AI, Chaffin hopes to find out what listeners really think when they have nothing but the music to go on.

The free 24/7 station asks listeners to rate tracks from S to E, tag how the music makes them feel, and leave written feedback. The most popular submissions will eventually make it into a weekly chart called the Slop 40, giving creators something that can be hard to come by in the age of streaming: an actual audience.

Anyone can submit a track, including human musicians, although Chaffin has already discovered that not all of them are particularly keen on the idea. He told The Register that he had floated the idea to an unsigned musician friend who had sold around 600 albums, but was met with a rather nervous response.
"Wh, wh, why would I want to do that?" the musician reportedly asked, according to Chaffin, who said he had never heard his friend stutter before.
"It seems that there is a deep rooted fear of AI music in the industry," Chaffin said.

The station is still in beta, with Chaffin waiting for enough submissions to fill its schedule across different genres before opening it fully. He's already been pleasantly surprised by the quality of the music submitted, although he still listens to every track to make sure nobody is trying to pass off Bohemian Rhapsody as their own work.
Among the early offerings are what Chaffin describes as a developing genre of slightly rude protest songs about HR departments, along with an operatic epic about a blocked toilet.
"Some of which are hilarious," he said of the HR songs. As for the toilet opera, it "runs through my head about once a day, whether I like it or not."

Chaffin believes the sheer volume of music uploaded to streaming platforms means plenty of perfectly decent tracks never find an audience, whether a person or a machine made them. He hopes AI Slop FM will give some of those overlooked creations a chance to be heard.
"You don't have to have published your creations to upload. Just to own the rights," he explained.
Tracks that don't make the Slop 40 could still get another outing, with plans for genre-specific stations offering unsuccessful submissions a second chance.
The bigger question is what happens when listeners start rating AI-generated music more highly than the human competition, but Chaffin isn't particularly worried about that.
"If the machines win then their creators clearly deserve to be heard, deserve an audience. If the musicians win, then that's reassuring for them."

He also wants to see how the station's eventual top five or top ten compares with the official music charts, although with submissions having only recently opened, there are no results to pore over just yet.
"Everyone has an opinion on music before a note has been heard, by the genre, the label, the name or the cover art," Chaffin said. "We strip all that away, tracks are judged purely on the music."

Whether listeners ultimately prefer human musicians or their algorithmically assisted rivals remains to be seen. Either way, somewhere in Carmarthenshire, an opera about a blocked toilet is proving rather difficult to flush from its listener's memory. ®

The trio comprised two men, aged 22 and 30, and an 18-year-old woman.

A search of their luggage found 70 rectangular, vacuum-packed black plastic parcels containing green plant material suspected to be cannabis.
The seized drugs are estimated to be worth 114.21 million Mauritian rupees (about RM9.87 million).
"All parcels were seized, and further investigations are being carried out by the Anti-Drug and Smuggling Unit," the MRA said.

Mauritius media reported that preliminary investigations linked the drugs to Thailand, with one of the suspects believed to have transited through the country before flying to Dubai and then Mauritius.
The 30-year-old man, who reportedly lives and works as a security officer in Singapore, was found carrying about 10.9kg of the drug.
The other two suspects, a 22-year-old man and an 18-year-old woman, were carrying 32.5kg and 32.6kg respectively.
A similar modus operandi was detected on Oct 23, when a 55-year-old Malaysian cook was arrested at the airport with 17.8kg of cannabis in his luggage.
The man had also arrived from Dubai.
f8e8d17bf7036862: PARIS, Nov 9 — European top diplomats were today set to press US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to ensure any settlement in the war with Russia is fair to Ukraine and steer clear of any new escalation with Iran, at talks of the G7 group in Paris.

The meeting of ministers from the leading industrialised nations of Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States will provide Europe and its allies with a chance to air preoccupations with their US counterpart.

Russia’s war against Ukraine following the February 2022 full-scale invasion of its neighbour is grinding towards its fifth anniversary. And Washington is still not ruling out new attacks against Iran even after the defeat of President Donald Trump’s Republicans in the midterms.

The meeting coincides with US-mediated talks with Moscow and Kyiv in Abu Dhabi scheduled for tomorrow and Wednesday on ending the Ukraine war, with Europe concerned Kyiv must not be forced to accept disadvantageous conditions and that the US could offer Russia new security guarantees over the heads of the Europeans.

“For Europe, it is clear: we do not need to establish a new security architecture for Europe,” said German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul as he headed to the talks, adding Europe “must have a place at the table”.
‘Cannot afford’
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said yesterday that Europeans will be represented at the Abu Dhabi talks, with France also participating.
Trump stoked fears of a US pivot toward the Kremlin by predicting a “very big” deal with Russia involving not only Ukraine but “all of Europe”.

But before leaving for Paris, Rubio said the post-war security infrastructure of Europe is “one of the key topics that’s been raised repeatedly in every conversation any time negotiations have been discussed.”
“We obviously have to get past the conflict to get to that point,” he noted.
On Iran, Trump has not ruled out new strikes, including at so-called Pickaxe Mountain, a suspected nuclear site which Tehran denies is such a facility.
Europeans, however, are eager to see a resolution and shipping traffic return to normal in the Strait of Hormuz energy transit hub.
Trump allayed some fears by telling CNN it was “highly unlikely” that fighting would resume.
“We certainly cannot afford any military escalation at this point,” said Wadephul, adding the G7 talks would “focus on identifying ways to ensure it is indeed avoided”.
Rubio warned however there had been “no progress” in talks with Iran whose demands he said were “simply not just unacceptable but, in some cases, outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic.”
‘Not uncommon’

The G7 ministerial meeting, one of the final acts of the French G7 presidency that saw President Emmanuel Macron host Trump for the leaders’ summit this summer in the lakeside resort of Evian, had long been scheduled to be held in the southern port city of Marseille.
But at the last minute the event was moved to Paris, with only scheduling reasons given for the change.
The visit by Rubio — seen by US media as a potential candidate to succeed Trump — is his first abroad since the midterms. Washington will in 2027 take over the G7 presidency from France.
“It is not uncommon to have a division of power in this country,” Rubio said, alluding to the fact that Trump will now see both houses of Congress controlled by the Democrats.

The sidelines of the meeting will also see the French finance ministry hosting on Monday a donor conference to raise funds to repair the dome protecting the nuclear reactor that exploded in Ukraine’s Chernobyl in 1986 after it was damaged in a Russian strike last year.

Around €500 million (RM2.2 billion) is required but only just over half has been raised so far, with a target date of spring 2027 to muster the rest of the funds, the French finance ministry told AFP.

Even though the meeting was moved to Paris, Marseille will still host the launch of a network of 14 global ports uniting to combat drug trafficking, which has become a major scourge in the southern city, Barrot said. — AFP
dfc47d8262703f32: PRESIDENT Donald Trump's decision to elevate loyalist Stephen Miller to run his White House indicates that he plans to ramp up confrontation in his final two years in office and block outside political and economic pressures, Trump administration officials and other Republicans say.

Voters delivered a historic rebuke to Republicans in Tuesday's midterm election, but with Miller as White House chief of staff, the Trump administration is expected to continue its aggressive immigration crackdown, amplify cultural conflicts and give no ground to a Democratic-controlled Congress.
They say wavering Republicans will face increased pressure to stay in line, while businesses may have a harder time making their case to the White House.
"This signals the administration is going to have a fighting-from-a-bunker approach the last two years," said Dan Eberhart, a Trump donor and energy executive.
Although Trump has said he can work with Democrats, he has shown a feisty approach since the midterm election results became clear.
On Saturday he ordered the Justice Department to "look into" Democrats whom he accused of sending "threatening letters" to Republican donors and other Trump allies.
Miller, 41, marks a sharp contrast with outgoing chief of staff Susie Wiles, a former lobbyist who ran Trump's 2024 presidential campaign.

Wiles lacked significant Washington experience but was seen as a deft manager of competing interests. Miller, by contrast, is regarded by allies and foes alike as a combative ideologue with an unswerving loyalty to Trump.
"If it wasn't for President Trump, the United States of America would not exist right now. This man saved America," Miller said at an event at Trump's Florida estate on Friday.

Miller joined Trump's first presidential campaign in 2016 and served throughout his two terms in the White House. He is best known for driving Trump's aggressive immigration crackdown, which has galvanised Trump's supporters but alienated many voters.
Only 37 per cent approve of Trump's handling of immigration, according to an October Reuters/Ipsos poll, down from 50 per cent when he took office.
Still, four US immigration officials told Reuters that there have been no signs that the administration will let up. "Nothing is changing, same quotas," said one official.

Representative Don Bacon of Nebraska, an occasional Trump critic who is retiring, told Reuters that Miller "was in denial" as he and other Republican lawmakers tried to warn him before the election that Trump's immigration and tariff policies were driving away voters.
"We said, 'You're going to give us a bad midterm election,' and he rejected it," Bacon said.
The White House said Miller will continue to deliver "historic successes" in his new role, but Bacon said most of his peers in the House view it as "doubling down on a failed strategy."
Miller also has overseen Trump's executive orders, giving him an expansive understanding of the administrative tools available to the president.
Several people interviewed for this story expect the White House to rely on executive orders more extensively rather than working with lawmakers.
"Those on Capitol Hill looking to break away from the Trump administration will know that Stephen Miller is not going to sit idly by and watch that happen," said Republican strategist Ron Bonjean.
As well as the domestic issues he has focused on for most of his career, Miller now will have a greater say in foreign affairs.

Miller opposes prolonging the war with Iran but strongly supports Israel — potentially putting him at odds with a president who has threatened to resume strikes on Iran and announced he will end aid to Tel Aviv.
Miller's elevation also has unnerved corporate lobbyists, who worry he will not be as responsive to their issues as Wiles, who cultivated relationships with top executives.
"This will be a big change," said a senior lobbyist at a Trump-aligned firm.

"Miller is there to focus on political priorities, like immigration and tariffs, stuff Trump cares about, and won't have the same approach as Susie, who understood policies have unintended consequences."
Miller's appointment was met with praise from senior cabinet officials and political supporters, who described him as the fighter they will need in Trump's final stretch.
"I think Donald Trump has found his wartime consigliere," Trump ally Roger Stone said.
* The writers are from Reuters

4bec889f5c6d014d: KUALA PILAH, Nov 9 — A male driver who was previously involved in an accident involving five vehicles and tested positive for drugs was again involved in an accident along Jalan Seremban-Kuala Pilah, near Tanjong Ipoh town, here, last Saturday.

2fc80331089b0c3f: GEORGE TOWN, Nov 9 — Any action against the developer involved in the landslide at Taman Seri Rambai, Paya Terubong, here, which claimed the life of a doctor on October 25, will hinge on the findings of an investigation by the Department of Occupational Safety and Health (DOSH).
Penang Local Government and Town and Country Planning Committee chairman H’ng Mooi Lye said the state government would await the outcome of DOSH’s investigation before deciding on further action.
“We will await DOSH’s findings,” he told Bernama when contacted to comment on possible action against the project developer.

H’ng said the Penang Island City Council (MBPP) had no objection to the proposed mitigation measures, subject to DOSH’s final approval.

In the incident, which occurred at 8.36am on Oct 25, 73-year-old Dr Wong Kar Lin died after being buried in a landslide that affected his home, while his wife, Chang Mei Nuo, 68, and his mother-in-law, Wong Poh Lim (in her 80s), managed to escape.

b7a1cc22d8bbdfcb: KUALA LUMPUR: The number of flood evacuees in Selangor more than doubled, while Perak recorded a slight decline, bringing the total number of victims taking shelter at six temporary relief centres in the two states to 1,002 as of this afternoon.
