0cd99ca5b269d52d: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 9 — The National Cyber Security Agency (Nacsa) recorded 5,110 cybersecurity incidents from January to September this year, compared with 5,837 incidents last year.

Nacsa chief executive Dr Megat Zuhairy Megat Tajuddin said the higher number of incidents recorded last year was largely driven by intrusion attempts and potential attacks, which were detected at an early stage.

He said Nacsa’s National Cyber Coordination and Command Centre (NC4) had also issued nine alerts and advisories in October and November this year, concerning security vulnerabilities affecting National Critical Information Infrastructure (NCII) entities and government agencies.

“It is important to understand that not all cybersecurity incidents have the same impact, and Nacsa’s main focus is on incidents which have the potential to disrupt the country’s essential services,” he told Bernama here today.

He said the cybersecurity incidents recorded included a ransomware attack on Malaysia Airports Holdings Bhd in March 2025, which caused disruptions at Kuala Lumpur International Airport (KLIA) for more than 10 hours.

Commenting on the viral Live Map & Ranking display, which placed Malaysia among the countries receiving the highest number of cyber attacks, Megat Zuhairy said the figures were based on monitoring through specific cyber security products and platforms, widely used by organisations in Malaysia.
“The sensors installed enable proactive monitoring of detected cyber activities and traffic, providing an overview based on data from these sources.

“Additionally, Malaysia is one of the key data centre hubs globally, and this position means that a large volume of international internet traffic passes through the country, either as a target of cyber attacks, or as a transit route to other destinations,” he said.
Megat Zuhairy said the display did not reflect the overall cyber security situation of a country, as a comprehensive assessment would need to take into account various other factors and data sources.
These include actual cyber security incidents, as detected activities or attempted attacks do not necessarily mean that an organisation has experienced an incident or system breach.

He said there was currently no specific global ranking or report comparing countries, based on actual cyber attack incidents. However, based on the National Cyber Threat Level (NCTL) assessment, Malaysia’s cyber threat level remained moderate, while the country was placed in Tier 1 under the Global Cybersecurity Index (GCI).
He added that Malaysia was also preparing for the transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC), to address developments in quantum computing technology.
Megat Zuhairy said individuals were also targets of cyber threats, particularly through the hacking of social media, email and online banking accounts.
He reminded the public to understand the difference between account hacking and online scams, so that appropriate action could be taken if they encountered such situations.

“Hacking occurs when another party gains unauthorised access to an account or system. Early warning signs include login notifications from unrecognised devices or locations, passwords being changed without the account owner’s knowledge, or messages being sent from one’s own account without authorisation.
“Scams, on the other hand, occur when victims are deceived into voluntarily handing over money or information, for example, through calls, messages or fake offers,” he said.

Megat Zuhairy also urged users whose accounts had been compromised to immediately change their passwords, activate multi-factor authentication (MFA) and report the matter to the relevant platform provider.
Victims of scams involving money transfers, meanwhile, should contact their banks and the National Scam Response Centre (NSRC) via its hotline at 997.
“Authentic precautionary measures are generally simple and practical, such as activating MFA, keeping devices updated and refraining from sharing personal information.
“The public should also be wary of posts which do not cite clear sources, use an urgent tone, or recommend drastic measures such as withdrawing all their savings,” he said. — Bernama
4d9ab16b057d12be: BRUSSELS, Nov 9 — The EU wants to name the next head of the European Central Bank by the end of the year, Eurogroup chief Kyriakos Pierrakakis said today, before ministers held their first discussions on a successor to Christine Lagarde.

Former Dutch central bank chief Klaas Knot and Spain’s Pablo Hernandez de Cos, head of the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), are the two candidates to replace Lagarde, who announced last month that she would step down in February.

“The ambition here is that the whole process would have completed itself by the end of the year,” Pierrakakis said before a Eurogroup meeting of euro area finance ministers, when the ECB race will be on the agenda.

Pierrakakis said that Dutch and Spanish ministers would present their candidates, and that later on Monday he would meet with Antonio Costa, head of the European Council, which represents EU member states’ leaders.
It will be up to EU leaders to appoint Lagarde’s replacement based on a recommendation by euro area finance ministers.
There will be fierce negotiations as ECB executive board member Isabel Schnabel and chief economist Philip Lane are due to be replaced as well.
The expectation is that the leaders agree on a package deal on all three, including Lagarde’s replacement.
“Perhaps this would facilitate things but again this is a decision that will be taken by the leaders,” Pierrakakis said.
Spanish Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo said Hernandez de Cos was the “right person for the position”, pointing to his decades of experience.
“He knows the ECB inside out. He’s been leading institutions such as the Bank of Spain, such as BIS as well. A steady hand, but always a profile to be able to find consensus,” Cuerpo told reporters.

Dutch Finance Minister Eelco Heinen said Knot was an “excellent candidate”, adding that “He has a very clear understanding of the ECB mandate and he has... a lot of experience to fulfil this position”.
EU governments want a deal as soon as possible.
Irish Finance Minister Simon Harris, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency, said he hoped Lagarde’s replacement would be chosen by December.
“It certainly makes sense to fill the vacancy as quickly as possible,” Harris said. “But it’s also about getting it right and getting the right person. It’s a really crucial appointment.” — AFP
862d12319af03692: SEOUL: Four cases of cheating using AI glasses have been reported at middle and high schools this year, the South Korean education ministry said Monday, Yonhap News Agency reported.

According to data collected from all 5,679 middle and high schools nationwide between Oct 27 and last Tuesday, one middle school student and three high school students were caught using AI glasses during their midterm or final exams.
The middle school and one high school are in Seoul, while the two other high schools are in North Jeolla Province and the southern island of Jeju.

Three of the four were caught while constantly touching their glasses, while the other was caught switching to AI glasses after the exam got under way. In the latter case, the proctor had been keeping a close eye on the student following a tip-off from another student, officials said.
All four students received zero scores on the affected exams in accordance with relevant regulations.

In addition, separate disciplinary measures were taken against the three high school students, such as three days of special education, four hours of community service and a five-day suspension. The middle school student did not face any official disciplinary action but was asked to perform on-campus volunteer work.
The education ministry said it plans to distribute educational materials to students detailing these cheating cases, along with guidelines for schools to prevent the misuse of AI glasses.
The ministry added that it will discuss further preventive measures with regional education offices and the Korea Institute for Curriculum and Evaluation (KICE).

The education ministry earlier said those caught cheating on the annual college entrance exam using AI glasses will face criminal charges and be barred from taking the test for three years, up from the current one-year ban.

111b66d97ab01eca: This week, as countries meet in Antalya, Turkey for the United Nations climate conference, one topic likely to dominate the conversation is artificial intelligence. The host has already called on countries to commit to ensuring that AI is designed, powered, and deployed in ways that support climate action.

But so far, industries around the world aren’t doing nearly enough to harness the technology to actually drive down the greenhouse-gas emissions heating up the planet, despite some very optimistic claims from AI companies.

In 2024, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman declared that AI would unleash “astounding triumphs,” including “fixing the climate.” The year before, in a 2023 op-ed, the head of sustainability at Google and her coauthor wrote that AI could reduce global emissions 5% to 10% by 2030.

Some academic researchers have examined these AI-related climate claims. A peer-reviewed study published last year, led by researchers at the London School of Economics’ Grantham Research Institute and the firm Systemiq, estimated that AI could help cut global emissions by the equivalent of 3.2 to 5.4 billion tons of carbon dioxide annually by 2035—roughly on par with the US’s annual energy-related emissions on the high end, even after subtracting AI’s own energy footprint. Those potential gains are mostly concentrated in three sectors: power, meat and dairy, and vehicles.

But projections like these are only as good as our willingness to test them against present-day reality. So is there evidence that the largest companies in these three sectors are beginning to integrate AI in line with the study’s projections, and if so, do the results match expectations? Or is the 2035 number still mostly aspirational?

Companies across these sectors have announced plenty of initial efforts to incorporate AI into various business practices. But an AI-assisted review of public information from significant market actors in each sector, conducted and reviewed by the second author of this piece, found that few have announced they’re pursuing the specific emissions-reducing routes that informed the projections in the study—and fewer still claim they’ve used them to achieve meaningful climate progress.

The power sector is where the earlier study’s underlying math is most concrete: AI-driven forecasting of supply and demand could increase the amount of renewable electricity that reaches the grid from already-built solar and wind facilities by up to 20%, which could prevent an estimated 1.8 billion tons of emissions a year.

Yet of the grid operators reviewed in China, the United States, and Europe, only one deployed a known meaningful, working AI program of this sort, according to the analysis. A partnership between the UK’s National Grid ESO and Open Climate Fix halved the grid operator’s solar-forecast error (the difference between the amount of incoming sunlight predicted and the amount that actually reaches solar panels), avoiding hundreds of thousands of tons of carbon dioxide a year. Beyond this example in the UK, though, many other grid operators in the EU, the US, and China had little to show in the public record in terms of the AI integration envisioned by the study.

The meat and dairy sector offers the starkest contrast between technology readiness and market reality. To achieve the 2035 emission reductions anticipated in the earlier study, AI would need to close the taste and cost gap between traditional proteins and alternative ones, such as lab-grown or plant-based burgers and milk substitutes.

In one of the clearest efforts to achieve this, the AI and food tech company NotCo recently formed a joint venture with Kraft Heinz using its platform Giuseppe, which analyzes plant molecular data to pinpoint combinations replicating the taste, texture, and smell of animal products.

But few other alternative-protein companies had such a deeply integrated way of using AI in product development, the AI-assisted review suggests. Meanwhile, the sector seems to be facing more fundamental problems, including stubbornly slow mainstream consumer adoption and declining funding levels. Most notably, venture capital flowing into cultivated meat fell from a $989 million peak in 2021 to around $83 million last year.

The transportation sector offers some hopeful examples of the type of AI integration necessary to achieve the study’s projections, particularly among battery manufacturers and ride-sharing platforms. CATL—which controls roughly 40% of the global market for electric-vehicle batteries—launched an AI system trained on more than 100,000 battery design cases and 600 terabytes of test data. It cut the time needed to screen candidate materials by two orders of magnitude, according to the company. Independent researchers also found that the ride-sharing platform Didi Chuxing was able cut per-trip emissions 16% on average by using AI-optimized routing to minimize detours.

There’s another big problem in the climate case for AI, though: Oil and gas companies are also interested in these tools for many reasons, including the potential to increase production of fossil fuels. Technology firms that committed to sustainability goals in the past should answer questions about how their tools could be used to boost old, dirty energy as well as clean, renewable energy.

Finally, it’s also worth noting that integrating AI is just the first step, and it remains unclear to what degree the technology can accelerate the sorts of improvements and innovations envisioned. AI also does little to shorten the standard paths to certifying, permitting, building, packaging, marketing, and selling any resulting products, facilities, or services.

The findings of the analysis, carried out by Anthropic’s Claude Code, were reviewed against public documents and media accounts to ensure their accuracy. It is possible that some companies and utilities in these industries are pursuing AI-assisted applications that would fit into the initial study’s scenarios but haven’t yet been disclosed publicly.

Greater and better-targeted AI integration and efficiency gains in these three sectors may well materialize, bringing the 2035 projections closer to reality. But it won’t happen without deliberate and sustained efforts to ensure that AI delivers more environmental benefits than harms.

Notably, so far the rapid adoption of AI models and buildout of data centers has driven a huge increase in energy consumption and emissions, and this has led major tech companies like Microsoft, Google, and others to fall well off track in their corporate climate goals. At this point it would be surprising if the sector even manages to zero out its climate pollution: Emissions associated with global data centers (which may handle AI as well as non-AI computing tasks) could exceed 300 million tons annually in 2035, according to the IEA’s base forecast.

Industry leaders must implement the technology in the ways that promise to do the most to drive down emissions. Corporate customers should select models with the lowest environmental impacts and opt to work with the AI developers doing the most to reduce their climate footprint. And states and regions need to do more to incentivize or require all these companies to operate in more responsible ways.
The need has never been more apparent.
Mary Nichols is distinguished counsel at the UCLA School of Law and the former chair of the California Air Resources Board.
Jeremy Tamanini is the founder of Dual Citizen, a sustainability research and advisory firm.

88a01ca20e07f7d2: MOSCOW: Russian investigative newspaper Novaya Gazeta was winding up its operations on Monday and preparing to quit its central Moscow office after holding its final editorial meeting, bowing to what it said was a campaign of state pressure that had made it impossible to carry on reporting.

The paper, founded by the last Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev with money from his 1990 Nobel Peace Prize, had kept going until now despite a sharp tightening of censorship after Russia launched its full-scale war in Ukraine in 2022.
But it announced late last month that it would have to close after it was designated a "foreign agent" and banks stopped processing reader donations on which it relied for its financial survival.
Its offices and the home of its editor were searched, and another senior journalist is under house arrest awaiting trial.
"The most awful thing is that we who lead editorial teams cannot protect our journalists," former editor in chief Dmitry Muratov told an audience in London last month.
Muratov shared the 2021 Nobel Peace Prize, dedicating it to six slain colleagues, including investigative journalist Anna Politkovskaya, who wrote about Russia's wars in the restive Chechnya region.

The Kremlin - which accuses foreign intelligence services of trying to stir discontent in Russian society - has said previously that some censorship is necessary at a time when Russia is locked in what it calls an existential struggle with the West over Ukraine.
Some hardliner war bloggers have accused Novaya Gazeta of systematically promoting an anti-Russian narrative, an allegation it has repeatedly dismissed as false.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov played down the outlet's closure on Monday, saying it was part of what he called "a standard rotational process" in which some media closed only to have their places taken by newcomers in what he said was a fiercely competitive media environment.
A long article on Novaya Gazeta's website described its journalists' operation to pack up and vacate their premises.

It quoted a senior journalist, Irina Vorobyova, as saying its spirit would survive like a "good virus" - "Not even a nuclear explosion could destroy it. It will continue in everyone who was part of it."
daed6fa86fdbaa3d: DUNGUN, Nov 9 — A total of 69 participants in the Projek Berkelompok Kelapa Kampung Dendang, here, claim that their income has been affected since the beginning of this year due to an influx of imported coconuts in the market from Indonesia since the start of the year.

Project head Mohamed Zakaria Awang, 66, said that most wholesalers and traders of coconuts and coconut milk here prefer to source imported coconuts from Indonesia because they are cheaper compared to local ones.
He said that the situation caused a decrease in demand for the Matang variety of coconuts produced by the project participants, which in turn affected their sales and income.
Some 5,000 coconut trees across 20 hectares cultivated by participants of the Kampung Dendang Coconut Group Farming Project in Dungun November 9, 2026. — Bernama pic
Overall, the participants of the group project planted 5,000 coconut trees over an area of 20 hectares in 2009 and started yielding results in 2012.

“Every month, the growers can harvest about 500 coconuts to sell to wholesalers and coconut milk traders as our source of income,” he said when met at the Projek Berkelompok Kelapa Kampung Dendang site here today.

Mohamed Zakaria said that currently, the coconuts produced by the project’s participants are being purchased by the Federal Agricultural Marketing Authority (Fama) at a price of RM1.10 each to help market the growers’ produce following the influx of imported coconuts in the market, compared to RM2.50 each which were sold to wholesalers and traders previously.
Unsold coconuts pile up following an influx of supply from Indonesia since early this year, affecting their income, during a site visit in Kampung Dendang, Dungun November 9, 2026. — Bernama pic
“All this time, coconut growers were able to earn more than RM2,000 a month, but that amount has dropped to around RM500 a month currently due to the drop in coconut prices.
“Meanwhile, imported coconuts from Indonesia are sold at only 80 sen each in the market, putting pressure on the prices of local coconuts,” he said.

Another project participant, Zahari Abdullah, 61, said that some participants are no longer interested in continuing the group project due to the decline in coconut prices since the start of this year.
He said that the situation caused some of the participants’ coconut plantations to no longer be properly managed, even though the trees were still producing yields.
Unsold coconuts pile up following an influx of supply from Indonesia since early this year, affecting their income, during a site visit in Kampung Dendang, Dungun November 9, 2026. — Bernama pic
“If this situation continues, we are worried that more participants will decide to leave this project because the sales results can no longer provide returns like before,” he said.
Meanwhile, Terengganu Fama director Muhamad Fadlee Hassan said that his team had purchased coconuts from the group participants from April 29 to November 3.
“The coconuts that are purchased will be marketed to local wholesalers and Fama retail outlets around the Kuala Terengganu district,” he added. — Bernama
712a242776f6bb89: IPOH, Nov 9 — A two-year-and-10-month-old boy went missing while enjoying a family outing at Dataran Sungai Jahang, Kampung Jahang, near Gopeng, around midday today.

Perak Fire and Rescue Department Operations Division assistant director Sabarodzi Nor Ahmad said a team from the Gopeng Fire and Rescue Station was dispatched to the scene after receiving a call at 12.06pm.
“The search involved the police, villagers and a nearby tour company, which assisted by providing eight rafting boats.

He said the search area was being expanded this afternoon, with a control post already set up at the scene.
Personnel from the Kampar Fire and Rescue Station were also assisting by monitoring the river downstream near Kampar, he said, adding that the search is still ongoing.
In a separate incident on Pulau Pangkor, a 38-year-old Myanmar worker is feared drowned after reportedly suffering a seizure before falling into the sea.

“Efforts to locate the victim are ongoing,” he added. — Bernama
d7f2a3371ca368a5: PETALING JAYA: Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has announced an additional RM2,500 in cash aid for eligible flood victims in Selangor, with payments expected to begin tomorrow.
In a statement, the Prime Minister's Office said the assistance was to help affected households replace essential items damaged or destroyed by floods.
It said the implementing agencies would announce the eligibility criteria and payment details.
Anwar also directed flood mitigation projects to be expedited to address recurring flooding.

The announcement comes as the number of flood victims taking shelter at relief centres in Selangor more than doubled to 583 people from 163 families as of 3.40pm today, compared with 215 people from 55 families this morning.
All victims were housed at four temporary relief centres in Kuala Selangor, reported Bernama.
In Perak, the number of flood victims in Hilir Perak fell slightly to 419 people from 124 families, down from 439 people from 130 families this morning.
Last Friday, Selangor menteri besar Amirudin Shari said the national disaster management agency and the state government would provide up to RM1,500 in aid to flood victims in the state.

The State Disaster Management Committee Secretariat said 284 evacuees from 85 families were taking shelter at the Teluk Intan Municipal Council (MPTI) Rest House Hall, while another 135 people from 39 families were at the MPTI Langkap Hall.

f96470cd7392c999: KUALA LUMPUR: Each eligible household affected by floods in Selangor will receive RM2,500 in special additional cash assistance, with payments expected to begin tomorrow.
Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim announced the assistance in a statement issued by the Prime Minister's Office.
The aid is intended to help households replace necessities damaged or destroyed by the floods.
"The implementation mechanism and eligibility criteria will be announced by the implementing agency," the statement said.
It added that Anwar had also directed that flood mitigation projects be expedited to address recurring floods.
Flood evacuees in Selangor rose to 583 people from 163 families as of 3.40pm, compared with 215 people from 55 families in the morning.
Selangor Menteri Besar Datuk Seri Amirudin Shari said on Friday that the recent floods were caused by unusually heavy rainfall.
He said the state was pursuing both long-term flood mitigation projects and immediate measures, but it was unrealistic to expect floods to disappear overnight.
The 2026/2027 northeast monsoon began on Oct 27 and is expected to last until March next year.

Malaysian Meteorological Department director-general Dr Mohd Hisham Mohd Anip said three to five episodes of continuous heavy rain were expected between November and January, potentially triggering floods in low-lying areas and riverine communities.

The department's National Weather and Earthquake Operations Centre senior director Maqrun Fadzli Mohd Fahmi said the risk of major floods would increase if prolonged heavy rain coincided with high tides.

In August, the Selangor and federal governments agreed on five measures to mitigate flooding in the Klang Valley following a meeting between Amirudin and Minister in the Prime Minister's Department (Federal Territories) Hannah Yeoh.
The measures include assessing the capacity of Batu Dam and Klang Gates Dam, identifying potential sites for new flood retention ponds, and coordinating river dredging and desilting works.
cf358d3dc11385df: NEW YORK: Tesla will have to refund Cybertruck deposits for many customers as orders far exceed production capacity, CEO Elon Musk said, following last week's announcement that the electric vehicle maker is winding down the pickup truck's production at its Texas factory.
"We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months but will have to return deposits for a lot of people," the billionaire said in a post on X on Monday.

The comments come after Musk said Tesla would add an extra production shift to fulfil outstanding Cybertruck orders before dismantling the production line next year to expand output of its Cybercab robotaxi.
The production wind-down is slated for mid-2027, Musk announced on Friday, with the resources being redirected to the Cybercab, a vehicle central to the automaker's autonomous-driving ambitions.

Tesla began delivering the Cybertruck in late 2023, but demand has fallen far short of Musk's expectations. US sales fell 48% to 20,237 units last year, according to Kelley Blue Book, well below Musk's earlier projection that annual Cybertruck sales could reach 250,000 vehicles.
07261f694213eec0: BATAM, Nov 9 — A 41-year-old Malaysian man has been arrested in Batam, Indonesia, after allegedly robbing a woman at gunpoint with an airsoft pistol, stealing her car and injuring a police officer while attempting to escape last Friday.

The suspect, from Melaka, allegedly threatened the 48-year-old woman with an airsoft pistol and a knife before fleeing in her Toyota Rush with valuables worth an estimated 292 million rupiah (RM73,000), Sinar Harian reported today.

Barelang Police Criminal Investigation Division chief Commissioner Tri Poerbowo said preliminary investigations found that the suspect had entered Indonesia on September 15 for a holiday but overstayed by 10 days after running out of money.
“He then planned a random robbery to obtain money to pay for his return journey to Malaysia,” he was quoted as saying by Indonesian media.
The victim had just paid her vehicle road tax and withdrawn cash from an automated teller machine (ATM) at Harbour Bay before getting into her car.
The suspect allegedly entered the passenger seat unexpectedly, pointed his weapon at her and ordered her to drive to the Bukit Senyum area.
Upon reaching the grounds of a residential development, he forced the victim to transfer money online into his personal bank account.
However, when the woman screamed for help, the suspect panicked, pushed her out of the vehicle and drove off.
A traffic police officer nearby witnessed the incident and gave chase, eventually intercepting the stolen vehicle.
The suspect refused to surrender and pointed his airsoft pistol at the officer before ramming into him, leaving the officer injured.
Police questioning revealed that the suspect had bought the airsoft pistol from an apartment security guard for one million rupiah.
The security guard has also been detained to assist in investigations.
If convicted under Article 365 of Indonesia’s Criminal Code for theft involving violence, the suspect faces a maximum prison sentence of nine years.
ba6a9d2f50339772: LARYSA Ryndova hurried to see her husband as if they were going out on a first date — makeup on and perfume spritzed in the car.
It was the first time she had laid eyes on 68-year-old Serhiy in 4-1/2 years — time he had spent trapped with others in the Russian-held town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine.
"I can't believe you are here," Larysa, 72, kept repeating, her mascara smudged with tears after they embraced outside a hospital in Kyiv.
"Honestly, I can't believe it myself," Serhiy replied.
They last saw each other in 2022 when Larysa fled to England to live with their son, three months into the occupation following Russia's all-out invasion of Ukraine.
Serhiy stayed to look after the family home, ending up stuck in the town peppered with Russian-laid landmines and facing a mounting humanitarian crisis.
"We hoped for better. Turned out, it got 'better'," he said sarcastically.
Oleshky's residents described living through constant drone attacks and without power and heating. Things got even worse this spring, when food deliveries stopped.
Serhiy got out on October 30 with hundreds of other residents, evacuated during a ceasefire that US first lady Melania Trump was involved in brokering, with the additional involvement of Pope Leo.
For all the joy of seeing Larysa — and the prospect of being reunited with his three children and six grandchildren — he had found his escape from Oleshky a devastating wrench.
"Your heart is torn apart at the thought of leaving everything behind. How can you? Your home, your family, the cemetery — all your relatives are there," he said.
"How will you ever visit their graves, keep them cared for?"
As Oleshky's evacuees were moved by buses and planes through occupied land, Russia and Belarus, Larysa set out on her own 2,000-km journey to meet Serhiy and bring him back with her to Britain.
"How haggard he looks," she said when she saw the first pictures of her husband crossing into Ukraine. "It's hard to recognise him."
Serhiy called Oleshky a "zone of death" where life under occupation could depend on the mood of an individual Russian soldier.

He survived on humanitarian aid that he had stockpiled during the occupation — noodles, grains, sometimes canned meat and fish. He tried frying up flatbreads with flour stored before the war, riddled with weevils.

"Sometime around April (this year), the people who used to bring us food died — two men. After that, all food deliveries stopped completely. There was nothing," Serhiy said over a cup of coffee in a Kyiv cafe.
Locals shared what they had. Some risked the dangerous 20-km journey on foot or bicycle to Radensk for supplies. Rare provisions were sold at severely inflated prices.
The local hospital ran out of supplies. Bodies were stacked up in the morgue, as forensic experts refused to risk the journey to the town to perform autopsies.
"Bodies are just lying there. Everything is leaking. When my neighbour died, I carried his body in there, and the smell was absolutely horrific," Serhiy said. "God forbid!"
Another neighbour asked him to bury her in her own courtyard if she ever got killed.
Serhiy said he probably would not have left the town himself had it not been for the evacuation. Landmines were laid out on all the roads and even in the town.
"They (Russian troops) had their own objective, as I understand it: to mine everything so they could keep everything under control," he added.
"A lot of people were killed in Oleshky. Someone would go out to pick a cherry plum and get blown up. Someone else would pick up a mushroom or a nut and step on a landmine."
Serhiy said Russian troops "had done a great job of cleaning up" to put on a show before the organised evacuations began. He didn't see a single burnt-out car on the way.
He said he felt sure he could have survived another winter, despite the ordeal of occupation and food shortages.
Larysa rolled her eyes, still wet with tears.
"I'll fatten him up with borscht and varenyky (dumplings)," she said.
* The writer is from Reuters

af88f9028914f21b: Rising memory prices are pushing more customers toward refurbished tech, suppliers say, with warranties of up to three years helping to make secondhand kit a less daunting purchase.
Memory costs have more than quadrupled this year as manufacturers prioritize more lucrative high-bandwidth memory (HBM) for servers powering AI datacenters.

Many enterprises are keeping equipment longer in an uncertain economy. Ben Caddy, senior analyst at Omdia, said suppliers were linking refresh discussions with opportunities to recover value from customers' aging kit.

By 2030, he predicted, 35 percent of "all the hardware sold for the channel will be taken back by partners," driven "by the sheer economic logic of taking equipment back, recovering value, and embracing more circular IT lifecycles."

This is already helping some customers "unlock some capital to put towards those [relatively] small refresh plans," he said while hosting a panel on circular IT at last month's Canalys Forums in Barcelona.
Refurbished smartphones are growing in popularity, but persuading customers to trade in their old devices remains a constraint on supply.
The same applies to PCs and other equipment, said Jon Sansom, MD at GreenSafe IT. "Availability is a challenge," he said.

Marcel Joosten, group director of marketing and digital commerce at tech lifecycle specialist XTENTEC, said the company now offers trade-ins when customers buy new kit. "We're actually financing the residual value" at the end of year two, three, or four, when customers return the equipment, he told the audience.

XTENTEC collects, refurbishes, rents, and resells equipment, and has an agreement with HP to renovate aging products, with a two or even three-year warranty available as "just an SKU on the list from HP."
Joosten said equivalent support, including HP Care Pack services, helped make refurbished equipment more attractive to buyers.
Customers want to cut their carbon footprint, and many public and private sector tenders require it. But the "most important thing" for many is trust, said Patrick Molberg, CEO of Advania Finance.

"The customers have to trust the refurbished equipment and have to trust the process. And I think one of the things that we have to be better at as a whole is that we kind of need to have a standard methodology regarding verification."

Work on verification standards with vendors including HP, Lenovo, and Dell is ongoing, Molberg said. He also argued that lifecycle services should be built into purchasing decisions rather than added three or four years later.

Joosten argued that listed US tech companies' focus on quarterly sales and market share can work against refurbishment. "That needs to change," he said. "I think there should be a market share figure for circularity." ®
149e8d90ee282f44: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 9 — Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim today announced a special additional cash aid of RM2,500 for heads of eligible flood-affected households in Selangor, with payments expected to begin tomorrow.

The Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) said in a statement that the assistance is aimed at easing the burden of victims in replacing household essentials damaged or destroyed by the floods, with implementation mechanisms and eligibility criteria to be announced by the executing agency.
“At the same time, the prime minister has also directed that the implementation of flood mitigation projects be expedited to tackle recurring floods,” the statement read.

Meanwhile, speaking to reporters after visiting flood victims in Kuala Selangor, Anwar said the additional RM2,500 aid is intended for families who have endured prolonged displacement and sustained substantial damage from the disaster.
He said the payout is expected to be disbursed starting tomorrow in coordination with the state government to facilitate distribution.

The prime minister said the additional aid, placed under the Prime Minister’s Department’s Implementation Coordination Unit (ICU), is being provided in view of the protracted flood situation and the heavier losses incurred by victims.
He said this assistance is in addition to the RM1,000 Bantuan Wang Ihsan (BWI) distributed under the National Disaster Management Agency (Nadma).

“Because some families have been displaced for a prolonged period, the RM1,000 aid is often felt to be insufficient given the heavier damage. Therefore, I am announcing an additional RM2,500 per family in Selangor for those who have faced extended displacement and extensive damage,” he said.
Earlier, Anwar visited flood victims housed at the temporary relief centre at SK Parit Mahang, Jeram, here, which is currently accommodating 154 evacuees from 36 families.
He said the visit was carried out to assess the victims’ situation firsthand, considering the floods that have persisted for several days, along with prevailing weather conditions and high tides.

The prime minister also expressed his appreciation to all federal and state personnel, as well as volunteers, including medical teams, who worked tirelessly to assist flood victims throughout the Deepavali long weekend. — Bernama
c5d429a9d8484309: MELAKA: Umno vice-president Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani took a break from the campaign trail today to join residents of Kampung Bukit Godek, Semabok, for a friendly game of checkers, locally known as dam haji.

Helmy said the impromptu match gave residents a glimpse of Johari's down-to-earth personality and his kampung roots.
"Datuk Johari came here and played dam haji with the villagers. He even won the match.
"It showed his true personality, the kampung side of him from his younger days," he said.
Earlier today, Johari attended a briefing with BN election machinery for the Ayer Molek and Pengkalan Batu constituencies.
Also present were BN's Ayer Molek candidate Datuk Mohd Ridhwan Mohd Ali and Pengkalan Batu candidate Siti Aisyah Mahmood.
Helmy is defending the Duyong seat against Pakatan Harapan's Poo Long Suan.

9eee008019b01003: BRUSSELS: Seorang lelaki bersenjata yang membunuh enam individu dalam kejadian tembakan di Krakow dan bandar Ostrowiec Swietokrzyski di timur Poland meninggal dunia di hospital, menurut polis, lapor Anadolu Ajansi (AA).

3e963db44dade84d: PETALING JAYA: Malaysia's former internationals lost 2-0 to their Western Australian counterparts in Sendayan, Negeri Sembilan, but the result was secondary to an occasion honouring the late M Chandran.

The unveiling of the Dato' M Chandran Challenge Trophy paid tribute to the former national captain, who brought the two groups together more than 20 years ago to celebrate their shared love of football.
Now an annual contest, the fixture carries his name and continues a relationship that has survived the end of playing careers and Chandran's death in 2019, aged 77.
His idea was simple: bring senior footballers from Malaysia and Western Australia together to play and build friendships beyond the pitch.
More than two decades later, his former teammates and Australian friends are keeping that tradition alive.
For Soh Chin Ann, who captained Malaysia in Sendayan recently, the occasion brought back memories of a teammate he also regarded as a close friend.
Having played alongside Chandran during one of Malaysian football's finest eras, Chin Ann remembered a natural leader whose courage, discipline and commitment set the standard for those around him.
"He was a leader in the truest sense of the word," Chin Ann said. "He embodied courage, discipline, determination and an unwavering commitment to Malaysian football."
Chandran understood the responsibility of representing the country, Chin Ann said, and earned the respect of his teammates through his character and example.
The naming of the trophy was especially meaningful because it gave lasting recognition to an initiative that had continued long after its founder was gone.
"What began as his vision for friendship through football has become a tradition that continues to bring people together," Chin Ann said.
The unveiling was also an emotional occasion for Chandran's wife, A Pushpalatha, who received a special souvenir from Chin Ann.
She said she was deeply touched that her husband's contribution and sacrifices for Malaysian football remained in the memories of those who had shared his journey.

"Throughout his life, Chandran gave so much of himself to football and to the country he loved," she said. "There were many sacrifices along the way, and to see his contributions recognised and honoured in this way means more to me than words can express."

For Pushpalatha, seeing the relationships he built through the game endure was a source of particular happiness. She believed Chandran would have been proud that the fellowship continued to bring people together.
Chandran's playing career took him from Selangor Indian Association to Chartered Bank, his employer at the time, where his performances attracted the attention of Selangor manager Harun Idris.
He was brought into the state team and helped Selangor enjoy success in the Malaysia Cup before establishing himself as one of the country's leading defenders.

He captained Malaysia at the 1972 Munich Olympics, where the national side faced the United States, Morocco and hosts West Germany. Two years later, the team won bronze at the 1974 Asian Games in Tehran.
Those achievements marked a memorable period for Malaysian football, with Chandran among the leaders of a generation that represented the country with distinction.

The Sendayan reunion brought together several of those former internationals. The Malaysian squad also included Ahmad Yusuf, Alex Soosay, Vincent Thambyrajah, Mohd Nor Yaacob, K Ravinchandran, Ramli Junid, Chow Siew Yai, K Gunalan, Reman Ragunathan, Kamarul Zaman Yusuff, John Engathasoo, K Gunasakaran and Manuel George.
Former national striker N Thanabalan managed the team, while fellow former international Santokh Singh took charge as coach.
Santokh said the contest went beyond the pursuit of a trophy, celebrating more than two decades of sporting fellowship and mutual respect.

Frank Houston, Chandran's close friend and captain of the Western Australian seniors, said the trophy would preserve the memory of the initiative and the values behind it: sportsmanship, friendship and a shared love of football.
Malaysian football may be searching for its next great chapter, but one of its finest stories is still being written by the men who came before.
Each time the two teams meet, they keep alive something Chandran began more than 20 years ago. His playing days ended, but the friendship he created continues to take the field.

4e0a85895128acf5: ANTALYA, Nov 9 — The world is entering a new reality where climate extremes are the norm, the United Nations chief Antonio Guterres warned today, urging leaders at the COP31 climate conference in Turkey to “get serious”.
“A supersized El Nino is colliding with a planet already superheated by manmade climate change,” the UN secretary general said in a statement.
“We have entered a new age of climate extremes.”

As leaders gathered in Antalya for the UN climate summit, Guterres called on them to “get serious by cutting emissions faster, accelerating a just transition from fossil fuels and delivering the finance and protection vulnerable countries need”.
His statement came as the UN’s World Meteorological Organization released a report indicating that 2026 has continued a streak of exceptional global temperatures, melting ice and rising sea levels.
Each of the past 12 years have been among the hottest 12 years on record, the agency said, with this year expected to be among the hottest ever.
‘Off the charts’

“What we are seeing gives new meaning to the phrase off the charts,” WMO chief Celeste Saulo told reporters in Geneva, cautioning that the current exceptionally strong El Nino could unleash more heat and extreme weather well into next year.
“We should prepare for another record-breaking year in 2027.”
The global average surface temperature between January and September this year was around 1.47 degrees Celsius above the pre-industrial average, the WMO said.
And this year’s El Nino — expected to be the strongest since 1950 at least — could push the figure higher by the end of the year.

Preliminary data shows 2026 figuring among the four hottest years on record, WMO climate information chief John Kenned told reporters, adding though that “with the El Nina developing, we might see when the final numbers come in that we’re close to the top”.
The naturally occurring weather phenomenon releases heat from the ocean, which this year has been the warmest ever measured, Saulo pointed out.
El Nino is declared when the sea surface temperature is half a degree above average in the tropical Pacific, but from now through January, WMO forecasts “it may be 3.8C above average”, she said.
The WMO also reported that the global sea level was the highest on record, freshwater was dwindling and glaciers were continuing a long-term retreat.
In 2025, the annual mass loss of ice was enough to fill five Olympic pools every second that year, it said.

At the same time, “we are supercharging our weather and El Nino will be a risk multiplier”, Saulo said, warning that “heatwaves, tropical cyclones, and rainstorms are intensifying faster than our historical baselines prepared us for”.
On a positive note, the WMO hailed a significant increase of countries with essential multi-hazard early warning systems in place, from 55 in 2015 to 136 last year.
It urged the COP31 to ensure more investment in the sustained global observations, data-gathering and forecasting needed for such systems to work.
“We cannot afford to fly blind,” Saulo said. — AFP

be05acecd4551f5d: PETALING JAYA: A 41-year-old Malaysian has been arrested in Batam, Indonesia, after allegedly robbing a local woman upon spending all his money while on holiday on the island.
Agung Tri Poerbowo, head of Barelang police's criminal investigation department, said the suspect who hails from Melaka arrived in Batam on Sept 15.
"He overstayed for 10 days as he did not have enough money to pay for his trip back to Malaysia. He had come to Indonesia for a holiday but spent all his money.
"The suspect then planned to rob a random person to get the money to return home," Agung said, according to Berita Harian.

He said the suspect's victim was a 48-year-old woman who had just withdrawn some money from an ATM. The suspect allegedly entered via the passenger side as the victim returned to her vehicle, and ordered her to drive to a housing area.

He then pulled out an airsoft pistol and a knife before ordering the victim to transfer a sum of funds to his bank account. She then screamed for help, causing the suspect to push her out of the vehicle and drive off with the car and her belongings.

A traffic policeman chased the suspect after hearing the victim's cries and managed to cut the man off. The policeman suffered some injuries after the suspect rammed him before the suspect was arrested.
Agung said checks revealed the suspect purchased the airsoft pistol from a security guard at a flat for one million rupiah. The guard has been arrested to assist in the investigation.
The suspect is being probed under Article 365 of the Indonesian Penal Code for use of force to rob a person, which is punishable by up to nine years in prison if convicted.
d4be944aac9437a0: PETALING JAYA: Seorang rakyat Malaysia ditahan di Batam, Indonesia, selepas merompak seorang wanita sebelum melarikan keretanya serta mencederakan anggota polis pada Jumaat lepas.

Setibanya di kawasan luar sebuah taman perumahan, suspek mengeluarkan pistol airsoft dan pisau sebelum mengugut mangsa supaya memindahkan wang ke dalam akaun bank miliknya secara dalam talian.
Mangsa kemudian menjerit meminta pertolongan, menyebabkan suspek panik sebelum menolaknya keluar dari kenderaan dan melarikan diri bersama kereta serta barangan milik mangsa.
Seorang anggota polis trafik yang terdengar jeritan mangsa mengejar kenderaan curi itu sebelum berjaya memintasnya.

Polis turut merampas kenderaan yang dicuri, wang tunai satu juta rupiah, sebuah beg, pistol airsoft bersama lima kartrij karbon dioksida serta sebilah pisau.
Suspek berdepan tuduhan mengikut Artikel 365 Kanun Keseksaan Indonesia atas kesalahan mencuri dengan kekerasan yang memperuntukkan hukuman penjara maksimum sembilan tahun.

52ce958774d00497: JAKARTA: Indonesia will tighten controls on state surveillance equipment and consider sweeps of its presidential palace for bugging devices, a minister said on Monday, following last week's discovery of illegal wiretaps on the president, top officials and more.

The wiretapping scandal led to the arrest of four senior police officers accused of unauthorised monitoring of phones, among them a former national police chief who had recently been appointed President Prabowo Subianto's chief of staff.
The government had said that the wiretapping scandal pointed to treason. An investigation is underway, and no formal charges have yet been announced.

Asked if authorities would sweep the presidential palace for covert electronic devices, senior minister for legal affairs Yusril Ihza Mahendra said "it is something we will consider as an anticipation measure."
"The government is also taking steps to ensure that, in the future, the wiretapping equipment held by certain agencies is not misused," he told reporters.

The scandal comes at a time when Prabowo faces growing public pressure over his costly social programmes and his administration battles to restore investor confidence in Southeast Asia's biggest economy after a series of setbacks that have caused havoc for its stock market and currency this year.
It has also put the spotlight on growing political tension in Indonesia and a rift between Prabowo and the influential two-term predecessor who once backed him, Joko Widodo.
Authorities have yet to reveal the full extent of the illegal wiretapping, which they say started after Prabowo took office in late 2024.
Among those monitored were business people, journalists, activists and political figures, whose identities have not been disclosed. It is not clear how many people were targeted.

Former police chief Listyo Sigit Prabowo, who is no relation to the president, is widely seen as a loyalist of Widodo. Listyo was reassigned recently to the post of presidential chief of staff but then sacked last week following his arrest over the alleged wiretapping.
Prabowo held a meeting on Sunday with 10 former police chiefs that included a discussion on the wiretapping scandal, deputy house speaker Sufmi Dasco Ahmad separately told reporters.
Minister Yusril said that the investigation came after the national police received a tip, which its new chief investigated and then reported to Prabowo.
"Following this report, an investigation was launched, and it has become apparent where the wiretapping devices were located," Yusril said, without elaborating.

Deputy public prosecutor Nur Anith Nabilah Rusli requested a jail term, citing humanitarian considerations as the case involved the accused’s own child, and to serve as a deterrent to others.

1c84b55cd928911f: ANTALYA: The world is entering a new reality where climate extremes are the norm, the UN chief Antonio Guterres warned Monday, urging leaders at the COP31 climate conference in Turkey to "get serious".
"A supersized El Nino is colliding with a planet already superheated by manmade climate change," the UN secretary general said in a statement.
"We have entered a new age of climate extremes."

As leaders gathered in Antalya for the UN climate summit, Guterres called on them to "get serious by cutting emissions faster, accelerating a just transition from fossil fuels and delivering the finance and protection vulnerable countries need".
His statement came as the UN's World Meteorological Organization released a report indicating that 2026 has continued a streak of exceptional global temperatures, melting ice and rising sea levels.
Each of the past 12 years has been among the hottest 12 years on record, the agency said, with this year expected to be among the hottest ever.
'Off the charts'

"What we are seeing gives new meaning to the phrase off the charts," WMO chief Celeste Saulo told reporters in Geneva, cautioning that the current exceptionally strong El Nino could unleash more heat and extreme weather well into next year.
"We should prepare for another record-breaking year in 2027."
The global average surface temperature between January and September this year was around 1.47°C above the pre-industrial average, the WMO said.
And this year's El Nino – expected to be the strongest since 1950 at least – could push the figure higher by the end of the year.

Preliminary data shows 2026 figuring among the four hottest years on record, WMO climate information chief John Kenned told reporters, adding though that "with the El Nina developing, we might see when the final numbers come in that we're close to the top."
The naturally occurring weather phenomenon releases heat from the ocean, which this year has been the warmest ever measured, Saulo pointed out.
El Nino is declared when the sea surface temperature is half a degree above average in the tropical Pacific, but from now through January, WMO forecasts "it may be 3.8°C above average", she said.
The WMO also reported that the global sea level was the highest on record, freshwater was dwindling and glaciers were continuing a long-term retreat.
In 2025, the annual mass loss of ice was enough to fill five Olympic pools every second that year, it said.

At the same time, "we are supercharging our weather, and El Nino will be a risk multiplier," Saulo said, warning that "heatwaves, tropical cyclones, and rainstorms are intensifying faster than our historical baselines prepared us for."
On a positive note, the WMO hailed a significant increase of countries with essential multi-hazard early warning systems in place, from 55 in 2015 to 136 last year.
It urged the COP31 to ensure more investment in the sustained global observations, data-gathering and forecasting needed for such systems to work.
"We cannot afford to fly blind," Saulo said.
f249f31bcc2da5af: HONG KONG, Nov 9 — Tech firms clawed back today some of last week’s losses fuelled by AI regulation worries, though gains were tempered by news of a probe into Nvidia boss Jensen Huang and claims of an affair with a Chinese spy.

Chipmakers and other companies linked to the artificial intelligence boom took a hammering in the days after tomorrow’s US midterms saw Democrats sweep both chambers of Congress in a rebuke to Donald Trump and his Republican Party.

The results suggested voters were angry at the president’s Iran war and tariffs, which have sent prices soaring, as well as a sharp kickback against the huge data centre buildout that has taken place across the country in recent years.
That has led to speculation the new Congress will seek to wind in tech firms’ construction drive, which could put thousands of jobs at risk.
The uncertainty comes with traders already nervous about when the hundreds of billions of dollars pumped into the sector would actually see a profit.

After taking a lashing on Thursday, Wall Street enjoyed a little stability at the end of last week, and Asia — which had suffered a hammering itself on Friday — largely followed suit to start this week.
Japan’s Nikkei 225 rose more than two per cent thanks to gains in Tokyo Electron, Advantest and Sony.

Taipei jumped more than four percent as the Tawainese government pledged support for the market, including curbs on short selling and the back-up of a US$15.2 billion (RM13.6 billion) stock stabilisation fund.
There were also gains in Hong Kong, Shanghai, Bangkok and Jakarta.
However, Seoul gave up an early rally to end lower, with chipmakers SK hynix and Samsung giving up most of their gains.

“Investors will be watching carefully this week to get a sense as to whether these gains are just short-covering, bargain hunting or the beginning of something more sustainable in nature,” said Sally Auld at National Australia Bank.

“Fears around AI regulation, the outlook for (capital expenditure) and free cash flow have been the driver of risk reduction in recent weeks and these issues are not likely to be resolved with any conviction in the near term.
“Nonetheless, the valuation of many tech stocks now looks less expensive.”
Nvidia probe

However, a little more uncertainty was injected into markets with news that Nvidia’s board was launching an investigation into whether Huang had been targeted in a foreign espionage plot following his admission that he was unfaithful to his wife.

The New York Times reported last month that US intelligence officials concluded a Chinese executive linked to a Singapore-based data centre company called Megaspeed had been funnelling information to Beijing.
The executive, Alice Huang — also known as Huang Le, and no relation to 63-year-old Taiwanese-born Jensen — developed a close relationship with the Nvidia boss, the Times said.

Nvidia is a global leader in producing chips used to train and run AI models and one of the world’s most valuable companies, and last year became the first to reach a market capitalisation of US$5 trillion.

Jensen Huang is a huge figure in the AI revolution and a close informal adviser to Trump, and the Times said the Nvidia boss’s extra-marital relationship could have revealed insights into Trump’s thinking around AI.

Technology analyst Dan Ives, at investment bank Yorkville Ives, said the crisis will at the very least spark multiple congressional inquiries and “create an overhang on the stock for a myriad of reasons”.

“This will add risk to the stock as he is so important to the Nvidia story and strategy globally,” Ives added. “This will also increase major scrutiny regarding selling chips to China, which remains a key battleground issue in DC.”
Oil prices extended losses on hopes for an end to the Iran war following last week’s huge Democratic victory.
Investors will be keeping tabs this week on the release of fresh US inflation data, after figures on Friday showed the economy created far more jobs than expected in October.

The figures will be key for the Federal Reserve in determining whether or not to hike interest rates when it meets next in December, with markets saying there is an 80 per cent chance of a lift. — AFP

ff24ba8d59b95a21: Welcome to Monday, the day upon which The Register offers a new instalment of "Who, Me?" – our reader-contributed column that shares your stories of messing up, 'fessing up, and somehow finding redress.
This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Oriel" who told us he once worked for a vendor of small business accounting software.

This story comes from a time when software shipped on CD-ROMs and users bought it off the shelf in actual shops. The vendor released a new version each year and always shipped it before a major holiday that's celebrated with a giant meal.
Oriel was part of the team whose job it was to get the package ready on time.
In the previous year, they flubbed the job because the program didn't always install itself on some PCs running Windows 95 or Windows ME machines system due to registry corruption.

"We wanted to increase our successful installation metrics, so in conjunction with the installation team, a key decision was made – by me – to force the updating of registry keys to enable the install," Oriel admitted. In his email to The Register, he asked the portentous question: "What could possibly go wrong?"

What went wrong was that not long after the software was shipped, the vendor's support lines started getting calls from customers who complained that after installing the accounting package none of their other software would work.
"Installing a new version of our application had borked the customer's machine completely," Oriel wrote.
The company decided the best thing to do was to tell affected customers they should go and buy a new PC – and that it would pick up the bill, no questions asked.
"In the week prior to the holiday, we replaced over 600 machines," Oriel told The Register.
Oriel and his developer colleagues were of course told to fix the problem but couldn't reproduce it nor figure out their mistake.

"To get a reproduction case we need a user's machine where the user had created a Windows Registry restore point prior to installing our application," Oriel explained. If the developers could find such a machine, the plan was to roll it back to the restore point, verify everything was in order before the customer installed the update, install the accounting software, and figure out the problem.
The company tasked its support agents with finding a customer willing to surrender their PC, which proved difficult because few bothered to create a registry restore point.
The day before the holiday, a customer volunteered their machine.

This customer was located a few hours away by road, so an engineer got the job of visiting on the morning of the holiday to pick up the stricken machine, give the customer a shiny new system and configure it to their specifications.
Said engineer did the job, which took so long he was invited to stay for the holiday meal, then returned to HQ with the broken box.
The next day, Oriel and his colleagues got to work and found a fix, then created a version of the accounting application that wouldn't break any more PCs.

Oriel was, of course, summoned into a meeting with senior execs to explain the situation and watched as they decided the best course of action was to pull buggy CDs from stores – which meant trashing CDs and packaging valued at $1 million.
Have you made a mistake that broke customers' kit, or cost millions? If so, don't make the mistake of not sharing your story with The Register and click here to email the column. ®
c35a133ff9697d5c: How much control do people retain over their personal information in a world increasingly shaped by AI?
Originally published on Global Voices
Illustration by Nshua Cali-Dibang. Used with permission.

This post is part of Global Voices’ October 2026 Spotlight series, “Big Tech and Authoritarianism.” In this Spotlight, we explore how Big Tech facilitates and hinders authoritarian governments and practices, and how these choices influence the Global South. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Every search, social media interaction, and conversation with an artificial intelligence (AI) tool can leave behind information about its user. Individually, these digital traces may appear insignificant. Collectively, however, they can reveal interests, habits, preferences and patterns of behavior that have considerable commercial and political value.

As AI becomes increasingly embedded in everyday life, technology companies are finding new ways to use data to develop their products, personalize services and generate revenue. While these developments offer considerable benefits, they also raise a difficult question: How much control do people retain over their personal information in a world increasingly shaped by AI?

The issue extends beyond privacy policies and user agreements. It concerns the growing power of technology companies to collect information, draw conclusions about individuals, and influence the digital environments in which people communicate, work, and access information.
The business of knowing more about us

In September 2024, the United States Federal Trade Commission (FTC) published findings from an investigation into nine major social media and video-streaming companies, including Meta, YouTube, TikTok, and Amazon-owned Twitch.

The FTC reported that these companies collected extensive information about users and, in some cases, non-users. The information included personal details, interests, online activities, and data obtained from other sources. The investigation also raised concerns about lengthy data retention, inadequate privacy protections, and the use of personal information in automated systems, including AI.

The report highlighted a fundamental imbalance: Companies can accumulate substantial information about individuals, while those individuals may have limited understanding of how their data is used or how to prevent certain uses.

AI adds another dimension to this problem. Data can help train models, improve recommendations, and power automated decisions. However, the greater the volume and variety of information companies can access, the more important it becomes to establish clear limits on its collection and use.

The concern is not that every company collecting data is necessarily acting maliciously. Rather, it is that systems designed to maximize commercial value from information can create incentives to collect more data than people reasonably expect or understand.
Inclusion at what cost?

For millions of people, AI offers opportunities that were previously difficult to access. Students can use AI tools to support learning, small businesses can improve their operations, and journalists can explore new approaches to research and production.

In countries such as Nigeria, where access to resources and professional services can be uneven, these tools could help narrow certain gaps. AI systems that support local languages and reflect diverse cultural experiences could also make digital services more accessible.

Yet inclusion should mean more than allowing people to use a technology. It should also mean ensuring that they understand the conditions under which they use it and retain meaningful rights over their information.

Many digital services are governed by lengthy terms and privacy policies that users may accept without fully understanding the implications. Some AI products also raise questions about whether information submitted through prompts, uploaded documents, or other interactions may be retained or used to improve models.

The precise practices differ between companies and products. Nevertheless, users need clear explanations of what information is collected, why it is needed, how long it is retained, and whether it may be used for purposes beyond the immediate service.
Without these safeguards, the benefits of AI inclusion risk coming with an invisible cost: reduced control over personal information.
When corporate power begins to resemble surveillance

The connection between big tech and authoritarianism requires careful examination. Authoritarianism is not simply the collection of data by private companies. It involves the concentration and exercise of power in ways that undermine accountability, rights, and freedoms.

However, extensive corporate data collection can create conditions that make surveillance easier. Detailed personal information can support profiling, targeted persuasion and the prediction of individual behavior. Depending on the circumstances, businesses, governments, or other actors may exploit these capabilities.

The risks become particularly serious when personal data can be accessed or shared without adequate safeguards, when automated systems make consequential decisions without meaningful oversight, or when people have little opportunity to challenge how their information is used.

Concentrated corporate power adds another concern. When a small number of companies control widely used digital platforms, AI services, and large pools of information, individuals may have few practical alternatives. Leaving a platform may mean losing access to professional networks, customers, communities, or essential services.

This does not mean that every AI system is a surveillance tool or that every technology company intends to restrict freedom. It means that the infrastructure of digital life deserves scrutiny because its capabilities can be used in ways that extend beyond their original commercial purpose.
Nigeria’s data protection challenge

Nigeria has a legal framework intended to protect individuals against the misuse of their personal information. The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 established the Nigeria Data Protection Commission and provides a framework for the lawful, fair and accountable processing of personal data.
Legislation is an important step, but effective protection also depends on implementation, public awareness, and regulators’ ability to hold organizations accountable.

As Nigerians increasingly adopt AI-powered services, questions about data governance become more pressing. Users need to understand their rights, while organizations must take responsibility for explaining their practices and protecting the information they collect.

There is also a wider question of representation. If AI systems are developed using data that inadequately reflects Nigerian languages, cultures, and social realities, their benefits may be distributed unevenly. Responsible AI governance must therefore address both the protection of personal information and the inclusion of communities whose experiences are often underrepresented.

UNESCO’s Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence emphasizes privacy, data protection, transparency, accountability, and fairness throughout the AI lifecycle. These principles provide a useful foundation for ensuring that technological progress respects human rights.
Innovation must not come at the expense of control

The challenge is not to reject AI or prevent companies from using data to develop useful technologies. It is to establish boundaries that allow innovation without making personal privacy an acceptable casualty.

Technology companies should minimize unnecessary data collection, communicate their policies clearly, provide meaningful choices, and strengthen protections against unauthorized access. Regulators must ensure that existing laws remain effective as AI capabilities evolve, while users need accessible information about the rights available to them.

Ultimately, digital inclusion cannot be measured solely by the number of people using AI. It must also consider whether those people can participate safely, understand the systems they rely on, and exercise meaningful control over their information.

As AI becomes more powerful, the question is no longer simply what technology can do with our data. It is who decides what can be done, who benefits from those decisions, and who has the power to challenge them.
The future of AI should not be defined only by what machines learn about us, but also by how much control we retain over ourselves.
Written by Nshua Cali-Dibang

a0f61c6c0cf5cc52: From Khin Nadarajah and Sri Nadarajah
The 2027 budget brings fresh momentum to Malaysia’s preparations for longer lives.

Its wider investment commitments, including RM25 billion from government-linked investment companies, provide a timely setting to consider how capital, housing and care can work together for older Malaysians.

The opportunity is to translate that momentum into responsible investment in care, housing, healthcare, technology and services that families can depend on. The task is to turn that momentum into services that families can depend on.

The scale is clear. Asean’s population aged 60 and over stood at 74.4 million in 2020 and is projected to reach 127 million by 2035. The speed matters, too. France had 115 years to make the transition to an aged society. Malaysia will have about 27 years.

The statistics department's preliminary estimates for 2026 put the population aged 60 and above at 4.2 million, or 12.3% of the total. These figures make healthy ageing an immediate infrastructure and investment priority.

The recent call by the finance ministry to invest responsibly in the longevity economy remains an important starting point. As proposals take shape, it helps to keep their purpose in view: preserving independence, supporting changing needs and creating lasting value for both families and investors.
Care becomes investable when we can show that the service works for people as well as the numbers work for capital.
We should begin with the person rather than the building.

The National Health and Morbidity Survey 2025 found that 60% of older Malaysians were pre-frail, representing about 2.4 million people. Another 10.7% were already frail. This strengthens the case for earlier support, before greater dependency develops.

Most people hope to remain independent and connected to familiar surroundings for as long as they can. Their needs may then change gradually, or suddenly after an illness or a fall. A useful care system must offer choices between living at home with support and receiving more intensive help. Day services, rehabilitation, home nursing, assisted living and residential care each have a place.

The surroundings matter, too. A home that worked well at 45 may be harder to manage at 75. Stairs, maintenance, transport and access to healthcare can become obstacles. This does not necessarily mean someone needs residential care. It may mean the environment needs to adapt so that independence can continue.

The property sector, therefore, has a role beyond supplying more retirement units. Adaptable homes, accessible public spaces, walkable neighbourhoods and connections to health and community services can help people remain active and involved. Independence should be understood through the life a person can lead, as well as where they live.
This has consequences for development. A well-designed building matters, alongside its continuing usefulness as residents’ needs change.

Early collaboration with the care operator can help align design, skilled staffing and the support families may need over time. Clear information about services and costs helps families plan with greater confidence.
For families, the real test is simple: will this place still be right for someone they love when that person needs more help?

These considerations also strengthen the investment case. Local demand, sustainable pricing, staffing, governance and long-term maintenance deserve attention together. An adaptable, operationally viable development can better serve residents and sustain investor confidence.
The reduction in service tax on elderly care, together with the exemption announced in the 2027 budget, offers welcome relief for families.

They also provide a useful occasion to consider affordability across the full range of needs, from accommodation and daily living to more intensive care. Middle-income families and lower-income households should remain part of that planning. Affordability cannot be added as an afterthought.

Developers, care providers, insurers, employers and policymakers each have a role in exploring practical ways for people to pay for support across different stages of needs. Different households will need different arrangements. Community services, rental options and supported access can complement ownership models, where local evidence and sustainable funding support them.

The announced allocation of more than RM40 million to train 8,000 people in elderly care reinforces the importance of the workforce. Training, supervision and staff retention deserve the same early attention as land and buildings. Investing in people helps turn a well-designed setting into dependable and trustworthy care.
The proposed Senior Citizens Bill is a further reminder of the value of clear responsibility and accountability.
Safeguarding, transparent fees, accessible complaints procedures and standards that can be monitored help families, operators and investors build confidence together.

The same care should guide how progress is measured. Alongside beds built and units sold, attention should go to residents’ social connections, consistent care, timely support and staff development. These outcomes help show whether investment is adding value to everyday life.

One of us, Sri Nadarajah, was born in Malaysia and spent much of his working life developing businesses abroad. That experience taught him to respect both ambition and execution. A promising idea must survive contact with the practical details: land, finance, operations, people and accountability.
Malaysia does not need to choose between commercial discipline and doing good. The strongest care investments will require both.
The budget provides momentum; thoughtful partnerships can carry it forward. Institutional capital has a role alongside government, communities and responsible private operators.

With local evidence, adaptable design and clear delivery responsibilities, Malaysia can build homes and services that remain dependable as lives change. That is how longevity becomes part of the country’s working social infrastructure.
Khin Nadarajah and Sri Nadarajah are the founders of Venus Healthcare, a specialist care provider.
