751583ab578911cd: The Federal Aviation Administration still uses computers that require floppy disks. But those are finally on the way out within the next few years.

Yes, it’s still 2026, and yes, you read that right: The FAA – the agency responsible for overseeing aviation safety in the US – is finally getting rid of four systems dating back to the 1980s that remain in use at more than 400 facilities around the country, the agency announced on Thursday.

“Good news America: floppy disks are out, 21st century tech is in,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in the FAA’s announcement. Only a few decades late, Sean, but we’re sure the flying public appreciates it.

The new system, known as Enterprise Information Display System (E-IDS), is designed to consolidate data from various systems into a common digital platform, allowing air traffic controllers to access operational information and alerts needed to manage flights.

E-IDS is replacing four legacy systems: Information Display System 4, used to track weather and operational info; the Automated Surface Observing System Controller Equipment Information Display System, which also relays weather information; the NAS Information Display System, which relays information about airports and other airspace conditions; and the En Route Information Display System (ERIDS), which handles information about flights.

The FAA said E-IDS will improve how Pilot Reports and Notices to Airmen (NOTAMs) are collected and distributed. The agency has had its share of air traffic control SNAFUs, including one in 2023 that temporarily halted domestic flight departures nationwide after someone accidentally deleted a file from the NOTAM system.

The FAA said it has already lined up five facilities to receive E-IDS upgrades: airports in Atlantic City, Nashville, and Rochester, New York, along with data processing hubs in Atlanta and Salt Lake City. The agency plans to install the system at 435 sites by the end of 2028.
That 2028 deadline echoes the ambitious three-year timetable Duffy laid out last year for overhauling the nation's air traffic control system.

Aside from the four systems E-IDS will replace, the FAA has a lot of outdated technology, with the Government Accountability Office saying in 2024 that 51 of the agency’s 138 ATC systems were unsustainable due to lack of parts and funding to sustain or replace them.

Trump’s Big Beautiful Bill allocated $12.5 billion for the FAA’s overhaul efforts, but that’s far short of what’s actually needed. In December of last year, the FAA said that it needed an additional $20 billion to handle upgrade costs, and that appears to still be the case.

"To continue modernizing our air traffic control facility, Secretary Duffy and FAA Administrator Bedford are calling on Congress to pass the Modern Skies Act," an FAA spokesperson told The Register in an email. That bill is asking for $30 billion to get ATC modernization across the finish line, the spokesperson added.

"It will modernize our air traffic control system, replace crumbling aviation infrastructure, and build world-class airports across the country," they said. In other words, the FAA wants to get rid of floppy disks, but it's probably not accurate to say they're "out," as Duffy put it.

The GAO said in September that the FAA was still well short of its financial needs, with an additional $10.2 billion needed for the second phase of upgrades, which has yet to receive a completion date.
As with so many government ambitions, budgets often get in the way, and this wider modernization effort still seems more ambitious on paper than the FAA may be able to deliver. ®

3e5ae70a61891983: On the eve of Donald Trump’s return to the presidency of the United States, in January 2025, Meta’s founder and CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, announced that changes would be made to his company’s moderation policies in the name of “freedom of expression”, which, he said, was under threat by global pressures for what he saw as censorship. The announcement signaled a rapprochement between Meta and the far right around a common goal: the deregulation of Big Tech. Since then, growing entanglement between major technology companies and the U.S. President Donald Trump administration has shown how the private interests of a small group can override the public interest. In recent months, allegations have been mounting that Big Tech companies, especially Meta, have been interfering in the Brazilian electoral process this year, aiming to undermine the reelection of President Lula (PT). This kind of accusation is not new. Over the past decade, a vast body of literature has exposed the mediating role played by digital platforms in foreign interference in elections around the world. These reports have also highlight the challenges of holding companies accountable for allowing these interference campaigns to be amplified. At our research group, NetLab UFRJ, we have spent years investigating how major digital platforms shape public debate and influence people’s perceptions of reality, often outside the regulatory and normative frameworks in force in Brazil. Meta in particular has become fertile ground for disinformation and boosting fraudulent ads, which already account for 10% of its annual revenue. Despite lawsuits and administrative actions brought by Brazilian authorities against Meta, complaints and requests from civil society for investigations, as well as reports published by the press, the company has shown neither the willingness nor the diligence needed to effectively fight this kind of content. Given this troubling track record, NetLab UFRJ created the “Big Tech Observatory” during the 2026 election campaign period in order to monitor how Meta and other digital platforms performed in two key areas: algorithmic recommendation and political advertising. The initiative set out to examine whether these companies would comply with the current Brazilian legislation established by the Electoral Supreme Court (TSE). The results of the analyses, however, told a predictable story. All were paid for in foreign currencies and boosted by pages with declared locations in other countries. The amount invested in this advertising is equivalent to that spent on prominent campaigns, including the race for Presidency and other executive offices. Brazilian electoral law expressly prohibits candidates from receiving cash or donations in-kind from abroad. This ban, however, did not prevent the ads from being displayed to Brazilian users of Meta’s platforms. According to the available information, not only the ads were allowed to circulate but they may have reached up to 171 million views in the country. But the irregularities in advertising do not stop there. Brazilian electoral rules prohibit electoral advertising from 48 hours before the polls to 24 hours afterwards. However, our analyses of both rounds of the 2026 election identified hundreds of ads in favor or against specific candidates that circulated on Meta’s platforms with no apparent restrictions. The company even allowed fake profiles posing as official channels of the Electoral Supreme Court to boost disinformation about a supposed “digital vote” which stated that people would be allowed to cast their vote from home on the day of the first round — something which does not exist in the Brazilian electoral system. In addition to these irregularities, Lula’s political campaign page was temporarily disabled by Meta without explanation, preventing it from running electoral ads. On September 23, his Worker´s Party (PT) reported they had been blocked from advertising on Meta’s platforms. In a statement released on October 16, the company rejected the accusations of election interference and attributed the temporary deactivation to an “incorrect anti-fraud review” carried out under an agreement with the federal government to fight fraud involving public programs. The effectiveness of the company’s anti-fraud measures, however, is questionable: an analysis carried out by NetLab UFRJ identified hundreds of fraudulent ads involving federal public policies circulating before and after September 23, indicating that those same measures were not able to stop this kind of content from running during the same period. Finally, we found signs of discriminatory practices in ad pricing. Based on data released by Meta, we estimate that for the first round Lula’s campaign may have paid between 33% and 43% more than his far right adversary Flávio Bolsonaro campaign to reach the same number of users on Meta’s platforms. Despite this substantial difference, limitations in the company’s transparency policies make it impossible to identify precisely which parameters and criteria are used to price ads and, consequently, to draw definitive conclusions about the mechanisms behind this disparity. Even so, studies conducted in other contexts, such as the United States, India and the Netherlands, also point to evidence of discriminatory pricing practices in the platform’s advertising. Other complaints made during the elections add to this overall scenario of negligence and show that, despite being worth billions and their strategic position at the forefront of technological innovation, major digital platforms invest little in protecting their users. For example, this 2026 election in Brazil saw several controversies involving WhatsApp’s image generation service, powered by the Meta AI artificial intelligence. Users reported being able to generate content favorable to Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign without difficulty, whereas they were not getting the same results for Lula. Meanwhile, the documentary channel Revelando had videos criticizing Flávio Bolsonaro removed from its Instagram profiles shortly after they were posted, without clear justification from the company. These episodes cast doubt on the consistency of Meta’s moderation and content control systems, exposing failures that call for greater investment and improvement. The situation is made worse by the absence of transparent criteria or guarantees of equal treatment in how ads are handled, how content is recommended, how advertising is priced, and how profiles and posts are moderated. Big Tech companies have developed predatory business models, and they are currently joining forces with political forces committed to deregulation in Brazil. This is part of a strategy to protect their businesses and expand their room for maneuver. Whether or not one side of the electoral race is being deliberately favored, it is indisputable that the major digital platforms continuously exercise the power to determine what gains visibility and what remains on the margins, with no transparency over their criteria and no mechanism for accountability. What is clear is that, for these platforms, defending their economic interests and maximizing their profits prevails above user rights, public interest, and democracy itself. 5cf47ee4d1b26dde: Linux can do many things, but good looks aren't always its strong point. Apple has rather more of a reputation in that department, and a crop of new projects is bringing Mac-style polish to the open source desktop.

Some are all-new, such as the Argentinian Lord OS, a whole new GUI desktop on top of Debian. Another, Cutefish, is a revival of a pre-ChatGPT project that never got as far as a complete release. Now it has version 1.0 for both x86-64 and Arm64, plus it's working on Mac binary compatibility via a work-in-progress layer called Reef. Ukrainian Desert OS is already at version 5.5 – practically a venerable elder in this company, despite appearing to be only about a year old.

Meanwhile, ClokeOS uses Xfce for its desktop, but underneath, the OS is based on Apple's FOSS XNU kernel. The project lead plans to offer compatibility with multiple types of binaries: Linux apps, plus Mac apps via Darling, and Windows apps via Wine.

This isn't new. Much as Cutefish has been revived, last year we reported on PearOS Linux, a very Mac-like skin on KDE Plasma. It has hooks in place for ambitious future features, such as Siri-style speech recognition.

What's striking is the number of projects appearing and the pace of their development. Some offer both x86-64 and Arm64 builds, with Raspberry Pi editions in certain cases. For human coders, this would be months of hard work, but if it's just checking an additional box in an LLM development tool, then why wouldn't you? It's almost no extra work, but it widens the potential audience.

Coveting Mac-like good looks is a longstanding urge among Linux users, and with legitimate reason. There's nothing wrong with Macs, even if you are mainly a FOSS user. Modern macOS, or OS X as it was called a decade ago, is a Unix underneath its shiny proprietary desktop, and many of the flagship Linux FOSS apps also have Mac versions, from Firefox and Thunderbird, via LibreOffice, to VirtualBox, plus less well-known but very handy apps such as Ferdium and Panwriter. We've written about the usefulness of FOSS apps on macOS before, including for reviving elderly Macs.

Just a couple of months ago, we published a two-part guide on how to give Xfce a macOS-like layout and then how to tweak it so apps fit in better. We focused on the functionality, though, not the looks – we don't really care much for such things. If it does matter to you, though, you're not alone, and there are lots of themes and skins to make Xfce look prettier.

Some of these are all-in-one packages that you can install on an existing distro to give it a new look. One recent example is Cupertino, developed with assistance from Claude. From a few years ago, there are Small Sur and Ventura-Xfce. From nine years ago, long pre-LLM, there is osXFCE.

We can see the appeal. From 2006 to 2020, Macs used Intel x86 processors, and those machines are now all falling off the end of Apple support – only four Intel models supported last year's macOS 26 "Tahoe," support for which is just starting to reach OpenCore Legacy Patcher. Earlier this year, The Reg FOSS desk upgraded his 11-year-old iMac to macOS 15 "Sequoia" with OCLP 2.5.1. The first experimental OCLP 3.0 release appeared last month, and it's now up to 3.0-rc5. This adds support for macOS 26, Apple's final major macOS release for Intel Macs. That puts a ceiling on future macOS upgrades for both home-built Hackintoshes and older Macs kept going with unofficial patches.

We gave LordOS a brief spin using its OVA virtual machine image. It installed and booted without trouble, and looks impressive. Last month, we wrote about ZacOS-9 and Mavernix, and similarly, we gave ZacOS-9 a very quick spin in a VM. The resemblance to our recent experience with ZacOS-9 went beyond appearances. In both, we found that the keyboard UI is largely missing: standard keystrokes didn't work. In LordOS, we found some menu options duplicated in two places in an un-Mac-like way, such as "About" options in both the app menu and the Help menu. The LordOS GitHub repository does not credit any LLM assistants, but it's gone though nine test releases in three weeks.

The inevitable end of life of x86 Macs is driving fresh interest in FOSS OSes. They offer a life extension for genuine Macs as well as the enticing prospect of Mac-like polish for existing FOSS OSes. Combine that with the fast, easy code generation offered by LLM coding assistants, and we think there's going to be a lot more of this. In 2025, we saw one macOS-like Linux project rebooted. This October, we saw two new ones. In November, we've found four more. We have a feeling that these are just the first trickles of what may soon become a flood. ®
0ac4496c2cca0cde: Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) now boasts a system for research into quantum error correction, combining IBM quantum processors with a high-performance compute (HPC) system based on AMD silicon.

The Quantum Science Center (QSC) at ORNL, funded by the US Department of Energy (DoE), unveiled what it calls a co-design platform for quantum error correction, marrying up quantum and HPC technology.

While useful, fault-tolerant quantum systems always seem to be at least a decade away, there have been notable advances over the past several years in the field of quantum error correction, according to ORNL. These include early demonstrations of protecting quantum information from environmental noise, which can cause loss of the fragile quantum states needed for computations.

"Solving the challenges of quantum error correction is essential to making quantum computing a practical tool for scientific discovery, which is a priority for Oak Ridge National Laboratory," said QSC director Travis Humble.

IBM Fellow and director of IBM Research Jay Gambetta said that it was no longer a question of whether error correction works, but how to accelerate and optimize error correction to build systems that scientists can use to tackle challenging problems.
"This new co-design platform for quantum error correction allows us to evaluate different approaches and determine the architectures, software and workflows that will scale," he stated.

ORNL's new tool combines an IBM Quantum System Two, equipped with the latest 120-qubit Nighthawk r2 quantum processors, and Umbra, a classical HPC system powered by AMD 5th Gen Epyc CPUs and Instinct MI355X GPU accelerators.

According to AMD, the CPUs provide the orchestration and general-purpose performance needed to coordinate everything, while the GPUs accelerate simulation, optimization and the parallel scientific computations surrounding quantum workloads.
Also part of the system are AMD Versal SoCs to provide the low-latency control, readout and decoding capabilities for the quantum circuitry.

ORNL says that this brings together the computing infrastructure needed for quantum error correction in a single environment, and opens it up to more researchers than ever before. They will use it to develop and validate quantum algorithms, workflows, and applications in an environment built for quantum-centric supercomputing, an emerging paradigm where quantum processors (QPUs), CPUs, and GPUs work together as one system.

IBM says that one promising approach the co-design platform cloud explore is hierarchical error correction. It describes this as using an inner code to protect qubits within a module, while an outer code wraps around the inner code’s logical qubits and adds a second layer of protection.

This approach could reach a trillion logical operations at a physical error rate of one in a thousand, IBM research suggested. These hierarchical codes rely on having powerful classical compute, and the co-design platform will give researchers a place to test and develop those ideas with GPUs in a low-latency environment, the firm states.

The co-design platform is likely to play a key part in the DoE’s Quantum Genesis Mission objectives. These include the recently announced Q Competition, an initiative to deliver a system with 100 logical qubits capable of performing hundreds of millions of fault-tolerant operations. It follows an executive order from President Trump to develop a full-blown quantum system by 2028.®

4c133974387388aa: Elon Musk has hit the brakes on the Cybertruck, announcing on X that Tesla will wind down production at its Texas factory around mid-2027.

Despite years of delays, the stainless-steel turd Musk claimed was a futuristic, apocalypse-proof tank straight out of Blade Runner is headed for a production wind-down after roughly four years, putting the Cybertruck alongside such automotive flops as the Edsel and the DeLorean.
We can’t even put the Cybertruck on the same tier as the Ford Pinto, as that deathtrap was produced for a decade.
The first Cybertruck lumbered off Tesla’s production line in mid-2023 before going on sale later that year, and it was practically right out of the gate that the problems began.

Within months of the first deliveries, recall notices began piling up on the monstrosity. Trim pieces were flying off, internal components were failing, cameras were malfunctioning – all in all, the thing has faced 11 recalls since hitting the road in late 2023, most recently in April 2026, when a defect in brake rotors was found to potentially cause cracks that could allow wheel studs to separate from their hubs.

Musk had pinned a lot of Tesla's hopes on the Cybertruck a few years ago, describing it during the company's Q3 2023 earnings call as "a great product" that would eventually generate "significant positive cash flow" for Tesla.

Musk said on that same earnings call that Tesla intended to ramp Cybertruck production up to 250,000 vehicles per year by 2025 to meet the over one million Cybertruck reservations he claimed Tesla had taken. Some Musk fans may still be waiting for their Cybertrucks, while others may have canceled their reservations after reading early reviews or experiencing the reality of driving such an ugly vehicle associated with a right-wing provocateur. Tesla hasn't disclosed how many reservations were canceled or converted into sales.

Even then, it was widely reported in recent years that unsold Cybertrucks were piling up around the US, with Tesla unable to move them even with repeated price reductions. Tesla has never shared Cybertruck sales numbers, but it’s estimated that only around 70,000 of the things have been sold in the past three years - not exactly a ringing endorsement of its marketability.
So that’s that for the Cybertruck - it’s safe to say it’s been a total disaster for Musk and Tesla. It never sold well, never became a boat, and will likely never be remembered fondly. ®

<!--kg-card-end: html--> Immediately after the UK banned a wide range of porn fantasies involving choking, breath-restriction, and relative roleplay, adult creators watched platforms remove hundreds of their videos — even when the creators thought they were in compliance with the law. These creators say they were blindsided by the removals, since the content didn’t seem to violate the law at all.
Creators are reporting one platform in particular, Clips4Sale, is purging content with little notice, “a precautionary measure.”

Some creators who’ve contacted Clips4Sale to appeal these removals have shared screenshots online of the reply the platform sends: “At this time, we have implemented a general restriction on content availability in the UK to ensure compliance with applicable regulatory requirements,” Clips4Sale support replies, according to these screenshots, viewed by 404 Media. “This is a precautionary measure and does not necessarily indicate that your clips contain prohibited content or violate our policies. We are continuing to review affected content, and additional clips will be made available to UK buyers as they are reviewed and cleared.”
In the UK, Face Sitting Porn Might Land You in Jail
The Crime and Policing Act, which goes into force on November 6, criminalizes possessing or publishing strangulation or suffocation porn, as well as some types of "close familial relatives" roleplay.

Updates to the UK’s Crime and Policing Act went into force on Friday. The law criminalizes a list of sexual acts, including downloading or publishing choking and incest roleplay content. The law is vague and overbroad, criminalizing “strangulation or suffocation” and “certain types” of incest roleplay. There's a lot of confusion among sex workers and fans about what this encompasses, and seemingly could include various kinds of gagging, face sitting, and roleplay. Violating this law, either as someone in possession of noncompliant content or publishing it, carries a risk of up to five years in prison.

UK-based creator Sophia Truee told me that Clips4Sale removed more than 75 percent of her content — 392 out of 506 videos — with the platform flagging it as requiring edits without noting what needed to change. Truee makes POV content where she’s alone talking to the camera. Many more creators have shared on social media that content that shouldn’t be in violation of the law has been caught in the crossfire on Clips4Sale specifically.

In an email sent to creators on Thursday, the day before the law went into force, Clips4Sale said it would be reviewing “both the video content and its details, including titles, tags, keywords, and descriptions” of content that creators have uploaded to the site. It told creators no action was required. “Affected clips will be hidden automatically starting November 6. If you'd like to make a clip available in the UK again, you can edit the content or its details as needed and submit the changes for compliance review.” Approved content would go back up, the company said.

Another message from Clips4Sale on creators’ dashboards said: “As we gain further clarity on the regulatory requirements, we expect to be able to make additional content available again to UK users, wherever permitted. These restrictions apply only to the UK and will not affect your content's availability in other markets where it is permitted.” According to the law, however, if creators based in the UK possess that content, they’re still facing jail time.

“Of course, we were all aware of the new Act coming in and prepared accordingly, but not for anything at this scale. We've had nothing since and they've been tweeting as normal,” Truee said. Clips4Sale launched in 2003 and caters heavily to fetish content. “It's a huge blow to this area of the industry, and I can only hope things will be communicated soon. We, as creators, understand how difficult it is to be a content site in this current climate, but communication has not been prioritized,” Truee said, noting that this is happening right before the holidays, with Black Friday being one of the most popular times for creators selling content. “For many, this will be devastating, as over 20 years of the work will have just been wiped.”

Are you affected by this new UK porn law, as a fan or creator? I would love to hear from you. Using a non-work device, you can message me securely on Signal at sam.404. Otherwise, send me an email at sam@404media.co.

Madame Caramel, another UK-based creator using Clips4Sale, posted on X that out of 900 clips she had available on the platform, she now has 198 left. Another creator, Goddess Kitty, wrote that the platform restricted 931 of her clips from UK audiences. “All of them [had] utterly NOTHING to do with the UK laws,” she wrote. There are many, many more creators across social media reporting that they’ve woken up to their clip sites gutted with no warning, even though their content wasn’t non-compliant by the letter of the law.

With the speed at which content has been purged en masse, and with some creators reporting instant rejections of content that should actually be compliant with the law, Clips4Sale may be auto-moderating with a very wide net, and sifting through reviews creators are now forced to send for legal content. This is something most social media platforms do to try to comply whenever over-broad laws or payment processor regulations hit.

Other platforms are also attempting to comply now that the law is in effect. LoyalFans has a notice on its homepage for fans addressing the new law. It says: “These changes may also apply to content you've purchased, downloaded, or saved privately on your devices. Non-compliant content in your Loyalfans account will be removed on November 5, with no further action required from your side. We encourage you to understand the new law and review any affected content you have downloaded, or stored privately, whether on your phone, computer, or cloud storage.”

LoyalFans updated its terms of use on Thursday to include strangulation or suffocation, in its unacceptable content list, “including any content, whether real or simulated, that explicitly and realistically depicts a person strangling or suffocating another person, such as applying pressure to the neck or obstructing the nose or mouth,” the terms now say. “This content is prohibited regardless of whether the participants consent, and even if it is fantasy-based, roleplay, or digitally created.” Several creators using LoyalFans have posted on social media saying they’ve had hundreds of videos removed from their accounts on that platform, too.

JustForFans, an LGBTQ and kink content site, posted on X earlier this week that creators should review their content and use its new “restrict this content” option to keep it from being viewed by users in the UK. The platform also said that it would be scanning every new video upload for consent requirements and content restrictions. “If we find content that should be restricted in the UK, we will restrict it and you can review it in a new section of your Media Center called Restricted Content. The page will tell you what we found and give you options right on that page to fix it: re-word a post, replace a video with another video, delete the video, or tell us we are wrong, and why you believe we are wrong. A staff member will review your changes,” it said.

“The UK's new pornography restrictions are creating a lot of uncertainty for adult creators, and we want to give our models options rather than simply take away their work. We're reviewing new and old content for potentially restricted material, blocking flagged content from UK viewers and giving models the ability to correct or challenge those decisions. Creators can also restrict individual videos themselves or block access from the UK entirely," JustForFans founder Dominic Ford said in a statement. “The law is nuanced and not particularly well-adapted to gay content. The spirit of the law is about protecting women, but some things don't translate directly to gay culture. For example, 'daddy' is an archetype, not a claim that someone is your actual father, so we're not treating those scenes as automatically prohibited. Our priority is to comply with the law without unnecessarily restricting content elsewhere. We also want models in England and Wales to understand that the law covers possession, not just publication, so they need to take extra precautions.”

The vagueness of the law, combined with the use of auto-moderation on sites like Clips4Sale, have come together to create a nightmare for creators. “This highlights the lack of protection sex workers and content creators have when laws aren't properly researched and clearly written. We do our very best to stay compliant and ensure everyone's safety by following the rules,” Truee said. “This highlights the unprecedented use of AI in moderation and the lack of clear instructions from the government.”

Clips4Sale told 404 Media in a statement: "The UK law carries criminal penalties for possessing or distributing consensual kink and fetish content made by consenting adults, meaning our creators risk arrest if we allow them to distribute banned content in the UK. Unfortunately, there’s no good guidance as to what content might or might not now be illegal. As a result, we’re being aggressive for the time being when it comes to limiting content. We know this is not what creators want, and it’s not what we want. Over the coming weeks, we hope to be able to clear clips that were limited during this precautionary period, after we’ve had a chance to review them more closely. This law is impacting an already marginalized community, mostly women, mostly queer or gender-nonconforming, heavily stigmatized and discriminated against. As with most sex censorship, the burden falls heavily on communities with the least amount of power. We will work with the UK government to comply with the law and our creators to keep them safe."
Updated Friday, November 6 1:03 p.m. EST with comment from Clips4Sale.
Updated 3:08 a.m. EST with comment from JustForFans.

f7bf69c583dfda3d: The US Department of Justice (DoJ) says its Super Intelligence Task Force (SINTF) is now up and running, after president Donald Trump ordered the move in a memo last month.

Headed up by director of national intelligence Jay Clayton, as well as associate attorney general Stanley Woodward and associate deputy attorney general Stephen Weiss, SINTF's responsibility is to protect the US's lead in artificial intelligence development.

Thursday's announcement, which was littered with the "super intelligence" Trumpism, said the task force will ensure the US's SI/AI leadership remains uncompromised by foreign AI "abuse," including by state and state-backed groups, criminal enterprises, individuals, or corporate entities.

Per Trump's October 13 memo [PDF], SITF will take "affirmative measures, as appropriate," to ensure the US stays ahead in AI development. It did not elaborate on what this nebulous phrase meant, but it can be reasonably assumed this means a breadth of proactive steps.

The memo also stated that the task force will organize the DoJ's criminal and civil lawsuits involving AI, recommend enforcement priorities concerning public safety and AI misuse, develop prosecution guidance for unlawful AI conduct, and feed into legislative proposals to prevent "burdensome regulation."
Addressing a Wall Street Journal tech conference this week, Pentagon CTO and SITF vice chair Emil Michael said the team would release details about its AI regulatory landscape later this month.
The task force will also shoulder various cross-departmental responsibilities, such as "deconflicting investigations, cases, and other matters" among departments and the offices of US attorneys.

According to quotes from senior officials, chief among the concerns facing ordinary US citizens are AI attacks that target individuals, as well as those that aim to disrupt critical infrastructure and other national security interests.
"The creation of the DOJ-SITF marks an important moment for the Department to help advance SI technologies and, at the same time, protect American innovation," said Weiss.

"The Department also has a responsibility to utilize law enforcement tools at our disposal to deter improper use of SI, harden regular reporting on SI risk and response, and ensure companies exercise vigorous internal controls so that SI technology behaves as intended. The Department is committed to protecting all Americans and our business interests."

Trump compelled the US to start using the term "super intelligence" in September, claiming "artificial intelligence," the widely used and original term coined in the mid-1950s, was a better descriptor for the technology's capabilities.
The US government's dedicated website for SI states that "America is in a race for Super Intelligence. We intend to win it."
It also highlights a number of initiatives the government has taken to promote its AI supremacy, including legal guidance to streamline federal approvals, leading to more data centers being built.
The pivot toward renaming the technology in all official capacities raised confusion at the time.

A somewhat contradictory move, the Trump administration heavily promotes its own AI innovators, but in one swoop essentially antiquated the trading name of arguably its most recognizable AI lab, OpenAI.

One financier previously floated the idea that Trump ordered the shift to boost the value of .si domain names, many of which have recently been registered using MAGA-related terms and resold for millions of dollars. There is no categorical evidence that the investments are linked to the Trump family, however. ®
1c4079f29568663f: Linux Mint 27 is expected next month, and it's starting to take shape. Its flagship desktop, Cinnamon 2.8, is already available.

The team behind the popular, beginner-friendly Linux just released Cinnamon 2.8, which will be the default desktop in Mint 27. Since 2014, Linux Mint versions have been based on the LTS releases of Ubuntu. Since a new LTS, Ubuntu 26.04 "Resolute Raccoon" arrived in late April, that means that a corresponding version of Mint is in development.

The Mint project blog post last month revealed the codename: "Adrien." This is the first male codename since Mint 1.0 "Ada" in 2006, based on the first ever Ubuntu LTS release, 6.06 "Dapper Drake", but the project has run through the whole alphabet since then (except for the letter “Y”.) That blog also revealed it will have a new alarm clock app, but the subsequent Mint Blog post imparted more information.

The Nemo file manager will gain a preview pane, there will be a new and much more capable system resource-monitor program called "Superlight", a new simple manager for compressed archive files (Zip and so on) called "Unfold," and a new, theme-able terminal emulator called "Velocitty." Mint also has a new Community Website, which uses GitHub to manage logins and eliminates the old website's dependency on PHP.

Probably the most significant new feature, though, is that Mint 27 will restore system hibernation. Ubuntu supported hibernation in its early releases, but it has been disabled as standard since 12.04 "Precise Pangolin." Enabling it again is regularly discussed, for instance back in 2020. As we discussed in some detail a year ago, it's a complicated subject and there's a lot that can go wrong.

It seems that Mint's Clément Lefebvre feels he can sort this, and we hope it works out. Support is included in the new version of Cinnamon, among a host of other changes. Its Wayland support is no longer experimental, although the X11 session is still there so users won't be forced to use the new system. The Network Manager applet has better, simpler VPN support and Wi-Fi encryption handling. There are multiple improvements across the desktop: better handling of sound devices, keyboard input layouts, touchpads and gesture support, HiDPI display handling, and better search in the Settings app. The window list control has been upgraded, more things happen in the background for faster desktop starts, and it has better handling and storage of authentication and credentials, including the same Rust-based "oo7" secret store we mentioned in Fedora 45. Screensaver handling is also mentioned – this is particularly problematic under Wayland, as XScreensaver maintainer Jamie Zawinski has covered with some feeling. The Mint blog mentioned this at the start of 2026, when Lefebvre announced the new, slower, annual release schedule.

Cinnamon is not the only desktop environment that has moved to embrace Wayland while also maintaining its support for X.org. Almost exactly two years ago, we reported that the LXQt 2.1 included preliminary Wayland support. That project is very much still in active development, led by Jen-Lee "PCMan" Hong, and version 2.5.0 just appeared, almost simultaneously with Cinnamon 2.8.

Before LXQt, "PCMan" developed the LXDE desktop – which is still around. There's an LXDE spin of Fedora 45, the Raspberry Pi OS uses some of its components, and last year when Debian 13 was released we also noted that its terminal emulator, LXTerminal, had just been updated. This release of LXQt removes its last dependency on an LXDE component – until now, it still used the old menu-cache.

LXQt 2.5 is based on Qt 6.10, and it draws upon some of the components of KDE Plasma. One of these is libkscreen, which manages screens for Plasma. Version 6.8 of this drops X11 support – as does Plasma 6.8 itself – and that broke LXQt's Monitor Settings applet. The team are looking for a workaround and plan to fix this in a minor point release. Aside from this, the desktop's taskbar-style panel has improved sizing support, icon handling, and auto-hide, but most of the improvements in this release are in around its QTerminal terminal emulator.
New LXQt versions usually appear twice a year, around April and November, so this version will likely be in Lubuntu 27.04 in about five months – and available in many other distributions, too. ®

108211fdc5c43380: New Glenn's return to flight has slipped to January 2027, according to the internal memo, viewed by The Register, from Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp, overshadowing the company's announcements of a new third stage and booster engine.
Blue Origin has been rebuilding after its New Glenn rocket exploded during a ground test in May, extensively damaging the launchpad.

A month later, the company's CEO, Dave Limp, said that Blue Origin "still plan[s] to fly again this year," which raised a few eyebrows in the space and rocket community. The detonation had pretty much destroyed the facility, and getting back into the launch business so quickly seemed optimistic.
That timetable has now slipped. In the memo, Limp praised the team's efforts but said: "We're proactively updating our anticipated launch date to January 2027."
A small slip given the damage, but one that leaves less breathing room before NASA's planned Artemis III demonstration mission, involving lunar technologies from Blue Origin and SpaceX, next year.

The delay emerged as the Bezos-backed company unveiled GS3, a third stage for New Glenn, designed for missions including direct injection into geostationary orbit and Earth-escape trajectories. The company said: "GS3 is already under contract for a cislunar mission with a government customer scheduled to launch in 2028."
Blue Origin says the stage is not required for its lunar lander architecture, although it could support sustained operations around the Moon.
The company also unveiled Northstar, a booster engine it says has half the parts and 30 percent less mass than its BE-4, while increasing thrust from 640,000 to 715,000 pounds-force.

The memo said the team had "found and fixed the issue that caused the anomaly," without elaborating. Limp said in August that the problem "originated at the main oxygen valve on one of the BE-4 engines" and that existing engines would need retrofitting, but did not explain how the valve failed or what changes were required.
The memo added that the company would "continue sharing progress updates on Voyager ." ®

3a8fc5690275a1d0: Millions of hunters will be in fields and wooded areas, where they can help spot and report any signs of screwworm. Michigan Department of Natural ResourcesFor the first time in over 50 years, an infestation of the flesh-eating fly known as the New World screwworm (Cochliomyia hominivorax) is spreading on the U.S. mainland, and it is putting livestock and other animals at risk. The New World screwworm doesn’t just attack cattle. All warm-blooded animals are susceptible, including deer and elk, as well as small game, waterfowl and pets. That means hunters headed to the field this fall may be the most important line of defense for spotting this destructive parasite and keeping it from spreading further. As co-directors of the Mississippi State University deer lab, we believe the country’s millions of hunters can serve as a powerful early warning system by keeping a close eye on the state of wildlife they see. Wildlife agencies are already asking them to be vigilant and report any signs of screwworm infestations. The problem with screwworm Unlike other blowflies, New World screwworm larvae feed on living tissue rather than dead tissue. They lay eggs in open wounds or mucosal openings, such as the eyes and nose of livestock, deer or elk. Screwworm larvae are fairly small but destructive. USDA Screwworm larvae later become flies. USDA Wounds as small as tick bites or scratches, as well as natural openings such as the umbilical stump on newborns or on deer’s pedicles, where their antlers grow and are shed, can attract these parasites. Once the eggs hatch, the maggots burrow into the animal’s flesh and feed, enlarging the wound and attracting more flies. Over time, this leads to infection and death. How the US eradicated screwworm in the past All warm-blooded animals are susceptible to the New World screwworm, but America has seen firsthand the harm they can cause to livestock. In the 1950s, livestock producers in the U.S. Southwest lost up to US$100 million annually to New World screwworm infections, equivalent to over $1 billion today. The New World screwworm fly lays its eggs in fresh wounds, where its larvae hatch and eat the flesh. Judy Gallagher/Wikimedia Commons, CC BY The nation was eventually able to eradicate the New World screwworm from the mainland in 1966 using a combination of treating infected animals and raising hundreds of millions of sterilized male flies and releasing them in infested areas. The New World screwworm has a life cycle of only about 21 days, and each female mates only once. Because of that, inundating areas with sterile male flies for a few months, which equates to a few generations of flies, can eradicate a screwworm population. Historical economic impact estimates of New World screwworm cases in the United States before 2025. USDA 2025 Over time, sterile flies were used to push the New World screwworm further south, where they had been contained behind the Darién Gap, Panama’s narrow border region with Colombia. Sterile flies kept the parasite south of Panama for years, but the movement of cattle and wildlife likely brought it north again. Since 2022, the parasites have been reproducing and moving farther northward. There have been hundreds of detections in Mexico and now in the U.S. The Florida Key deer infestation Wildlife have received far less attention than livestock during screwworm infestations, with one exception: In July 2016, the New World screwworm was detected in the Florida Keys in an endangered deer population: the Florida Key deer (Odocoileus virginianus clavium). Signs of a New World screwworm infestation in an animal’s wound. USDA At the time, the Florida Key deer population was estimated at only about 800 to 1,000 individuals. Because they were endangered and isolated, primarily on the islands of Big Pine Key and No Name Key, they were monitored more closely than most wildlife. U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service biologists established quarantine zones. They inspected more than 16,900 animals – dogs, cats, a pig and a raccoon were also found with larvae – and they released 150 million sterile flies across the area. The islands lost 9% to 20% of the total Key Deer population, but the New World screwworm was declared eradicated there on March 23, 2017, less than a year after it was discovered. Screwworm is back In June 2026, screwworm was back in the United States. A rancher discovered the first New World screwworm case in a calf near La Pryor, Texas. A few more cases were confirmed in livestock and domestic animals in Texas and New Mexico. The number of cases in animals had passed 120 as of Nov. 7, 2026, including in two elk reported by hunters in Texas. The U.S. government has started ramping up production of sterile flies to try to keep the parasites from spreading. The state of Texas encouraged ranchers and others to report any signs of screwworm after the first cases appeared there in 2026. Joel Angel Juarez/Getty Images Although there have been only a couple of cases reported in wildlife, that isn’t necessarily reassuring. Wildlife are far more likely to carry the parasite without being detected. Once the screwworm is detected, treatment would also be much more complicated for wildlife than for livestock, because wildlife cannot be treated individually and thus are more dependent on the use of sterile flies to eradicate screwworm. For this reason, quickly identifying areas with New World screwworm and targeting those areas by releasing sterile flies would be more important than ever. Tapping an army of conservationists: Hunters Fortunately, there is an army of conservationists across the country who spend much of their time afield. These conservationists are also known as hunters. According to the latest U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service National Survey of Fishing, Hunting, and Wildlife-Associated Recreation, nearly 11.5 million hunters pursue big game and spend part of the fall and winter in the field hunting ungulate species such as deer and elk. Hunters can be the first line of defense in tracking screwworm infections in wildlife. Lovz2hike via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA White-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus) hunters alone are expected to harvest about 6 million deer during the 2026-27 season and will observe millions more. Hunters also review tens of millions of wildlife pictures collected each year by game cameras used for scouting. That level of surveillance can’t be matched. New Mexico’s Department of Agriculture has already called on hunters to report any suspicious larvae, particularly in Grant and Otero counties, where screwworm has been found in livestock. Hunters of all kinds, everywhere, can help. What to watch for as a hunter If you’re a hunter, be on the lookout for wounded animals, especially those with visible maggots, and for unusual behaviors such as restlessness, lethargy, or biting or licking wounds. Do not move harvested animals from the field if they show signs of a New World screwworm infection. Doing so could further spread the parasite. Instead, contact the area’s state wildlife agency, the U.S. Department of Agriculture office or a local veterinarian immediately. As hunting seasons get underway across the country, an army of conservationists will be in the field, and they have an important role to play in detecting and managing screwworm’s spread. Hunters already contribute to conservation through license fees, excise taxes and keeping wildlife populations at healthy densities. In the face of New World screwworm, their observations may be most valuable for protecting livestock. This article, originally published Nov. 6, 2026, has been updated with a rising number of cases. 996a31376cbe5e02: I’m not the sort of person who typically pays for a house cleaner. I’m too frugal, and I kind of enjoy putting on a podcast and going to town on my tub with a Magic Eraser. But when I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist. I wanted my apartment to feel like The Jetsons, even if just for an hour.

I was also motivated by journalistic interest. In order to ensure an authentic experience, I didn’t tell Tau Robotics, the startup behind the X post, that I was a journalist—though I did use my real name, so it’s possible someone looked me up. Tau’s long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but they’re not quite there yet: For now, the robots are piloted remotely by humans, who watch what’s going on via cameras mounted in the robots’ heads and wrists. As the robots clean, they collect data that Tau will use to train up their more independent descendants. Every counter successfully wiped and T-shirt successfully folded will help the models that power the robots learn to do better on the next go-round.

Because this data is so valuable to Tau, the company charges less for cleaning than one might expect for such a cutting-edge product. At the time I booked, Tau was offering $30 for an hourlong cleaning with a single robot; now the charge is $60 per weekly cleaning with two robots, or $100 for a one-time visit. But even at the cheaper rate of $30 per hour, Tau’s robots aren’t a great bargain. They are thorough but slow, so if you, like me, are tempted to stand around watching them for their entire visit, it would probably be a better use of your time to just take care of the cleaning yourself.

But the robots are physically capable of cleaning, and they’re undeniably cute. Tau has armed each four-and-a-half-foot-tall robot with a 3D-printed “head” with antennae that allow it to communicate with Tau’s headquarters, as well as two 3D-printed claw “hands” (the more humanlike alternatives apparently aren’t durable enough, and claws do surprisingly well for most cleaning tasks). Mine was wearing a Tau Robotics shirt, and grippy socks so that it didn’t scratch hardwood floors.

With all the human support they need, the robots are closer to radio-controlled cars than Waymos. Many tasks, such as making the bed and folding laundry, require what’s called kinematic guidance: The human pilot performs the necessary motions, and sensors transmit those movements to the robot, which copies them. These kinematically guided tasks produce especially valuable training data. Tau’s AI models might not have solved laundry folding yet, but learning from the examples of robots that have completed the task in the real world is how they’ll get there.

But according to Tau cofounder Cornelia Weinzierl, to whom I came clean as a journalist a few weeks after the cleaning, the robot can already complete some other tasks—such as vacuuming and mopping—without any human help. If Tau succeeds in using all the data it is collecting to train truly autonomous cleaning robots, they could even become San Francisco’s newest tech tourist attraction as Waymos become more commonplace countrywide.

The cleaning robot that came to my building last month was already a bit of a spectacle. It arrived in a blue minivan, out of which it was helped by Weinzierl and another Tau employee. That’s when the robot encountered its first obstacle: the eight stairs leading up to the building’s front door. I’d come down to greet Weinzierl and the robot, so I had a front-row seat to its struggles with my steps. It climbed as if it were drunk. Each successful step was as likely as not to be followed by a stumbling backward stagger that erased all its progress—though, impressively, it never entirely lost its footing.

When I later discussed my experience with Weinzierl, she explained that the robot sometimes walks strangely because it is operated remotely from Tau’s headquarters, and the short signal transmission delay can affect its coordination. “The amount of work and time that we spend just optimizing, for example, timings and connectivity is crazy,” she said.

Inside, the carpeted staircase leading up to my apartment defeated the robot entirely, and Weinzierl had to lug it up the last few steps. This, it turned out, was not typical. As the robot cleaned, it repeatedly stalled out, something Weinzierl attributed to it overheating in the unseasonably hot weather—until she heard from one of her colleagues that the heat had shut down not the robot but the equipment that its human controller was using to watch its progress through my apartment. Without remote assistance, the robot couldn’t clean, and so it, and Weinzierl, departed before my booked hour was up. (Back in September, Weinzierl or another Tau representative remained with the robot throughout its visit, but she says that’s no longer necessary.)

You can’t fault Tau on customer service, though. Weinzierl quickly emailed me to apologize, comp the visit, and offer me another on the house (minus whatever price I assign to my data privacy)—and that was all before I told her I was a journalist. I scheduled the next cleaning for about a month later, after a couple of trips out of town, and it went much more smoothly—the robot got up my stairs without much assistance, though still with the drunken stagger.

In the hour it was there, it did a creditable job of cleaning my kitchen (though it didn’t brave the stove) and even saved me my most dreaded cleaning task, the toilet. That was its most impressive performance: Three times the head fell off its toilet cleaning wand, and three times it managed to reattach it by poking around with the handle until it made contact at just the right angle.

The robot is still rough around the edges, which is to be expected for a product in beta. It repeatedly left my taps dripping, it knocked over a (closed) bottle of olive oil, and it couldn’t manage to right an air purifier that it had toppled. But I easily forgave all those missteps because of how charming it was. As I watched it wipe down my countertops, I felt the same fond gratitude that I feel when a Waymo delivers me safely home after a night out.

Still, it’s not all slapstick and whimsy. If Tau Robotics or its competitors succeeds in training robots to clean autonomously and inexpensively, people could lose their livelihoods, and the United States is a long way away from implementing policies to take care of those left unemployed by AI.

But Weinzierl maintains that someday turning over cleaning work to robots could make a lot of sense. “Cleaning is not a job that a lot of people really actively want to be doing—there’s high turnover, there’s a high risk of injury,” she said when we spoke after the cleanings. “We need people, and we don’t have them, and no one wants to do it.” She said that the company is also starting to consider someday deploying the robots for other dangerous or physically challenging jobs, such as mold remediation and home health care.

Tau Robotics still has a long way to go: The amount of data needed to train robots to do the varied and complicated tasks of apartment cleaning is probably enormous, and the company has completed only a couple hundred cleanings so far. But it’s remarkable that there are now humanoid robots able to clean your toilets and mop your floors, even if they need quite a bit of human help to do so. The Jetsons no longer feels quite so far away.
