<!--kg-card-end: html--> There's a BlazeTV YouTube video whose thumbnail shows the presenter with his arms around Anakin Skywalker and a gender-flipped Draco Malfoy called Malfoid. “Total Chud Victory?” It says. The video's title: “Young Right is Reclaiming Culture and Liberals Are Mad About it.”

BlazeTV posted the video on November 2, the day before Democrats swept the midterms and started a political realignment in America so overwhelming that Republicans lost control of all the most powerful state positions in Texas.

The video is a profound misreading of the political and cultural moment. It reminded me of stories of the Bolsheviks seizing the Winter Palace to discover tarot card playing courtiers who had no idea a revolution was happening in the streets.

<!--kg-card-begin: html--> <!--kg-card-end: html--> The American version was watching defense contractor Palmer Lucky dress up like Harry Potter on Halloween while standing next to his Malfoid wife. And it was Elon Musk — who spent roughly half a billion on the election only to see his chosen candidates fail — posting an AI generated picture of Anakin Skywalker sitting at the head of a happy fascist Star Wars family two days before the midterms.
This is what they stole from us pic.twitter.com/q1GnpjF394
— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 1, 2026

The online right has dominated American culture for a decade, or at least has dominated political narratives picked up by the mainstream media. Its memes and conspiracies drove news cycles. At first, the right’s memes filtered from random people on obscure Discord channels to Reddit’s r/the_donald or 4chan to Trump’s Twitter feed. More recently they’ve come from AI slop farms, from Musk, or from the administration itself. Powered by a well-funded media and podcast ecosystem, Fox News (and a propensity for shamelessness) its comedians, podcasters, and pundits became powerful celebrities and influencers, at least within Elon Musk’s X.

This insular, often inscrutable world has given us Ben Shapiro, Nick Fuentes, Gamergate influencers, the streamer Asmongold, and a revolving door of characters who have shuffled interchangeably between Twitterverse celebritydom and actual government; Kash Patel, DataRepublican, Laura Loomer, Pete Hegseth, RFK Jr., Dan Bongino, the list goes on.

It has been said many times that “Twitter is not real life,” and that posting too much anywhere will rot your brain. Never has that been more apparent than now: Much of Trumpworld spent the week before an election in which they would get utterly trounced using AI to generate barely legible Anakin and Malfoid memes for an inconsequential ingroup on the social media platform run by the biggest loser on the planet.

“It certainly seems like it has had its high water mark and that reality has FINALLY caught up with the Republican Party,” Michael Senters, a PhD candidate at Virginia Tech who studies online and gaming culture, told 404 Media.

In 2016, 4chan posters talked about “meme magic” — the pseudo-ironic belief that pictures on the internet could manifest great change in reality. According to legend, Trump strategist Steve Bannon was running a World of Warcraft gold farm when he realized the angry gamers could be harnessed into a powerful reactionary political force. Bannon and others would successfully parlay Gamergate into an endless culture war that’s dominated online life in the Trump era.

During the midterm livestream of Bannon’s War Room podcast, his guest read exit polls that suggested the right-wing had lost young men — a group long thought to be its strongest soldiers. The split between the parties was even, the guest explained. “That can’t be right,” Bannon whispered, signalling he’d lost touch with the constituency he’d harnessed on behalf of Trump ten years ago. As the election results began coming in, right-wing podcasters, livestreamers, and newscasters across the internet went through at least a few of the stages of grief. First they struggled to understand what was happening, suggesting the votes must be wrong. Eventually, many of them ragequit.

"Okay, I'm going to be honest. I'm absolutely rage quitting. I'm so frustrated. I am so unbelievably frustrated. I'm so mad. I think Trump didn't do 50 different things he should have done. I think he should have gone a thousand times harder. I think that he wasted his time selling trinkets and nonsense,” Asmongold said as the returns came in. He lives in Texas where Democrats swept in a shock victory.

“I wish that there were more people who thought like me that weren’t sorry about it. But you know what? There’s not. So it’s just me. And that’s fine. It’s fine. It’s OK,” he said, his voice catching in his throat.

Asmongold (@Asmongold) realizing in real time that he's a total fucking moron who got duped by the most cartoonishly obvious con-man of all time and ragequitting his election night coverage pic.twitter.com/XgtnqNjAaf
— kilo (@kilotonics) November 4, 2026

Many right-wing personalities went into Tuesday somehow expecting to win despite a disastrous war, a disastrous economy, disastrous polls, and a doddering president whose closing argument seemed to be more about his ballrooms, golf courses, and the Reflecting Pool than anything else. Since Trump was re-elected, these same people have called everyone else out of touch, convinced by their X algorithm and prediction markets that no blue wave would materialize. The media has similarly spent many thousands of words suggesting that Bluesky is an out-of-touch leftist echo chamber while mostly failing to suggest anything of the sort about the AI-pilled Silicon Valley executives, bots, and racists shitposting on X. Tuesday’s election wipeout highlights how detached from reality the Malfoid/Anakin-shipping, X-brained billionaires and their acolytes have actually become.

“Blueskywave. Those of us on here, across the board, were out of touch. I see no other conclusion,” Joe Weisenthal of Bloomberg's Odd Lots podcast (who is a serious, good journalist), said in a post on X after the election amidst a sea of Anakins tonguing Malfoids.
"I see through the lies of the Democrats."
VOTE STRAIGHT TICKET REPUBLICAN pic.twitter.com/i1HjdHdAn7
— Utah College Republicans (@UtahCollegeReps) November 1, 2026

The meme game and general demeanor of Trump and his followers has grown wildly tiresome in his thus far-disastrous second term. Under the guidance of White House Communications Director Steven Cheung, official government accounts have posted racist Halo memes, used AI to put a studio Ghibli face on anti-immigrant propaganda, and fully embraced Malfoid and Darth Vader as cultural heroes. The base on X loved this stuff. No one else did.

As our friend Gita Jackson over at Aftermath wisely put it immediately before the election, "The idea that they can meme magic their way into a red sweep by posting about Anakin Skywalker a lot is pure desperation [...] Their values have been rejected by popular culture at large, and they are now resigned to exist in the margins.”

Senters said the midterms showed the hard limits of memes as a political tool. “The power that memes have has always been, in my opinion, the power to help define linguistic and community lines in the amorphous space of the Internet. You create a community when you ‘get the joke’ behind a meme but memes generally don't persuade,” he said. “I'll be curious to see if the government accounts will continue to post these far-right cultural memes in the wake of the defeat or if they'll change their tune at all. Like do they double down on the meme posting to try to rally their base? Because it very clearly had ZERO appeal to anyone outside their base.”

Yet the right-wing has spent the last ten years acting as if their memes had moved the country politically. “They deluded themselves into believing that memes carry persuasive power and that their bubble on X represented material reality in a meaningful way when that was no way close to the truth,” he said. “They saw how many ‘numbers’ the Malfoid and Anakin memes did on X and convinced themselves that this was a real cultural awakening moment and that the volk were on their side.”
It cannot be overstated how culturally significant Anakin poasting is. I dont think you could engineer a better anti-progressive memetic virus in lab if you tried.
— Max (@minordissent) October 31, 2026

Alyssa Mercante, an internet culture reporter who is writing a book about politics and video games called Rage Game, agreed. “I think what it's really showing is that when you start to get a little bit too deep in the weeds of this hyper online culture war stuff, it cannot escape the internet,” Mercante told 404 Media. “It is not working anymore. The material reality of America is just not good enough.” Gas prices are up. Everything is more expensive. And ICE has killed Americans in the streets.

“This conspiratorial mindset is wrecker mentality. It is just destructive for the sake of destruction. There is no goal beyond pulling away any sort of legitimacy from the media or from democracy,” Mercante said. “When you get so deep in the weeds of this anti-establishment conspiratorial thought process, you just can't make anything or do anything of value. You're just upending tables and pointing at them and laughing.”

Democrats crushed Republicans who leaned into the online culture war during the midterms. Bo French — an overt racist who ran for railroad commissioner in Texas — sent text messages to voters that depicted himself as Master Chief from Halo. His opponent beat him by more than a million votes.

In Nevada, Halo composer Martin O’Donnell ran as a Republican for a House seat and lost to incumbent Susie Lee. O’Donnell announced his campaign on Discord and leaned hard into an extremely online gamer identity. “He’s like, ‘I wrote the Halo music and I’m voting for Trump and you should too.’ He did a Halo LAN party campaign fundraiser. The imagery was him as Master Chief,” Mercante said. “This dude is like: ‘My personality is gamers, gamers are not woke and they're resisting this [...] and Trump is the person that is going to help us resist,’ and he's polling like absolute dog water.”

It’s been 12 years since Gamergate set the tempo for online culture wars and a decade since Trump won in 2016. In 2026, Star Wars, Halo, Harry Potter feel dated in a way they didn’t back then. “What 22-year-old kid is going to be like ‘they took Halo from me.’ They don’t know Halo to have it taken away from them,” Mercante said.

She stressed that so much right wing online culture is about distraction — she likened it to jingling keys to capture the attention of a baby. “If the economy is the number one issue for both Democrats and Republicans going into the midterms, no amount of Malfoid scissoring Anakin Skywalker is going to change that need for people to be in a better financial position,” Mercante said. “The tech oligarchs pushed this stuff straight into our eyes for two years straight unfettered [...] And I wake up and gas is this expensive? I don’t care if you take a Taylor Swift song and make JD Vance walk out to it.”

“[They] really thought that this would just last forever,” she added. “When you build up a meme presidency, eventually the cards just collapse underneath you, and there's just nothing to show for it.”

Though this midterm signals a move away from Gamergate-style culture war politics, both Senters and Mercante cautioned that this type of rhetoric is still dangerous, and can still be destructive. “They’re still very good at doing propaganda on the internet — they wrote the book in many cases,” Mercante said.

23d2c05a48e2b2f0: When a human picks up a coffee cup, we use predictive processing based on our understanding of the world. For a robot, picking up a cup requires extensive training and simulation. (Unsplash)Today’s artificial intelligence technologies have become remarkably good at generating text and ideas that seem profoundly human. Chatbots powered by large language models such as ChatGPT, Claude, Google Gemini and Perplexity AI can write poems, brainstorm and find solutions to complex problems. The developers of these products drew heavily on the human brain for inspiration, creating artificial neural networks based on the workings of human neurons. Their systems now produce outputs that often resemble the outputs of human thinking. AI and the human mind, however, do not work the same way. Similar results do not necessarily mean similar processes. “World models” are an emerging technology that could help AI systems move closer to human “thinking” by helping them learn to anticipate what might happen and use that prediction to act. Still, AI will not perceive, learn or understand the world as humanity does. Read more: Cyber attacks? Bioterrorism? To ‘Pace the Frontier’ of AI effectively, we must improve our anticipatory thinking A falling cup, a complex prediction Imagine reaching for a cup at the edge of a counter. The cup may fall and smash if you misjudge the distance, grip it too loosely or move too quickly. For humans, grabbing a cup like this is routine. Yet this simple action relies on the complex ability to anticipate what might happen next. Our minds constantly try to stay one step ahead by understanding events and their causes. We can foresee the mess that would result from moving an overfilled cup or imagine a sofa getting stuck in a doorway even before we buy it. These predictions draw on expectations that form when we interact with the world. What we anticipate can, in turn, impact how we perceive the world and how we act. One influential family of theories, known as predictive processing, proposes that perception works partly in this way. The brain generates expectations, compares them to the information it receives and makes adjustments when the two don’t match. Let’s return to the example of the cup. Imagine reaching for an empty cup that you believe to be full. Your hand, expecting a heavier object, lifts it with more force than necessary. The cup rises abruptly and feels almost weightless. That mismatch provides feedback that helps correct the movement and update your estimate of its weight. What we anticipate shapes our actions, and what happens next updates our expectations. All this happens just to pick up a cup. Does AI predict differently? Even for today’s robots, reliably manipulating cups can require extensive training and simulation. The challenge involves learning how the physical world behaves and predicting the consequences of an action. Chatbots using large language models also make predictions, but of a different kind. They learn to predict the next word or fragment of text. This apparently simple way of predicting can nevertheless produce remarkably capable systems able to solve complex problems. Take the sentence: “A hand bumps a cup near the edge of a table. The cup…” Having learned patterns from enormous amounts of data, a chatbot might continue with “tips over the edge and falls to the floor.” It can do so by predicting patterns from a dataset and without ever physically handling a cup. However, being able to describe plausible outcomes does not necessarily mean a chatbot has learned why they happen. Teaching a robot to anticipate This is where world models kick in — a broad family of AI approaches that aim to predict how situations evolve and, in some cases, how actions may change them. These models can learn from videos, simulations or recordings of what robots see and do. For a domestic robot, this could mean anticipating that gripping too tightly might break the cup, or that a wrong movement could tip it over. By incorporating actions, motion and sensory information, preliminary research shows these systems can help connect predictions with what happens in the physical world. A world model could eventually make the same predictions we do about a cup. And as it learns from actions and sensory feedback, the resemblance to us may become increasingly hard to ignore. Still, arriving at the same prediction does not tell us what knowledge supports it or how that knowledge was acquired. Same prediction, same cognition? To us, a cup is not only a cylinder on a table. It can be graspable, breakable, yours, mine, too hot or almost falling. Our understanding connects the cup’s physical properties to a network of possible actions and consequences. Predicting that the cup will fall reveals only a small part of that understanding. And this understanding develops quite early. Studies suggest that infants just a few months old already have basic expectations about how physical objects behave. Child-development researcher Jean Piaget proposed that children build knowledge through acting on the world. As this knowledge develops, they become able to mentally anticipate consequences without having to carry out each action. For humans, learning involves more than accumulating information about cups. It involves connecting experiences when reaching for one, feeling its weight, seeing it spill and eventually imagining what might happen without even having to try it. Using world models, AI can also learn from actions and sensory feedback, in addition to videos, simulations and other data. Like humans, they can learn to interact with the world. The question is how their experiences contribute to the knowledge they build and use. AI could definitely come closer to anticipating what might happen and using that prediction to act. This alone, however, does not show that AI perceives, learns or understands the world as we do. As AI gets better at replicating the results of human cognition, distinguishing performance from process will only become more important. 90ee2db57b22d50a: The US midterm elections have shifted the balance of power in Congress, delivering a massive blow to Donald Trump and his Republican party. This has implications both at home and possibly abroad, including for US policy towards Ukraine; an issue that was hardly mentioned during the campaigns. But even if Ukraine did not figure much in the election, the question in US politics of what to do about the war has not gone away. Indeed, in the weeks and months before the result was announced, Trump had been busily rowing back on US support for Ukraine. This was despite much opposition, even from some Republicans. Crucial intelligence to Kyiv about Russian strikes was cut off, before later being reinstated, while critical military aid was reduced. Trump also decided to suspend several sanctions on Russia. This move was denounced by President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine as only helping Russia, but justified by Trump as being “in the national interests of the United States” and also a decision that might help his party’s electoral chances by reducing gas prices. In the end, none of this helped Trump and the Republicans. Yet few commentators believe that the midterm results, disastrous though they have been for Trump, will have very much impact on his foreign policy outlook and his policy towards Ukraine in particular. “The Trump administration’s foreign policy is like a car going down the highway,” said James Green, a research fellow at the Centre for European Reform and former Congressional aide in Washington, recently. “Congress has the ability to slow that car down, maybe make it put on a turn signal, but it’s going to be very difficult for Congress to change the overall route over the next two years.” In part, this has to do with how foreign policy is determined in the US. Congress is not without some influence. It can hold hearings, subpoena executive branch officials, as well as exercise control over the purse. Yet as commander-in-chief and head of state with a vast foreign policy bureaucracy supporting him, the president retains significant foreign policy powers. The Democrats are also unlikely to make Ukraine front and centre after the midterms. They will have other more important fish to fry, the most critical being how to make sure they come up with a candidate and programme that will win them the White House in 2028. Yet Ukraine is a cause which many Democrats and quite a few Republicans have championed for some time. Nor are they likely to forget what ordinary Americans think about Russia and its leader, Vladimir Putin. The war in Ukraine may not be something they think about on a daily basis. On the other hand, as the Pew Research Center showed in 2025, 67% of Americans distrust Putin while six in ten view Russia as an enemy. Democrats may not wish to become embroiled in a European war. But having just scored a sweeping landslide victory, they may well calculate there is a good deal of political mileage to be had now in escalating their attack on a weakened Trump if his foreign policy towards Russia and Ukraine continues in their view to reward an aggressor while making the victim of that aggression look like an obstacle to a settlement. Pushing for a peace deal? If the midterms result presents a series of opportunities for the Democrats, while posing a challenge to Trump, it also presents Putin with a possible opportunity. The Russian leader may well try and exploit Trump’s domestic position by offering some kind of settlement that would allow the US president to claim a victory. US, Chinese and Russian officials have already been holding talks about a summit when the heads of state travel to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit later in November. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov has said Russia hopes to finalise the meeting in the coming days. Trump is similarly keen on such a meeting. He told reporters in October that Ukraine would be discussed at the meeting, adding: “I would meet in order – anything I can do to end the war, whether somebody is there or not, whatever I can do to end the war.” This might sound reasonable enough. However, deciding the fate of a sovereign country which won’t be at the negotiating table, and coming to some kind of “great power” deal with two authoritarian countries that involves Ukraine losing 20% of its territory, is almost certainly something an emboldened Democratic party in Congress will not take lying down. Nor, according to most military experts, would it be wise to concede anything to Russia when its war against Ukraine appears to have run into the ground. According to the Institute for the Study of War, Russia may have “secured a temporary advantage in the skies over Ukraine through their jet-powered drones and the shortage of Patriot missiles that can intercept their ballistic missiles”. But as the institute also points out, unless western military aid dries up entirely, a Russian victory is by no means inevitable. A war that most experts, including the CIA, predicted would be over in a matter of months is thus likely to go on. Trump is unlikely to change his mind about Russia and Ukraine. Russia in his mind’s eye will continue to be regarded as a potential partner, and Ukraine a country that has taken assistance from the US and given “absolutely nothing back except grief”. But now, with his back to the wall politically and the Democrats in charge of Congress in a country that has just passed a decisive verdict on his presidency, shaping his own agenda in relation to Russia and Ukraine is likely to prove more difficult. Michael Cox was a founding director of LSE IDEAS and is an associate fellow at Chatham House.
c2cc4bd675b22592: Québec’s flagship sovereignist party, the Parti Québecois (PQ), formed a minority government in the recent provincial election. The party essentially rose from the dead after a 12-year absence, dethroning the right-wing nationalist — but not separatist — Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ). For Canadians, the PQ is typically associated with sovereignty referendums. Yet, despite the PQ victory, estimates place Québecois support for sovereignty at between 27 and 31 per cent, a far cry from the 49.42 per cent who voted to separate in the 1995 referendum. This figure aligns somewhat with the popular vote received by the PQ, which, at 28 per cent, is the lowest popular vote share of a sitting government in the history of the province. The PQ’s victory therefore should be understood in light of three factors: low public support for the PQ and for separatism, Indigenous resistance to Québec independence and a global context where statehood doesn’t necessarily shield against interference or expand diplomatic leverage. Lukewarm mood on independence The combination of Québec’s multi-party system and its “first-past-the-post” electoral system means governments are often formed on less than a majority of the popular vote. In six elections between 2007–2022, an average of 53.9 per cent of votes failed to translate into seats, according to electoral expert Mercédez Roberge. This explains how the separatist PQ was able to form government despite the measured lack of enthusiasm for separatism in the province. In fact, even leaving room for the possibility that leftist Québec Solidaire supporters also support independence (though the party does not necessarily prioritize it), a combination of the popular votes earned by parties that explicitly do not support independence suggests that 58.24 per cent of the electorate don’t want to separate from Canada. PQ leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon’s statements following his party’s victory reflects a generally lukewarm mood towards independence in the province. During his campaign, Plamondon mitigated his promise to hold a referendum during his first term by stating it wouldn’t be held while Donald Trump remained president of the United States. In the meantime, Plamondon has prioritized housing and cost of living issues, and has signalled to the English-speaking community that “we’re all in the same boat.” Plamondon’s prudence is paired with various assertions of Québec autonomy. In his first month as premier, he’s antagonized the federal government by skipping the recent Canada-European Union summit. Under the CAQ, antagonism was more often directed at Québec’s increasingly ethnically and religiously diverse population. Without dropping this inward-facing orientation to nation-building, the PQ’s swipes at Ottawa suggests it will return to stoking more familiar Québec-Ottawa tensions. But in a country with longstanding debates about provincial autonomy, none of this is new or indicative of separatist sentiments. The recent PQ victory is more akin to detecting a faint pulse in a terminally ill patient than a spectacular jolt back to life. Read more: Unruly provinces? That’s what the Fathers of Confederation expected — and planned for Changed scene from 1995 The PQ has formed a government in a situation different from 1995. Domestically, First Nations have increasingly affirmed their place in Canada’s tapestry. In 1996, the Royal Commission on Aboriginal Peoples published its five-volume, 4,000-page report making 440 recommendations. Among them were recognizing Indigenous Peoples as self-governing nations and creating Indigenous institutions, including an Indigenous parliament. Montréal riot police watch a fire burn underneath a Oui sign after the No side won the Québec referendum in October 1995. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Tom Hansen In 2015, the Truth and Reconciliation Commission published its final report, which included 94 calls to action to address the harms of the residential school system and advance reconciliation across areas that include child welfare, education, health, justice and culture. The following year, Canada officially adopted the United Nations Declaration for the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. The document became federal law in 2021. Finally, since 1995, at least 19 modern treaties have been concluded or come into effect. It would be misleading to claim, however, that the relationship between Canadian governments and Indigenous nations has radically changed in the last 30 years. Plamondon’s absence from the First Nations-First Ministers meeting recently held in Ottawa is an example. Québec’s minister responsible for relations with First Nations and Inuit wrote that the premier’s absence was aimed at prioritizing direct nation-to-nation meetings with Indigenous nations on “notre territoire (‘our territory.’)” This phrasing takes Québec’s territorial sovereignty as a given, treating it as a non-negotiable precondition that other nations must accept before dialogue can even begin. By prioritizing provincial self-determination, it implicitly subordinates Indigenous sovereignty. Claiming these talks are “nation-to-nation” rings hollow when one party unilaterally dictates the terms of engagement. The premier’s decision to skip the meeting was criticized by the Assembly of First Nations of Québec and Labrador (AFNQL) and the Native Women’s Shelter of Montréal, who wanted Québec to be at the table in Ottawa. Plamondon would do well to remember that in 1995, multiple First Nations within Québec’s boundaries refused forcible inclusion into a new independent state, notably those whose rivers provide the bulk of the province’s hydroelectricity. Modern risks of independent statehood Internationally, separatist sentiments today have more to do with populism than with the decolonization efforts that played out in the second half of the 20th century. In a climate of survival-of-the-fittest foreign policy, sovereignty in the form of an independent state does not guarantee the same freedoms or capacities it might have in 1980 and 1995. As U.K. political scientist Michael Keating suggests, self-determination is no longer fixed to a single people or territory. Nations today are largely regarded as contested constructs, and territories are multi-layered with various cultural and ethnic populations. Additionally, sovereignty doesn’t shield a state from the decisions of another, as recent American tariff policies are showing Canadians all too well. Read more: 3 ways Canada can navigate an increasingly erratic and belligerent United States Keating’s argument aligns with Indigenous political theories of relational autonomy: today sovereignty is experienced less as something a nation possesses and more as a continuously negotiated relationship. American threats to Canadian sovereignty and Greenland’s self-determination suggests that secession would not necessarily improve upon Québec’s ability to negotiate its position within the broader international order. In short, in a world where even the U.S., a superpower for decades, is experiencing the costs of fractured relationships, a convincing pitch for Québec separatism would have to take into account similar costs. The pulse of Québec separatism persists, though the body sustaining it is weighed down by internal fractures and a punishing political landscape. 030f04b0abd3fc88: When European Union officials Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa recently joined Mark Carney on the docks of Montréal’s Old Port for the Canada-EU Summit, Canada’s prime minister presented closer ties with the EU as a good deal for Canadian households. He argued a closer relationship promised more choices and lower costs for families at a time when American tariffs are causing pain on both sides of the Atlantic. In April 2025, my colleague, Léandre Benoit, and I argued that the newly elected Carney would pursue a pragmatic and globally engaged liberalism, definitively aligned with Europe. The Montréal summit confirms that alignment. The meeting’s firmest commitments concern democracy, while much of its economic measures are still to be carried out. With autocracies gaining ground around the world, and with Trump’s United States no longer a reliable ally — although that may shift with the Democratic rout in the U.S. midterm elections — Canada and the EU have found in each other stable liberal partners who take democracy seriously. Read more: What Liberal Mark Carney’s election win in Canada means for Europe What Montréal delivered On the economic side, the results of the summit are quite modest. Of the 20 measures announced, two are concluded agreements: one is a digital trade agreement and the second is a treaty that lets the European Investment Bank finance Canadian critical minerals projects. The remaining measures are promises to be negotiated, for example on the Erasmus+ education program and on LNG exports. For a summit sold as offering relief for household budgets, few of these announcements will have an impact on Canadian kitchen tables any time soon. Left out of the final statement was the most ambitious and symbolic proposal: Carney set June 2027 as the deadline for Canada to become the European Union’s first “associate member,” a category that exists nowhere in EU law. Read more: What Canada could gain from joining the EU’s Erasmus+ program, and what’s unresolved Allies in defending democracy The associate membership process is driven by shared values. Canada, one of the few established democracies to have avoided democratic backsliding, has strong institutions where no reforms are needed before it qualifies to be a partner of the EU. Even though the details of associate membership are still unclear, the partnership’s significance is in “elective affinity,” as Carney had set out in Strasbourg in September when addressing the European Parliament. So far, security and defence are where these shared values have produced concrete results. The joint statement warns that hybrid threats now target Canadian and European institutions, and it promises an early-warning system against foreign interference and disinformation. This is a clear acknowledgement that Russian aggression goes beyond Ukraine and that defending democracy has become a matter of national security. In the current global context where holding states accountable via international bodies is under threat — for example, the recent American sanction of the International Criminal Court — both the EU and Canada need each other more than ever in protecting their liberal values and their security. The joint statement stretches Canada’s commitment along Europe’s whole eastern flank through the EU Common Security and Defence Policy, from the Arctic to the Black Sea, and frames it as a reinforcement of NATO. Beyond the balance sheet While a Canada Pulse Insights poll found that 73 per cent of Canadians support the idea of closer ties with the EU, the status of “associate member” is a problem in Europe. Germany and several other member states oppose the label. At home, Conservatives argue that the summit produced zero tariff removals or trade-barrier eliminations, and they’ve also raised concerns about what the agreement would mean for Canada’s independence and sovereignty. Judged on tariffs alone, the critics might have a point — after all, the EU cannot undo U.S.-imposed trade penalties. Diversifying away from Canada’s top trading partner demands both political will and time. In the meantime, the summit’s true value lies in the political message it sends. By offering a country outside Europe a place close to its family, the EU is saying that being European is as much a matter of values as of geography. If the process works, it could become a model for other partners outside Europe. For Canada, the membership would make clear to the U.S. and Canadian voters that the country has other partners and options beyond its southern neighbour. The Montréal summit gave Canada a safe harbour on the other side of the Atlantic. What holds the two partners together is a shared conviction that democracies must stand together as autocracies gain ground, beyond trade deals. By June 2027, we’ll know whether that conviction survives the doubts of some European capitals and whether Canada becomes the EU’s first associate member in name as well as in spirit. a85f9b6a75e39be3: The DRC is in the seventh month of an Ebola outbreak. AP Photo/Sebastien Kitsa MusayiI visited a family of 19 in Sierra Leone in 2015. By the time I arrived, eight had died. The other 11 were left to live with the grief and fear of what might happen next. I am a medical doctor and epidemiologist, and at that time I was serving on an African Union Ebola response mission. The 2014-16 epidemic in West Africa caused more than 28,600 cases and 11,300 deaths. Over roughly six months in Sierra Leone, I saw how quickly the disease could overwhelm families and health services. That’s also when I learned that good medical advice can fail if people do not trust those delivering it. Some families buried relatives secretly, despite warnings. In certain communities, funeral practices included washing the body and sprinkling water on mourners, which risked exposing people to infected bodily fluids. Simply repeating instructions did not help. But those of us working in the field found that working with families to make burials safer while respecting their grief helped them to mourn their loss while stopping the virus from spreading. More than a decade later, those experiences have returned to my mind. The Ebola outbreak now sweeping across parts of Central Africa is different from the one I responded to. Still, one lesson remains: Timely international support makes a huge difference. A growing outbreak The current outbreak was declared in the Democratic Republic of Congo, or DRC, in May 2026. By Oct. 28, 2026, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported 10,305 confirmed cases and 4,996 deaths across five countries, with new updates daily. The DRC accounts for nearly all of those cases and deaths. This is already the second-largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded, after the 2014-16 epidemic. The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, whereas the 2014-16 epidemic involved a different Ebola virus. No vaccine or specific treatment is currently approved for Bundibugyo. The World Health Organization warns that late detection, deaths outside health facilities and sustained transmission in the DRC remain serious concerns. The DRC has extensive experience with responding to outbreaks, and African institutions are coordinating a continental response. Africa has the expertise and leadership. What it needs right now is sustained support that reaches the front line – quickly, safely and accountably. Crossing borders Ebola follows human movement. In October, Kenya reported infections linked to a traveler who had passed through Uganda from the DRC. Nigeria also reported an imported case around the same time. Symptoms can appear between two and 21 days after exposure, and people are generally not infectious before symptoms begin. A traveler may therefore pass a temperature check and become ill days later. These events show why countries need to share information quickly, verify travel histories and maintain contact tracing across borders. In response to the 2014 Ebola outbreak, American healthcare workers set up makeshift clinics like this one outside Monrovia, Liberia. Abbas Dulleh/AP What international support looks like now International partners are, in fact, contributing. In September 2026, the United States reported US$887 million in Ebola-related health and humanitarian assistance. The U.K. announced a contribution of roughly £78 million ($104 million). In October, the World Bank described $426.6 million in current and planned financing for the DRC and neighboring countries. And Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention reported nearly $3 billion in international pledges following a September mobilization effort. But pledges are not the same as supplies delivered or services provided, and these contributions are coming late in the outbreak. In 2014, Britain helped expand treatment and safe-burial operations in Sierra Leone. The U.S. mobilized logistics capacity in Liberia, while France assisted Guinea. And African Union health workers served alongside local teams and other partners. That cooperation saved lives, though the global response was slow to scale up. It has been discouraging for me to see that today’s response has not built on that experience without waiting for the outbreak to grow further. According to the WHO, massive cuts to international aid over the past year diminished a quicker response. The success of international collaboration will be measured in how many contacts are reached, how rapidly patients are tested, how many health workers have protective equipment and are consistently paid, whether women can still deliver babies safely, and whether remote communities can get care. Building connections with everyday people My experience in Sierra Leone in 2014 taught me that trust is essential to outbreak control. Families need credible explanations, timely information and opportunities to ask questions. Local health workers, faith leaders, survivors and community organizations can help bridge the gap between an emergency response and the people it seeks to protect. That gap can be large even when a disease is widely known. A colleague and I conducted a study involving 440 secondary school students in Nigeria in 2014, and we found that 95.4% had heard of Ebola. Yet only 42.3% identified fever as a possible symptom, and only 33.2% recognized the risk associated with certain burial practices. Seeing that awareness of the disease alone was not enough, we subsequently began Ebola education activities in local Nigerian schools. The need for reliable information from trusted sources remains in 2026. Risk messages must be consistent, culturally sensitive and practical. This works only when communities are partners in recognizing illness, seeking early care, contact follow-up and safe, dignified burials. Even in times of emergency, health workers cannot treat communities simply as audiences for instructions. Reaching affected communities In August 2026, Africa CDC and the WHO jointly called for expanded laboratory and treatment capacity and faster delivery of supplies. But in the DRC, insecurity and displacement due to ongoing conflict, in addition to poor roads, can prevent supplies and patients from reaching treatment centers. These obstacles may also keep laboratories from receiving samples and contact-tracing teams from visiting households. The ministry of health is not equipped to resolve these problems. The response therefore requires cooperation among health authorities, humanitarian agencies, local government, transport services and those responsible for civilian safety. There are signs that investments in these services are helping. In October, the World Bank reported that supported detection timelines in the DRC had improved. This meant new cases were being detected within one or two days by September, a huge improvement from the 10-day detection timeline early in the outbreak. The Tumaini vaccine trials started in the DRC at the end of October 2026. ‘Tumaini’ is the Swahili word for hope. AP Photo/Dieudonne Dirole Looking to the future Because Bundibugyo virus lacks an approved vaccine or specific treatment, this outbreak also demands carefully conducted research. The Tumaini vaccine trial, begun in Bunia, DRC, in October 2026, is an important step toward a potential vaccine. The hope is that this effort will prevent more families from experiencing loss. I still remember the 11 survivors in that Sierra Leone household I visited back in 2015. I never learned what ultimately happened to them, but more than a decade later, I still think about them. Olayinka Stephen Ilesanmi was the past West Africa Regional Program Lead for Africa CDC.

d3e82c516963b892: From Hartini Zainudin
I am dismayed! I read an FMT report about a young man and his biological father who lost their citizenship case.

A Malaysian father went to the Kota Bharu High Court with a DNA report from our own chemistry department proving the young man beside him is his son. To add insult to injury, he left with an order to pay the government RM4,000!
The son was born in Golok in June 2006 and was carried across the border at three months old. He has lived here for 20 years. He has no birth certificate and no nationality anywhere in the world.
The court ruled that because his parents could not prove they were married when he was born, the law must look past his Malaysian father entirely and treat him as the child of his Thai mother alone.
I read the news report and I am still angry; it is outrageous.

In fairness to the judicial commissioner, he applied the law as it stands. Section 17 of Part III of the Second Schedule of the Federal Constitution states that for a child born out of wedlock, any reference to the father is read as a reference to the mother.
The Federal Court confirmed this in the 2021 landmark case CTEB & Anor v Ketua Pengarah Pendaftaran Negara, on almost identical facts: a Malaysian father, a Thai mother, no registered marriage.
Citizenship by operation of law is fixed at the moment of birth, and nothing that happens afterwards can change it.
So the fault lies with the law, and with those of us who have left it standing. Whatever its purpose in 1957, the rule now overrides a laboratory result that settles paternity beyond doubt.
Our own government chemist confirmed who this boy's father is. Our own constitution then told the court to ignore him.

I have spent close to 20 years recovering abandoned babies, sitting with young mothers once they are traced, and working with children in detention. I know how a birth goes unregistered. The clinic across the border is closer. The couple married in a religious ceremony and never registered it. Someone told the father the paperwork would cost money he did not have, or get him into trouble. The child made none of these choices ... none!

The child carries the consequences for life anyway. No identity card, no exam certificate in his own name, no legal job, no passport, no registered marriage. When he has children of his own, the problem passes to them. Statelessness is inherited. How is what’s happening to him his fault?

This is far from a rare case. The national registration department (JPN) registered 542,363 births of children born out of wedlock between 2006 and June 2017, the most recent national figure on record.
We have no count of how many have a Malaysian father who wants to claim them. The law has never asked.

The court says this young man should look to his mother's nationality. He left Thailand as an infant with no birth record. Anyone who has tried to obtain documents from a country they cannot remember, with nothing to prove they were born there, knows what that answer is worth.
We fought hard to protect foundlings and the overseas-born children of Malaysian mothers. The children of unmarried Malaysian fathers are still waiting. Four things would change that:
Amend Section 17. A Malaysian parent, mother or father, married or not, should be able to pass on citizenship where parentage is proven, including by DNA.

Use Article 15A properly. The home ministry should publish clear criteria and timelines for registering children like this one, treat a chemistry department DNA report as sufficient proof, and give written reasons for every refusal.
Stop pursuing costs against stateless applicants. A young man with no nationality should never be billed RM4,000 for asking the court who he is.
Make late birth registration reachable. Border births, unregistered marriages and families afraid of the system need a simple, safe route to register, years later if necessary.
A father stood up in court and did the honourable thing by saying: this is my son, and here is the proof. Most of us would call that responsibility. Our law called it irrelevant.
Until Parliament fixes Section 17, I hope the home minister asks for this file and grants this young man what the court could not. He has waited 20 years already.
Hartini Zainudin is co-founder of Yayasan Chow Kit, founder of Kasih Madhya, and co-founder of Voice of the Children.

aa77b635d887aeb9: A sweeping bit of legislation designed to cut red tape could speed up the buildout of energy infrastructure in the US.

With the dust barely settled on this week’s momentous midterms, the Senate is set to vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) on November 9. It’s a plan that could finally start an overhaul of the slow, complicated process for getting energy projects approved, as part of something called permitting reform. People on both sides of the political aisle have been pushing for this type of change for some years.
The key question is whether this will cut greenhouse-gas emissions from the US energy sector or push them higher still.

The federal permitting system is designed to protect the environment against industrial pollution from large projects like power plants, transmission lines, and natural-gas pipelines. Today, permitting is governed by a range of laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act and the Clean Water Act. And if there’s one thing you might know about the current state of permitting in the US it’s that it’s slow and incredibly complicated.

So in its 417 pages, BAAJA attempts to tighten things up. The bill has provisions that narrow the sorts of projects that need to apply for federal permits and others that enact deadlines in hopes of speeding up a process that today can take years. (There are also specific provisions about transmission planning, mining, and the rest of the kitchen sink; this thing is dense.)

One thing to know about this bill is that it’s largely technology neutral: It opens the doors for the buildout of projects involving both fossil fuels and renewables. So there’s a weird mishmash of legislators and outside groups supporting it.

The bill’s four sponsors in the Senate are two Republicans and two Democrats. The White House has backed this permitting reform bill, with its Council of Economic Advisors finding that it would reduce review times and have economic benefits like boosting GDP.

Clean energy groups like the American Clean Power Association have largely come out in favor of the bill too, with the group’s analysis finding that it could unlock 350 gigawatts of new clean energy for the grid.

Some environmental groups, however, oppose the bill, or parts of it. An assessment from the Natural Resources Defense Council says the parts about transmission could have substantial benefits for the grid, but the narrowing of environmental reviews could be damaging for public and private lands.

Many in the climate world have long been calling for permitting reform, arguing that renewables stand to benefit more than fossil fuels. The thinking is that solar and wind power are some of the cheapest sources available today, so if we unlock the ability to build more energy, they are likely to win out economically.

A few early analyses have tried to quantify just what BAAJA would mean for emissions in the US. One, from the think tank Rhodium Group, found that in the best-case scenario, the bill would cut economy-wide emissions by 4%, reduce annual energy bills by $78 per household, and add 200 gigawatts of new clean energy by 2040. In the worst case, emissions would stay about the same.

Another report, from the nonprofit research group Resources for the Future, found that the bill could cut power-sector emissions 6% by 2041 and save more than $350 billion on system costs by midcentury.

But there are some concerns that this permitting bill’s real effect would be to open the floodgates for new natural-gas plants. As data centers have put more pressure on the grid, a wave of such plants have been announced.

“You get down to a trade-off between essentially growing the clean electricity industry on the one hand and then, as a compromise, growing the fossil-fuel industry on the other,” says Kevin Kircher, an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue.

To quantify that trade-off, Kircher also modeled the potential emissions effects of the bill and found that if BAAJA had been in place in 2025, energy sector emissions would have been higher than the actual baseline. Health and mortality risks associated with air pollution would also have increased.

This bill is scheduled for a Senate vote on November 9, well before the next Congress takes control. It’s not clear what the dramatic victories for Democrats might mean for the legislation, which was expected to pass the Senate with largely Republican support if a few Democrats got on board. Democrats could decide to wait for next year, when they’ll have control of both chambers. But any deal would ultimately need to win Trump’s signature, limiting what a future bill might be able to change.

In a world where permitting new projects is easier, we’ll see more clean energy, but we’ll see more natural gas, too. And while prices could get lower, that could push demand for electricity higher, leading to more emissions overall.
Simplifying the permitting system and cutting red tape is a worthy goal. But when it comes to emissions, it still really matters what, exactly, you want to build.
cf403874a276142d: Chinese women are challenging marriage pressures and redefining what it means to be single.
The marriage market at People’s Park in Shanghai, 2013. Photo by Jpbowen via Wikimedia Commons, licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0.

On weekends at Shanghai’s People’s Park, umbrellas covered with handwritten sheets of paper line the paths. Parents stand beside them, exchanging information about their unmarried children: age, height, education, income, and whether they own an apartment. It is one of China’s most famous marriage markets — a place where private hopes and social expectations meet in public since 2005.
For years, the word shengnü (剩女), literally translated as “leftover women,” hovered over many of the women whose profiles appeared there.

The translation sounds strange in English because the original Chinese carries a sharper meaning. The character sheng (剩) does not simply mean “remaining.” It suggests something left behind, something unused. In everyday contexts, it can describe leftover food — something that has passed its ideal moment and may eventually be discarded.

When the term became popular in China in the late 2000s, it was used to describe unmarried urban women, often highly educated professionals, who were considered “too old” for marriage after their late twenties. The label was not just a description of marital status. It turned a personal choice into a social judgment.

But today, if you search Chinese media, the phrase shengnü appears far less frequently than it once did. Instead, a more neutral term, zhonggnü (中女), literally translated as “middle or in-and-between women,” is now more often used to describe unmarried women in their thirties in both mainstream media and social platforms.

While the word has faded, many of the expectations behind it remain. The language around unmarried women has become more circumspect, though still pointed. Instead of openly calling women “leftover,” conversations often appear in softer forms: concerns about women being “too picky,” warnings about missing the “best age” for marriage and childbirth, or questions about why a successful woman still has not found a partner.

Instead of using the neutral term zhonggnü, which still highlights women’s age, some women have created new terms and spaces on social media platforms, such as Xiaohongshu and Douban, to discuss these pressures on their own terms. For example, they have reframed the marriage debate to cuīhūn (催婚) — the repeated pressure from family members to marry — and kǒnghūn (恐婚) — the fear or hesitation surrounding marriage itself.
These words reveal a shift. The conversation is no longer only about why women are failing to meet expectations. Increasingly, women are asking whether those expectations should be followed at all.

On Xiaohongshu, a user writing under the name “十元尼美” (Ten Yuan Nimei) described seven years of pressure to marry, beginning when she graduated from university. By 30, she wrote, the pressure had eased — not because her family had accepted her choices, but because people arranging introductions considered her too old for the matchmaking market. At 34, she said, her parents had almost stopped asking.

Her advice to other women began with creating physical distance. Moving from her home province of Hunan to Beijing had largely confined her parents’ pressure to phone calls; later, she moved to Spain. “Sometimes, freedom comes not from persuasion, but from distance,” she wrote.

Other posts question the pressure itself. One shared by the account “渭北春天树” carried the title —“Pressuring someone to marry is, at its core, a form of expulsion.” (催婚的本质是一种驱逐) These conversations no longer see shengnü or unmarried women as a problem, but are turning the conversation on its head to scrutinize traditional conservative family values.

Some women have even embraced and reclaimed the characterization of shengnü as a form of empowerment. Online, some social media posts explicitly recast the label through a play on Chinese characters: 剩, meaning “leftover,” becomes 胜, meaning “victorious,” with the same pronunciation, shèng. A Xiaohongshu post shared by an account named “Kevin” declares: “I’m not a ‘leftover woman’; I’m a ‘victorious woman.’” It advocates remaining single rather than settling, pursuing personal growth, and enjoying time alone.

In another post, the creator “小李存钱记” addresses her mother’s worries about her being unmarried at 30. “I’m not a leftover woman! I’m a victorious woman!” reads the text across the image. She describes juggling several jobs and building an online following, presenting her work and earnings as evidence of her worth. The reframing rejects marriage as the measure of success, while placing considerable emphasis on professional achievement and financial independence.

These posts do not erase the social stigma of the term shengnü. Rather, they show how users are challenging the label by questioning family pressure, sharing ways to escape it, or replacing “leftover” with “victorious.” Yet the language of victory raises another question. If an unmarried woman must point to her earnings, career, or independence to defend her choices, how much room is there simply to be single?
16de4ca3c25d3eed: In an emergency, a human might someday ask a robotic assistant to fetch a wall-mounted defibrillator located down the hall. But if the robot has incorrectly labeled the defibrillator as a fire extinguisher in its stored memory, it may not know where to find the life-saving device. This robotic assistant could benefit from a new memory system created by MIT researchers. The system identifies entries in a robot’s memory that might be wrong and corrects the descriptions of mislabeled objects.  In the future, this method could make household or industrial robots better able to perform complex, multistep tasks, such as clearing a dining room table or working alongside human collaborators to assemble a piece of machinery.  Called UQ-DAAAM (which stands for Uncertainty Quantification for Describe Anything, Anywhere, at Any Moment), the system compares multiple descriptions of the same object, seen from different viewpoints, to quantify the robot’s uncertainty about what it saw.  It then selects additional views to reduce the uncertainty and combines these captions into a more accurate description of the object, which it saves to memory. The researchers also employed a special technique to streamline this process so a mobile robot can continually update uncertain memory entries in real time.  When compared to baseline methods, UQ-DAAAM boosted the robot’s confidence and improved the accuracy of its answers to questions about objects, their locations, and when it saw them.  “Contrary to ChatGPT, when we think about physical AI, it is not enough to simply put a disclaimer cautioning that sometimes the robot might be wrong. Allowing a robot to know what it doesn’t know is going to be essential for this technology to be deployed safely and have a positive impact on society,” says Luca Carlone, an associate professor in MIT’s Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics (AeroAstro), principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS), director of the MIT SPARK Laboratory, and the senior author of the paper presenting UQ-DAAAM. He is joined on the paper by co-lead authors and MIT graduate students Harry Zhang and Nicolas Gorlo. The research will be presented at the Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems.  Amending memory This new method builds on the researchers’ prior work, DAAAM, a robot memory system that uses a vision-language model (VLM) to richly describe objects in scenes a robot captures with its onboard cameras. These descriptions are stored as detailed captions in a 3D map-based representation of the robot’s environment that it can call upon later to answer questions.  But the robot sometimes sees objects only partially or from far away, or its camera might capture blurry or poorly lit images. In these cases, DAAAM might describe these objects incorrectly, such as by mistaking a gray chimney for a squirrel perched on a rooftop. “With no way to correct itself, this wrong memory would persist as the robot proceeds in its environment, which could impact downstream applications,” Zhang says. UQ-DAAAM integrates uncertainty quantification into the DAAAM framework. It allows the robot to measure its confidence in the accuracy of object descriptions and fix incorrect captions as it travels through an environment. While on the move, the robot constantly collects and stores images of the world around it. Many of these images show the same objects captured from different angles. UQ-DAAAM uses these additional viewpoints to identify and correct unreliable descriptions. First, it calculates the VLM’s confidence level in the words it generated to describe a potentially mislabeled object. Then, it measures consistency by comparing this description to captions of images that describe the same object from different vantage points. “We fuse both sources of uncertainty into a single number that captures how certain the VLM is in its overall understanding of the object,” Carlone explains. If that number exceeds a certain threshold, the uncertainty is too high, and UQ-DAAAM will refine the caption by using additional images of the object. It does this using a heuristic, or simple rule, that determines which additional viewpoints will reduce the robot’s uncertainty about the object. For instance, it might choose an image captured a few frames later that clearly shows smoke emanating from the chimney.  The researchers mathematically proved that this heuristic can identify the best frames to select without rerunning the VLM, dramatically reducing the amount of computation.  “The key challenge Nico and Harry had to overcome is how to combine VLMs with uncertainty quantification into something that is running in a fraction of a second on a robot that is moving,” Carlone says. Remembering with confidence Once it has identified additional captions that will reduce its uncertainty about the object, the system uses an LLM to fuse them into a single object description. To boost accuracy, the LLM puts more weight on new captions and those with less ambiguity. This refinement step is able to resolve ambiguities for about 92 percent of the objects in the robot’s environment, while only requiring two additional captions per object. It increased the accuracy of object descriptions by 5 percent compared to the state of the art. UQ-DAAAM also provided more accurate answers to questions about the objects it observed, where it saw them, and when it last encountered them than baseline methods. “Performing this uncertainty quantification procedure across the entire map the robot generates allows it to improve its understanding of what it has observed,” Gorlo says. Next, the researchers want to use UQ-DAAAM to guide different types of robots, like mobile robotic manipulators, and apply their uncertainty quantification techniques to other domains.  In addition, they are studying the use of UQ-DAAAM to identify areas of high uncertainty the robot could revisit to improve its understanding of the environment. They are also exploring uncertainty quantification in systems that predict the future state of a robot’s environment. This research is supported, in part, by the U.S. Army Research Laboratory and the U.S. Office of Naval Research. Carlone is currently on sabbatical as an Amazon Scholar; this article describes work performed at MIT and is not associated with Amazon.
2e0612d18143103c: Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.
Synthient’s depiction of the outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.
Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.

“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”

All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.
1c5f8252381c9e95: Menurut ahli falsafah dan sejarawan Perancis yang terkenal, Pierre Nora; terdapat satu hubungan erat antara sejarah dan memori. Akan tetapi Nora menegaskan, dalam banyak keadaan memori adalah lebih utama dan dalam banyak keadaan mengatasi sejarah. Ini kerana memori adalah pencarian kebenaran yang objektif a search for objective truth atau satu himpunan bagaimana ia pernah terjadi, a recollection of how it really was.

Sedangkan sejarah tidak sebebas memori, dan kadangkala perlu dikendala. Ini kerana sejarah selalunya mempunyai aspek ideologi dan boleh dimanipulasi, ideological and manipulative. Idea dan gagasan Nora mengenai pertentangan memori melawan sejarah ini boleh ditemukan dalam banyak karya-karya beliau, antara lain The Present. Nation. Memory; Between Memory and History. Problems of Memory Places; World Celebration of Memory; History as Protection from Politics; dan dalam kerja beliau yang paling masyhur, Places of Memory.

Mengapakah Nora lebih berpihak kepada memori berbanding sejarah, sedang beliau adalah seorang sejarawan? Menurut Nora, beliau pertamanya ingin meluruskan semula sejarah dengan membersihkannya dari fakta tertentu.

Fakta-fakta sejarah ini pada Nora telah dimanipulasi oleh agenda politik dan hanya memori secara kolektif yang dapat membetulkan keadaan ini. Nora dalam kerja-kerja akademiknya menyorot bagaimana gerakan politik, pengukuhan identiti kebangsaan Perancis, dan agenda kelompok tertentu boleh mencemarkan sejarah. Tugas sejarawan sebenarnya adalah memelihara atau melindungi memori ini.

Atas alasan inilah Nora melancarkan gagasan beliau yang dikenali sebagai Places of Memory. Bagaimanapun cabaran untuk meluruskan sejarah dengan mencari memori yang benar ini bukanlah mudah, memandangkan memori itu sendiri terputus, tambahan pula tradisi sendiri akan hancur atau ditinggalkan, dan inovasi mengambil tempat sehingga memori kolektif itu sendiri ikut terjejas. Nora menyatakan, memori yang benar hanya datang dari ruang-tempat memori berjejak memory places atau mnemonic places, yang hadir membentuk ruang memori.

Nora menafsirkan konsep places of memory (lieu de memoire) ini sebagai satu fenomena yang signifikan, terzahir ketara atau tidak ketara, yang mana kerana kenekadan masyarakat atau pengaruh zaman telah membentuk sebagai satu lambang warisan untuk bangsa;

Memori kolektif terbentuk oleh kerana memori berjejak ini yang termanifestasi secara benda, fungsi dan lambang. Memori berjejak dalam bentuk benda misalnya adalah monumen, tugu, memorial, perkabungan, penyanjungan, wajah pada stem atau duit kertas, acara yang bersempenakan memori ini, nama jalan; dan lain-lain. Memori yang terputus memerlukan memori berjejak ini supaya dapat diingat kembali dan sekaligus dimurnikan semula sejarahnya. Sesuatu hanya ‘menjadi sejarah setelah memori berakhir, selagi memori dipugar secara kolektif maka sesuatu itu belum menjadi sejarah meskipun sudah berlaku pada masa lampau’; dalam erti kata lain ‘sejarah akan terus hidup jika terus dikenang’.

Harus diingat, memori berjejak Nora selalu dikelirukan oleh ramai sebagai satu tempat, ini kerana terjemahan suntuk place of memory itu dikait dengan physical place, padahal ia telah kehilangan tempat dan lebih kepada simbol atau tanda, kesan, atau jejak.

Saya selalu mengangankan, atau mencita-citakan agar nama Wan Azizah Wan Ismail terlekat dalam memori Malaysia, di saat beliau masih bernafas dan masih hidup. Beliau memiliki tempat dalam memori negara. Saya khuatir meletakkannya dalam sejarah. Ini kerana seperti mana dilihat oleh Nora, sejarah boleh mengalami pemesongan. Buku sejarah boleh diubah oleh pihak yang menang. Sejarah boleh dipadam. Tetapi memori misalnya tidak boleh dipadam. Yazid bin Muawiyah sebagai contoh cuba memadam sejarah mengenai cucu Rasulullah. Dia gagal. Ini kerana Zaynab al Kubra, puteri Fatimah dan Saidina Ali menghidupkan memori abangnya itu dengan segar dan harum. Ia menjadikan kesyahidan itu sentiasa hidup.

Sejarah telah membuktikan bahawa wanita di alam Melayu bukanlah kelompok yang pasif atau hanya berdiri di belakang kejayaan seseorang pimpinan masyarakat. Antara fakta dari lipatan sejarah alam Melayu, dapat dikenali sosok seorang Permaisuri bernama Pramodawardhana yang bertanggungjawab di belakang Kerajaan Majapahit dan Pembangunan Borobudur yang inklusif. Dari era kesultanan hingga ke zaman perjuangan kemerdekaan dan era pemodenan dan digital masa kini, wanita Melayu telah memainkan peranan yang amat signifikan sebagai pemimpin, diplomat, pendidik, usahawan, pemikir sosiobudaya, dan tiang seri utama dalam keharmonian nusa bangsa.

Di saat berlakunya krisis dalam masyarakat, wanita terbukti menjadi penyelamat. Seperti dilakukan oleh Tengku Ampuan Intan Tengku Alang Hussain yang menjadi Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan antara tahun 1869-1872 iaitu ketika berlakunya pertelingkahan untuk merebut kuasa. Watak sedemikian muncul lagi di zaman kita, dengan nama Wan Azizah Wan Ismail.

Selaku timbalan perdana menteri (2018-2020) dan pemimpin di Kementerian Pembangunan Wanita, Keluarga dan Masyarakat (KPWKM), Wan Azizah ketika itu telah melancarkan Pelan Tindakan Kebangsaan Menangani Punca Perkahwinan Bawah Umur (2020-2025). Pelan ini merangkumi strategi menyeluruh berasaskan lima punca utama yang digariskan menerusi kajian mendalam, iaitu kemiskinan sosioekonomi, kekurangan akses kepada pendidikan, kepincangan maklumat kesihatan reproduktif, kelonggaran undang-undang, serta persepsi dan stigma masyarakat. Saya membayangkan bagaimana kiranya memori Wan Azizah ini disuburkan terus. Dan memori itu diberi nyawa apabila lima punca di atas terus dikaji dan diberi solusi oleh sebuah universiti. Kita ahli akademik mengkaji dan memberi solusi, atas nama Wan Azizah. Berbahagi pahala.

Satu lagi tonggak utama dalam perjuangan pemerkasaan wanita yang sentiasa Wan Azizah tekankan ialah pengiktirafan terhadap golongan suri rumah yang memerlukan perlindungan keselamatan sosial yang sewajarnya. Di tangan beliau lahir program i-Suri dan i-Sayang yang hari ini mesti diteruskan sebagai usaha menangani jurang perlindungan sosial. Kerajaan ketika itu melancarkan Skim i-Suri di bawah Caruman Sukarela Insentif Suri bagi memastikan suri rumah berdaftar dalam sistem eKasih mendapat tabungan hari tua di Kumpulan Wang Simpanan Pekerja (KWSP) dengan bantuan insentif kerajaan.

Memori atau legasi kerja bekas timbalan perdana menteri ini mesti dibaja. Ia mesti diberi, bak kata Pierre Nora, sebuah tanah pamah, sebuah watan dan tekad yang dapat menampang places of memory (lieu de memoire) tersebut. Kalau ada rezeki harapnya memori Wan Azizah ini akan dapat ditegakkan di kala beliau masih hidup, dan di kala saya masih berkhidmat sebagai ahli akademik.

36d4af5b6e476e47: From Clement Stanley
Malaysian Indian People’s Party, a Perikatan Nasional component, decided to skip the Melaka state election as a matter of principle, or so they say.
MIPP president P Punithan said the party would not compromise its principles simply to secure seats in the Nov 14 polls.

MIPP’s struggle, he declares, is to defend the interests of the Indian community with dignity and principles, and “that the community’s voice and interests deserve proper recognition and representation in the political landscape”.
In short, MIPP likely does not want to be seen as token for the opposition coalition’s supposed inclusiveness.
Which, in essence is fine. After all, how can a party market itself as an outfit that champions the Indian cause when it finds itself marginalised?
It is just horrible branding — apart from the fact they lost their deposits in the Johor election — which could be a factor as to why seat negotiations failed.
Yet, MIPP’s dilemma is also, to a certain extent, MIC’s.
What role does MIC play in the bigger scheme of things with respect to its affiliation with Barisan Nasional?
Would MIC be willing to accept the fact that it is by and large irrelevant and a “diversity hire” of sorts?
Are they content being pliant to Umno, BN’s lynchpin, since such an arrangement may guarantee a government post?
Or will they only display bravado, via empty threats to quit BN, before the party’s AGM?
To MIPP’s credit, they were brave to acknowledge where they stand in PN. It is now time for the MIC to do the same.
Pliancy and bravado, however, also bring us to MCA.
Mocked as being Umno’s lapdog for the longest time, MCA leaders walked out of BN’s candidate announcement over seat allocations, also over principles.

The party, its president Wee Ka Siong said, cannot be pushed around and deserves to be treated with dignity. Wee also later called out BN chairman Ahmad Zahid Hamidi on his claim that talks held after the walkout were “positive”.
Whether one believes it was just “wayang kulit”, the bravado eventually secured three seats for MCA to contest at the Melaka election.
But can MCA consider this a win?
The optics will definitely boost its morale.
Perhaps this will give MCA something to build on. Perhaps they believe that by riding on the tailcoats of a BN-PN pact they will win over more Chinese support for the party.
But truth be told, their victory would be somewhat hollow if they won based on the support of the non-Chinese voters.
Be that as it may, MCA must surely know they are no force to be reckoned with amongst the Chinese electorate.
But, if survival is the name of the game, then by all means be indebted to the Malay support for putting them back in a position of power in Johor, Negeri Sembilan and now very likely, in Melaka.
MCA now need only ask themselves, “How high?” when told to jump by the likes of Umno and PAS.
Clement Stanley is an FMT reader.
