a40b144ab5da56eb: From a layperson’s perspective, following the legal back-and-forth in the Malaysian courts can be rather taxing.
It often appears to be a war of words, legal arguments, constitutional interpretations and courtroom strategies, all aimed at persuading the presiding judge or judges.

Beneath the pomp and pageantry inherited from the British legal system, however, lie issues of profound constitutional significance that may or may not affect our lives today, but could have far-reaching consequences for generations to come.

When Malaysia was formed in 1963, several safeguards were negotiated to protect the interests and autonomy of North Borneo (now Sabah). Among these was Point 11 of the Inter-Governmental Committee (IGC) Report, under the heading tariffs and finance.
It provided that “North Borneo should retain control over its own finances, development and tariffs, with the right to formulate its own taxation policies and raise loans on its own credit”.

One can argue that the spirit and substance of this safeguard are found in the constitutional expression of Article 112C of the Federal Constitution, read together with Section 2(1) of Part IV of the Tenth Schedule and Clauses (1), (3) and (4) of Article 112D.

These provisions form the constitutional basis for Sabah's entitlement to a special grant equivalent to two-fifths (40%) of the net revenue derived by the federal government from Sabah, subject to the relevant constitutional provisions.

Former Sabah minister Yap Pak Leong revived the historical significance of this arrangement, maintaining that the 40% revenue-sharing arrangement was a fundamental condition underpinning Sabah's decision to join in the formation of Malaysia.
"Right from the start, I emphasised this share of 2/5 revenue to be a condition for Sabah to become part of Malaysia.”
He further stressed that without this safeguard being enshrined in the Federal Constitution, Sabah would not have agreed to participate in the formation of Malaysia.

The role Sabah and Sarawak played in forming Malaysia must be recognised, unlike the federated states of Malaya. The Borneo states negotiated separate terms under the IGC, one of which is Sabah’s entitlement to 40% revenue sharing of all taxes collected in Sabah.

From what I understand, the federal government is not objecting to Sabah’s right to the 40% revenue sharing, but to the High Court judgment on Oct 17, 2025, in favour of the Sabah Law Society (SLS), directing the federal and state government to commence a review within a stipulated period.

Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim himself promised during the last state election that the government would not appeal the High Court’s decision, but for whatever reasons, it seems he has reneged on that promise to the Sabah people.
On another point, one cannot help but question the position taken by the state government in these proceedings.
Having entered the case as an intervener at a relatively late stage, the state government appears caught between competing legal and political considerations.
Yet, arguably, it should have been at the forefront pursuing Sabah's constitutional entitlement.
The state government possesses the political mandate, institutional authority and constitutional standing to negotiate directly with the federal government.

Rather than allowing the matter to become an extended courtroom battle initiated by SLS on behalf of the people of Sabah, it should be exercising that authority to secure a meaningful and just resolution for Sabah's 47 "lost years".

In another case, another NGO, Sabah Action Body Advocating Rights (Sabar) has taken the federal government to court on February 27, 2025, disputing the validity of the Territorial Sea Act (TSA) 2012, which limits the State's maritime boundary to just three nautical miles.

While the Sabah state government may have its own reasons for not initiating legal challenges regarding Sabah's rights, and Sabahans are not privy to their arguments, it is only fair to ask where the Sabah government stands in relation to these key court challenges.
The position is unlike in Sarawak, where the state government has led similar challenges.

Importantly, after more than six decades since Sabah agreed to become a part of Malaysia, one uncomfortable reality remains: according to official statistics, Sabah continues to record the highest poverty incidence in the country.
That is a sobering indictment of the development gap that persists despite Sabah's immense natural resources and its contributions to the Malaysian federation.
The legal arguments may continue. Appeals may be filed, constitutional provisions may be debated, and lawyers may argue over jurisdiction, procedures and remedies.
But beyond the courtroom, ordinary Sabahans continue to face the realities of poverty, inadequate infrastructure, water and electricity shortages, and limited economic opportunities.

The fundamental question is this: after more than 60 years in the Malaysian federation, should Sabahans still have to fight in court for constitutional assurances that were meant to protect their interests from the very beginning?

The 40% entitlement should not be treated as a political bargaining chip, nor should its fulfilment be reduced to a battle of legal technicalities. It is a constitutional matter rooted in the historical terms and safeguards surrounding the formation of Malaysia.
It is about justice, constitutional accountability and the future of Sabah.
The people of Sabah have waited long enough. Following Lord Hewart CJ’s well-known dictum, “justice must be seen to be done”.

c6b1da594a8a831d: Over 60% of Floridian voters voted to cut property taxes, which has been surging in recent years. AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell)Many Florida homeowners cheered on Nov. 3, 2026, when more than 60% of voters approved a constitutional amendment to significantly reduce property taxes. Under the measure, Amendment 3, a homeowner’s tax break known as a homestead exemption would go from the current US$51,400 to $150,000 in 2027 and increase again to $250,000 in 2028. By shielding more of a home’s assessed value from taxation, this exemption effectively lowers homeowners’ tax bills. New Florida residents who buy a home would also reportedly be eligible for a property tax break, but on a more phased-in basis. But the measure comes with a hefty price tag. The Florida Legislature’s research arm estimated the measure would reduce annual revenue from property taxes by $11.8 billion. This translates to a 30% reduction in revenue for Florida counties and a 13% cut for smaller municipal governments. While homeowners will get some relief, the budget crunch due to the lower tax revenue will affect other Floridians in more adverse ways. As economists who have been following the debates over Amendment 3, we argue that local governments will struggle to fund basic services with less money. And we expect more sweeping economic consequences as well – including less affordable residential housing and a broader shift of the tax burden away from relatively wealthier homeowners to those who are less well off. How Amendment 3 would work Much of the political momentum for Amendment 3 came from a rise in the cost of living and frustration over rising property taxes. These now average just over $3,000 annually but can run much higher for Floridians with more expensive homes. In addition to raising the homestead tax exemption, Amendment 3 lowers the cap on annual assessments on rental and commercial properties from a 10% increase to a 5% increase. Since property taxes are based on an asset’s assessed value, this language effectively limits but doesn’t rule out tax hikes for businesses. So landlords, for example, could still see meaningful annual tax increases as their properties go up in value – costs that would likely be passed on to renters. Amendment 3 makes clear that school-related property taxes are exempt from these tax cuts. It also lists some theoretical limits on how local governments should use tax dollars, as a way to ensure continued funding for essential services such as public safety, infrastructure or obligations for employee retirement benefits. But it also states that funds may be used for “expenditures approved” by local and county governments – ambiguous wording that suggests these stipulations can be breached. Who pays the bill? Florida property taxes are levied and collected by some 640 local government entities. There’s no state income tax, so any reductions in property tax revenue directly affect local and county governments. With tax revenue slashed, businesses, landlords and owners of other non-homestead properties like second homes would almost certainly see their taxes go up. This is a typical pattern: When governments cut property taxes for some groups, taxes shift to other groups. Essential public services, including fire and police departments, could face sharp budget cuts due to the shortfall from lower property taxes. Orange County Fire Rescue Department via AP This dynamic is likely to play out with local governments as they try to keep revenue stable: Amendment 3 would force them to hike taxes in other areas to make up for the shortfall. This could include increases in state and local sales taxes, an expansion of the list of goods subject to sales taxes, or a hike in “documentary stamp taxes,” which are required on documents such as deeds, bonds and mortgages. State and local governments could also impose higher fees for specific services, such as solid waste treatment and stormwater utilities. Another option is to hike permits and inspection fees, fuel taxes or other service charges such as vehicle registration fees. Finally, local governments could raise tourism-related taxes, such as on food, beverages and hotels. But this recourse wouldn’t help counties with limited tourism, and such revenues fluctuate in any event. In the end, though, essential services would still almost certainly be affected. Funding for police, fire and emergency medical services is primarily the responsibility of local governments, and, for most counties, they make up the largest line item in their annual expenditures. Reducing property taxes would amount to a direct hit, especially in smaller, less-populated counties. And if local governments do raise sales tax rates to the extent they can, lower-income Floridians will bear a disproportionate burden as they spend much more of their income on consumption. They’re also far more likely to rent than own a home, so any increased rents would take a bigger toll. A looming affordable housing crunch? Less noticed in the debate over Amendment 3 was how it would affect the state’s affordable housing shortage. We argue that the structure of the property tax cut will likely create more incentives for counties and developers to build commercial structures instead of more residential housing. When developers build residential homes, they require a basic level of public services to support residents and the local infrastructure. In fact, property taxes in much of Florida effectively subsidize residential home development: For every dollar that a homeowner pays in property taxes, it costs county governments around $1.20 to provide those services. This gap will only grow when property tax revenues fall. From the standpoint of local and county governments, then, it may make more sense to focus on commercial or industrial construction as a way to keep tax revenues stable. But with fewer homes built at the expense of business construction – from manufacturing to data centers – the supply squeeze will only drive up prices and rents for the workers who are needed for those jobs. Now that Amendment 3 is on the books, Florida’s county and local governments will confront major trade-offs. We believe that state officials will come to realize how much of a change has been made – and how quickly their priorities may have to shift. This article has been corrected to note that the current homestead exemption is $51,400 and that new Florida residents who buy a home are eligible for a property tax break on a phased-in basis. eeff4737bf340d02: Voters respond to economic and political messages and experiences. AP Photo/Lindsey WassonAs Democrats and Republicans look at the overwhelming results of the 2026 midterm election, it’s worth remembering what has become a political axiom in America: “It’s the economy, stupid.” Democratic strategist James Carville famously said that to presidential candidate Bill Clinton in 1992, but he might have said “it’s energy prices” instead. The cost of energy underlies much of the economy, making energy and politics inseparable, especially when gasoline prices rise. Midterm elections have historically been difficult for incumbent presidents and often shift the balance of power in Washington, D.C. Many factors affecting gasoline prices are beyond a president’s or Congress’s control. Prices for crude oil and petroleum products such as gasoline are set on global markets as the results of economic forces of supply and demand. Even the companies that produce oil don’t have as much influence as people might think, because of how that oil gets to refineries: Over 60% of the world’s crude oil is transported by ocean tankers, with 20% of global supplies traveling through the Strait of Hormuz, which has been closed, or nearly so, for much of 2026 as the conflict with Iran drags on. When energy prices rise, other prices, such as food, follow. Sudden spikes in gasoline prices can contribute to higher inflation, both regionally and nationally. Voters pay attention to those changes, and incumbents are less likely to win reelection. For the 2026 midterm election, gasoline prices were the highest of any previous election. That put Republicans in the precarious position of defending their record. Four American presidents – Gerald Ford, Jimmy Carter, Ronald Reagan and Joe Biden – confronted the consequences of severe inflation and high fuel prices during midterm elections. Oil embargo, Nixon and Ford Richard Nixon was the first modern president to truly face an energy crisis that became political. In retaliation for U.S. support for Israel during the October 1973 Yom Kippur War, Arab members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries cut oil production and imposed an oil embargo on the United States. OPEC oil production fell by 5% a month, and crude oil prices rocketed 184% from prewar levels of $4.31 to $10.31 per barrel in March 1974. Nixon’s federal price controls on petroleum didn’t prevent U.S. gasoline prices from increasing 32%. When Nixon resigned over the Watergate scandal in August 1974, Gerald Ford took office. Inflation was 12.3%, and gas prices were still high. Right before that year’s midterm election, Ford launched the “Whip Inflation Now,” or WIN, campaign. But Republicans lost 48 House seats and five Senate seats. “WIN” didn’t work, and by the 1976 presidential election, gas prices were over 60 cents a gallon – adjusted for inflation to late 2026, that’s $3.49. Ford lost his reelection bid to Jimmy Carter. Carter’s struggles In Carter’s first two years in office, starting in 1977, the monthly average price of unleaded gasoline in the U.S. stayed high and even climbed slightly. Inflation hit 9% in 1978. In the 1978 midterm election, Democrats lost 15 House and three Senate seats. Inflation continued to climb, and by the 1980 presidential election, gas prices were twice what they had been in 1976. Plagued by those figures and the Iranian hostage crisis, Carter lost the 1980 election to Ronald Reagan. Reagan enters the picture Reagan implemented “Reaganomics” by cutting taxes and regulations, reducing government spending, tightening monetary policy and removing the remaining price controls on petroleum. By the mid-1980s, increased oil production from U.S. and non-OPEC nations led to an oil glut, lowering the average price of crude oil and U.S. gasoline price from previous highs. In the 1982 midterms, Republicans lost 26 seats in the House and gained one in the Senate. Reagan won reelection to the presidency in a landslide in 1984, but the challenges for incumbents remained in the 1986 midterms. Though crude oil prices were $15 a barrel and gas had dropped to 82 cents a gallon, Republicans lost five seats in the House and eight in the Senate. Trump’s first round In the lead-up to the midterms during Donald Trump’s first term as president, crude prices had risen about 24% from when he took office in January 2017 to October 2018. And gas prices were up 22%. In the 2018 midterms, Republicans lost 41 House seats but gained two in the Senate. Democratic Party supporters react to the results of the 2018 midterm elections, when their party won control of the U.S. House of Representatives. Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images Biden years Over the course of 2020, COVID-19 restrictions slowed the U.S. economy. U.S. crude oil production fell as gasoline demand plummeted by 40%. Prices rose because of pandemic-related supply chain backups. And from Election Day in November 2020 to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the average price of unleaded gasoline in the U.S. rose by 66%, from $2.11 to $3.52 per gallon. Also, as pandemic restrictions lifted and the economy began recovering, demand for gasoline rebounded, straining supplies. Upon taking office in 2021, Biden took steps to curb rising energy costs, including releasing oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve in March 2022, which the Treasury Department suggested helped prevent gasoline price increases of $0.17 to $0.42 per gallon. But other Biden policy moves made it harder to increase energy supplies. He canceled the Keystone XL pipeline project that would have brought more petroleum into the U.S. and suspended new oil and gas leases in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge and the Gulf of Mexico. He also recommitted the U.S. to the Paris climate accord, under which countries have promised to cut their greenhouse gas emissions, generally meaning moving away from fossil fuels as an energy source. In June 2022, inflation reached 9.1%, a 40-year high. And U.S. gasoline prices reached an all-time high of $4.929 per gallon; adjusted for inflation, that’s $5.60 a gallon today. The 2022 midterm election wasn’t as bad for Democrats as they might have feared, though it wasn’t a success: The party lost nine House seats and one Senate seat. That’s a reminder that energy prices aren’t the only factor in voters’ minds when they are casting ballots. Trump’s second term During the first 12 months of Trump’s second term, crude oil prices fell 4.5%, U.S. oil production rose 3.3%, from 13.3 million to 13.7 million barrels per day, and the AAA national average price of regular unleaded gasoline fell 4.5%, from $3.12 to $2.98 per gallon. On Feb. 28, 2026, U.S. military action against Iran disrupted Middle Eastern oil production and oil tanker traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. Initially, shipment volume plummeted, though by the end of September it had recovered to 82% to 92% of prewar levels. Overall, Middle Eastern crude oil exports are averaging around 24 million barrels a day, exceeding prewar levels in part because of increased use of pipelines out of Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Because of the war with Iran, AAA’s national average price of unleaded regular gasoline has increased by almost 40%, from February’s $2.98 price to $4.15 a gallon as of Nov. 3, 2026. Implications As the preelection polling had suggested, voters held Trump accountable for high gasoline and grocery prices, as well as an unpopular war. It was a reminder of a basic economic and political principle: When the economy is doing well, voters are more likely to support incumbents and their parties. And when voters are pessimistic about the economy’s future, they are inclined to vote against incumbents and their parties. Michael A. 31bba1eca5b3b896: Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech’s largest AI buildouts. But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position.

Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat against Ken Paxton. Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor against the Republican incumbent, Greg Abbott. At the state level, Democrats will take control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. At the industry’s DCD conference in Ashburn, Virginia, on Tuesday, panelists lamented that Texas had been the easiest place to build for years—until September. That’s when Abbott, perhaps seeing the increasingly bipartisan distaste for these facilities, began changing course himself.

Developers said the governor’s office had stopped responding to their emails. On September 21, Abbott directed a key state regulator to halt data center permits. Many panelists at the conference were expecting this to mean that existing projects might be slowed and new ones could be halted altogether.

The governor-elect indeed seems eager to do that. Hinojosa supported tax breaks for data centers in 2023 as a way to boost construction jobs, but during her campaign she began pushing for a full-fledged moratorium.

That would be a problem for the hyperscalers of Big Tech, which have ambitious plans for AI training facilities in the state. The scale of projects already underway in Texas is massive. The Stargate Frontier data center in Shackelford County is projected to serve 1,820 megawatts—about as much as the nation’s largest data center, SpaceX’s Colossus 2 in Tennessee, and more than twice as much as the largest data center currently operating in Texas. Nexus Hubbard, also under construction and intended mostly to serve Anthropic, has a planned size of 6,400 megawatts and is the second-largest data center being built in the US, behind only Meta’s Hyperion project in Louisiana.

The potential for Democrats to order delays to these projects or moratoriums on new ones adds to growing anxiety that the AI buildout could stall. Banks and lenders are already getting pickier about the projects they back. And given the extent to which the data center buildout is underpinning growth in the economy right now, those forces combined could have ripple effects.

Voters around the country, though, were unambiguous in the midterms, sending a similar message on everything from state ballot questions to national offices. Voters supported efforts to protect ratepayers from increases in their electricity bills caused by data centers, and they favored some larger bans on new data centers altogether. If we needed any more convincing that Big Tech has fumbled its effort to sell voters on the idea that AI-powered abundance will make health care better, goods cheaper, and scientific breakthroughs more common, this was it.
A key question is whether the Texas counties with the largest data center presence were part of the reason these Democrats got elected, or if the anti-data-center vote came from elsewhere.

It’s complicated: The counties where much of the data center buildout is happening are around Dallas. Dallas County and others closest to it predictably went blue, but nearby Ellis County, which leads in permitting requests for data centers, went for Greg Abbott and Ken Paxton. Cameron County, near the state’s southern border, is a hot spot for data centers and voted blue in the midterms, which was a shift. But Mitchell County and Scurry County, where a bunch of projects in west Texas are located, went red.

This is a big deal, because no single office in the state decides whether a project goes ahead or is halted. Decisions often reflect an interplay between city governments, county officials, and state offices.

Local officials who have some say over data center development may resist sweeping restrictions from the state. And Democrats pushing for a moratorium might also face pushback from the construction unions that supported some of their campaigns. So while the blue wave spells a death knell for Texas data centers in theory, election winners may find that following through on their opposition once in office is much more complicated than campaigning on it.

74ed475c846c9cfc: I’ve been locked in to my various screens since results from midterm elections started to roll in last night. And it didn’t take long to see the beginning of the blue wave: Democrats took control of both the US House of Representatives and the Senate, a dramatic swing from Donald Trump’s victory two years ago.

While the results are striking, we probably won’t be seeing some of the big climate and energy policy shifts that have come in recent years as Congress and the presidency have changed hands. Instead, we’re entering a period of divided government, with a Congress that will likely do battle with Trump’s White House over the next two years. But even if the federal government isn’t likely to pass laws that overhaul energy and climate policy, the midterm results could be a big deal for energy, especially at the state and local level.

Let’s step back for just a moment to put these results in context. Readers might remember huge laws affecting climate and energy that were passed in just the last four years. The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act included massive support for clean energy, including tax credits and government grants and loans. Then the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act essentially slashed much of the support and financial incentives in the IRA from two years before.

What those two laws had in common was a period when the government was entirely united, with the Senate, House of Representatives, and presidency all controlled by the same party—the Democrats in the first case and the Republicans in the second.

Now Democrats have captured a majority in both the Senate and the House. But Donald Trump is still in the White House. And crucially, neither chamber is anywhere close to a two-thirds Democratic majority. That’s the ratio that would be needed to override a presidential veto.

So even if Congress puts together new legislation to boost climate measures and clean energy, Trump will need to sign it—and that dramatically narrows the scope of what might happen legislatively between now and the next election.

There could be some bipartisan compromises. One interesting bit of legislation to watch immediately after the election is what happens with permitting reform. In late September, a bipartisan group of senators put forward a bill that would overhaul how new energy projects are reviewed and approved in the US. The law aims to cut red tape and speed up the permitting process.

The Senate is set to vote on that package, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, on November 9, before the new Congress takes control in January. The White House has supported the bill, and it could pass the Senate if just a handful of Democrats join the Republican majority. But now, we might see Democrats wait until next year to try to renegotiate a deal, though anything would still need to pass muster with Trump.

With Democratic control of Congress, we’ll likely see much more scrutiny of Trump and agencies controlled by his appointees. Democratic leaders have already signaled plans to go after leaders like EPA commissioner Lee Zeldin over cuts to staff and investments. Democrats will have the power to subpoena cabinet members and open investigations.

Looking beyond the national results, a major trend to watch moving forward will be local action. Democrats swept local control of Pennsylvania, and officials there have signaled plans to support renewable energy and efforts to cut greenhouse-gas emissions. Democrats also took control of the Georgia Public Service Commission for the first time in 30 years. The group regulates electric utilities, essentially controlling much of the grid’s buildout.

Among the broadest effects of these election results, though, will be for the data center industry. According to tracking from Ballotpedia, there were 41 local ballot questions related to data centers. And overwhelmingly, voters chose to restrict their development. Nearly every single one of these measures looks set to come down against data center development, as of the morning of November 4.

And AI critics fared well in their races, too. Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the governor’s seat in Texas, ousting Republican incumbent Greg Abbott. During her campaign, Hinojosa called for a law to completely pause data center development; if passed, it could have major implications for both the state’s grid and the data center industry more broadly.

We might not see dramatic new climate- or energy-related federal legislation between now and the next major US election. But many voters signaled, and quite loudly, that they wanted a change. We’ll see how much will shift in the next two years, and where that leaves us.

0a73cffbe155abce: Repeated giving may give the impression that companies care more. useng/iStock via Getty Images PlusPeople tend to think more highly of companies that give to charity on a monthly or weekly basis rather than donating an annual lump sum worth the same amount. This is what I and five other marketing researchers found when we conducted seven studies involving more than 150,000 people. The Journal of Marketing Research, which is peer-reviewed, published our article on the results in early 2026. My co-author Alexander B. Park and I led the team. Our goal was to discover whether the way a company communicates with the public about its donations affects how much credit it gets from consumers for those gifts. Across seven studies, we found that companies earn more goodwill when they give consistently – say, US$20,000 a month – instead of making a single $240,000 gift. On average, consumers also said they were more likely to buy from those companies. To test this premise, we did two real-world studies. First, we partnered with GiftAMeal, a U.S. company that runs a free app for diners. Each time someone takes a photo of their meal at a participating restaurant and shares it on social media, GiftAMeal donates to a local food bank. We ran two versions of GiftAMeal’s Facebook ad, which together reached 67,576 people. One said the company “donated 25,000 meals every month” last year. The other said it “donated 300,000 meals” last year. Both were true, and everything else about the ads was the same. We found that people who saw the monthly version were about 21% more likely to click on the ad. Next, we worked with Salt + Smoke, a Midwestern barbecue restaurant. When we emailed 75,514 customers who subscribed to its newsletters, half read that the company would give $5,000 a month from September through December to a small, local charity that supports early childhood education programs. The other half read that it would make a one-time donation of $20,000. Subscribers who read about the monthly donation pledge were nearly twice as likely to click through to the restaurant’s website as those who read about the one-time gift pledge even though the total was the same. Then we ran online experiments with more than 7,400 people to learn why and when consistent giving makes people view a company more favorably. We found that, on average, when a company gives monthly, people see its charitable support as a more genuine commitment to the causes. Why it matters U.S. companies gave nearly $44 billion in 2025 alone. And this kind of giving is popular with the public. In a 2022 survey, 88% of Americans said it’s important for companies to make the world a better place. Companies frequently promote their donations with the largest numbers they can muster. For example, Microsoft announced that the software giant and its employees donated $256 million in 2025; Walmart and its foundation say they have donated $2 billion in 2026. Yet boasting about big numbers may not impress people as much as emphasizing the consistency of donations. This may help explain why companies often struggle to convey their charitable efforts in ways that win people over. Even if companies give only once a year, they can indicate that they are engaged in a steady pattern of giving. For example, they can make their annual gifts on Giving Tuesday every year. Donating on the same day or as part of the same fundraising campaign every year can signal an ongoing commitment, not a one-off. What still isn’t known We don’t yet know how long the reputational boost companies may get from recurring donations might last, or whether those donations can translate into long-term customer loyalty. It’s also possible that what we found would not apply during emergencies. For example, consumers might be happy to see a company make one big gift right after a hurricane when a local community’s needs are immense. What’s next Along with Park and Cynthia Cryder, a Washington University in St. Louis marketing professor, I’m now studying other ways that corporate philanthropy can affect how much credit companies get for doing good. So far, we’ve found that companies may earn less goodwill when they ask customers to chip in to their charitable campaigns. People seem to expect companies to carry more of the load themselves. The Research Brief is a short take about interesting academic work. MIT Technology Review Narrated: The agentic web is here

In 2001, a decade after inventing the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision: an internet navigated by autonomous software agents that address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves.

At the time, the idea seemed far-fetched. But a quarter-century on, AI agents are beginning to make it a reality. They can triage your inbox, do your grocery shopping, and even access your bank accounts.
This new era is being called the agentic web, and it will inevitably transform the internet. Whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess.

416b7eba9f32ddf4: A sales representative asks an AI agent for customer pricing, and the agent pulls data from multiple sources: restricted pricing systems, internal communications, and archived quotes. The output looks accurate to the agent, so a second agent uses the data to draft the proposal for the sales rep. No human checks either handoff. When it’s discovered that the proposal includes unapproved, confidential, and sensitive information, no one can trace where the problematic data entered the workflow or how it spread across systems, files, and agents.

This scenario illustrates why AI governance needs to evolve, rapidly and dynamically. As more enterprises begin to use agentic AI in daily workflows, they’re realizing that they must manage more than static files; they must manage moving and fragmented data that is continuously ingested, copied, summarized, transformed, reused, and redistributed in new forms. In short, AI security isn’t a tool problem; it’s a data visibility problem.

Consequently, traditional security approaches built solely around applications, systems, networks, or endpoints are no longer sufficient. Securing agentic AI at scale requires understanding how data moves. Teams, therefore, need to establish data lineage in order to effectively manage governance, accountability, and trust across human, agentic, and hybrid workflows.
